## Making an out-of-range index unrepresentable

### FD-26 no surveyed system refuses a bad index with a length index alone, and the four whose seam is closest to this tree put the length on the value and let a refinement name the preceding binder

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question: what does a language give up, and what must it add, so that a string or byte-buffer type carries its length in its type and an out-of-range index is a static type error? **Ten systems were read at their own sources, nineteen pins. The practice SPLITS into two families and the split is the answer.** **Family A puts the length in the type** (Idris 2, Agda, DML, ATS) and pays for it with a dependent pair at every boundary. **Family B puts the length on the value as a pure function and bounds the index with a refinement that names a preceding value binder** (F*, Low*, LiquidHaskell, Dafny), and refuses exactly the same bad call with no index at all. **This tree's measured blocker, `load: unknown name s` at `docs/arcs/parts/diagnostics-L5.md:261-268`, is the Family B capability.** The tree already has Family A machinery and already has refinements, and it has neither of them pointed at `Str`. **A length-indexed `Str` is one of two routes and the sources price it as the more expensive one.**
- measured: **1. THE TREE'S OWN MACHINERY, COUNTED AT HEAD `ec494bf` BY GREP OVER `lib/`, AND NOTHING IN THE TREE RECORDS THIS.** **Refinement seats: 5.** Two are function-argument seats, `lib/ports/sock.port:69` (`(refine I64 (> 0))` on `sock-recv`) and `lib/memory/mem-linear.chiral:27`. Three are `data` constructor fields, `lib/runtime/proc.chiral:28`, `:42`, `:43`. Two further `(refine ` hits in `lib/` are neither: a parser error string at `lib/surface/parse.chiral:392` and the erasure case at `lib/lowering/compile-front.chiral:69`. **Type-level index seats: 33**, every one of the shape `(-> (0 n I64) ...)`, in five files: `lib/ports/pool.port` 3, `lib/memory/mem-linear.chiral` 3, `lib/memory/mem-region.chiral` 6, `lib/protocol/grid.chiral` 6, `lib/protocol/vt-parser.chiral` 15. A 34th occurrence is prose inside a comment at `lib/module/loader.chiral:452`. **Every erased binder in `lib/` is `I64`-typed; there are zero of any other type.** **Every one of the 33 indexes a linear resource**, `(Pool n)`, `(Region n)` or `(Grid n)`, and is paired with a `(1 x (T n))` seat. **`Str` and `Bytes` are indexed nowhere:** `grep -rnE '\(Str [a-z]|\(Bytes [a-z]' lib/` returns nothing, and `lib/surface/syntax.chiral:29` declares both as `t-primty`, a bare primitive. **The two kinds of machinery meet in exactly one seat in the whole tree**, `lib/memory/mem-linear.chiral:27`. **The three probes in `diagnostics-L5.md` §2 all reproduce today against `bin/chirality`:** `(-> (0 n I64) (=> Str I64 (refine I64 (<= n)) Str))` checks at exit 0; applying it as `(sub-safe 3 "abc" 0 99)` fails `load: cannot prove refinement` at exit 1; and `(=> (s Str) I64 (refine I64 (<= (str-len s))) Str)` fails `load: unknown name s` at exit 1.

  **2. HOW THE INDEX IS SPELLED, AND THE TWO SPELLINGS ARE NOT EQUAL IN COST.** **`Fin n` is an inductive and its values are unary.** Agda declares AGDAFIN:34 "data Fin : ℕ → Set where" with the successor case AGDAFIN:36 "  suc  : (i : Fin n) → Fin (suc n)", so the index 1000 is 1000 constructors before any compiler optimisation, and the lookup takes it as its own type, AGDAVEC:59 "lookup : Vec A n → Fin n → A". Idris 2 spells the same pair, IDRISVECT:16 "data Vect : (len : Nat) -> (elem : Type) -> Type where" and IDRISVECT:144 "index : Fin len -> Vect len elem -> elem". **The systems that target machine code refuse `Fin` and use a singleton over a machine integer plus a constraint, and DML states the reason.** The purity requirement on index objects is what forces it: DMLPOPL99:223 "connection to run-time values by using" singleton types, DMLPOPL99:228 "which contains just the integer" n, and DML says this is what makes the application possible at all. Its array signature is DMLPOPL99:3615 "sub <| {n:nat} {i:nat | i < n}" over DMLPOPL99:3616 "'a array(n) * int(i) -> 'a", where DMLPOPL99:3597 "is a singleton type which contains only" that one integer. **ATS ships the same spelling over a C `char*` today.** Its indexed string type is ATSBASICS:525 "string_int_type(n: int) = string_type" where ATSBASICS:523 "string_type = ptr // = char* in C", and its indexing function is ATSSTRING:176 "  (s: string(n), i: size_t(i)):<> charNZ" under the static quantifier `{n:int}{i:nat | i < n}` at `ATSSTRING:175`. **ATS's substring is PRB-24's and PRB-47's function with the bad call unrepresentable:** ATSSTRING:339 "  (str: string(n), st: size_t st, ln: size_t ln):<!wrt> strnptr(ln)" under `{n:int}{st,ln:nat | st+ln <= n}` at `:338`. ATS indexes bytes the same way, ATSBASICS:613 "typedef bytes (n:int) = @[byte][n]". **The singleton spelling is this tree's `(0 n I64)` plus `(refine I64 ...)` with one piece missing: a machine integer whose type-level value is itself.** The tree can bound a seat by an index; it cannot yet say that a given `I64` value *is* the index.

  **3. THE FOUR SYSTEMS CLOSEST TO THIS TREE'S SEAM CARRY NO INDEX AT ALL, AND THEY REFUSE THE SAME CALL.** **F* makes length a function of the value and lets the refinement call it.** FSTARSEQ:26 "val length: #a:Type -> seq a -> Tot nat", then FSTARSEQ:32 "val index:  #a:Type -> s:seq a -> i:nat{i < length s} -> Tot a", and the slice is FSTARSEQ:64 "val slice:  #a:Type -> s:seq a -> i:nat -> j:nat{i <= j && j <= length s} -> Tot (seq a)". That last line is the signature `diagnostics-L5.md` §4 Shape B wanted and could not construct. **LiquidHaskell does it with a measure and names the capability.** LHTUTOR:106 "measure vlen :: Vector a -> Int" then LHTUTOR:112 "assume (!) :: x:Vector a -> {v:Nat | v < vlen x} -> a", and the tutorial calls the enabling feature Dependent Refinements, LHTUTOR:140 "signature for `length` names the input with the binder" and LHTUTOR:142 "the signature for `(!)` names the input vector `x` so that the index" can be constrained against it. **Dafny does it with a field.** DAFNYTYPES:2755 "The length of an array is retrieved using the immutable `Length`" and indexing is admitted DAFNYTYPES:2763 "For any integer-based numeric `i` in the range `0 <= i < a.Length`,". **In all four, the type of the carrier is unchanged and the bound is stated at the seat.** The single capability they share and this tree lacks is a refinement atom that can name a value binder introduced earlier in the same arrow.

  **4. WHERE THE LENGTH COMES FROM AT A BOUNDARY: THE PUBLISHED NAME IS THE EXISTENTIAL, AND FAMILY B HAS NO BOUNDARY PROBLEM.** Idris states the use directly: IDRISDPAIR:986 "One use for dependent pairs is to return values of dependent types" IDRISDPAIR:987 "where the index is not necessarily known in advance", and gives the other name at IDRISDPAIR:1016 "Dependent pairs are sometimes referred to as" Sigma types. DML calls it a weak dependent sum and says what it is for: DMLPOPL99:3121 "pressed using an existential dependent type, also called weak" DMLPOPL99:3122 "dependent sum. Also, existential types can mediate between" dependent and ordinary ML types, which is how a library function of unknown length is given a type at all. ATS spells the existential in the type itself, ATSBASICS:535 "typedef String = [n:int] string_int_type(n)" and ATSBASICS:536 "typedef String0 = [n:int | n >= 0] string_int_type(n)". Idris's conversion from an unindexed carrier is IDRISVECT:342 "fromList : (xs : List elem) -> Vect (length xs) elem", which computes the index from the value. **For Family B the question does not arise**: a string read from a socket already has a length, because the length is a function of the value rather than a parameter of the type.

  **5. WHAT BECOMES UNWRITABLE, FROM THE SOURCES.** **Any function whose output length depends on a runtime predicate stops returning the carrier and starts returning a pair.** In Idris's own `Data.Vect` that is IDRISVECT:656 "filter : (elem -> Bool) -> Vect len elem -> (p ** Vect p elem)", and the same for `nubBy`, `nub`, `delete`, `partition`, and IDRISVECT:396 "mapMaybe : (f : a -> Maybe b) -> (xs : Vect len a) -> (m : Nat ** Vect m b)". DML states the cause: DMLPOPL99:3105 "express the length of the resulting list since it depends on" the predicate, so the length is inexpressible in the constraint domain. **The pair is not free at runtime.** Idris's own source carries the price as a comment: IDRISVECT:697 "deleteBy : {len : _} -> -- needed for the dependent pair", an implicit at unrestricted multiplicity, which is a `Nat` that survives erasure. **Concatenation needs arithmetic on indices, and the one mainstream language that added const generics refused to do it.** RFC 2000 states its own position: RUSTCONSTGEN:308 "minimal unification of abstract const expressions possible - it essentially" does not unify them. The feature that would allow it is still marked RUSTGCE:13 "Warning: This feature is incomplete; its design and syntax may change." on a tracking issue open since 2020. **A function over two carriers of different lengths needs two index binders**, which in Idris is the ordinary case and in this tree would be a second `(0 m I64)` on every such seat.

  **6. ERASURE: FAMILY A ERASES THE INDEX AND LOSES `length` WITH IT; FAMILY B ERASES THE LENGTH AND PAYS AT THE CALL SITE; RUST KEEPS IT AND PAYS A WORD.** **DML proves the erasure and states there is no reason to keep the index.** DMLPOPL99:1903 "We define the index erasure function" and DMLPOPL99:1816 "dices at run-time|there is simply no need to do so. Clearly," this would change only if runtime type-checking became necessary. **ATS's indexed string erases to a bare pointer**, ATSBASICS:525 "string_int_type(n: int) = string_type" over ATSBASICS:523 "string_type = ptr // = char* in C", so the index costs nothing in the C output. **Idris 2 uses the same quantities this tree uses and names the consequence.** IDRISQTT:13 "``0``, meaning that the variable is *erased* at run time" is the tree's `(0 n I64)` in another notation. The consequence is that a length function must un-erase the index: IDRISQTT:393 "vlen : {n : Nat} -> Vect n a -> Nat", and a caller whose own index is erased is refused with IDRISQTT:410 "m is not accessible in this context". **Low* is the sharpest case, because its output is C.** LOWSTARLIB:345 "The length is available in ghost (proof) code only: just like in C, one" LOWSTARLIB:346 "cannot compute the length of a buffer at run-time. Therefore, a typical" LOWSTARLIB:347 "pattern is to use refinements to tie together a buffer and its length, as we" saw earlier, and the published pattern is a runtime length passed beside the buffer: LOWSTARLIB:350 "let do_something (x: B.buffer UInt64.t) (l: U32.t { U32.v l = B.length x }): St unit =". That signature is the constructible form `diagnostics-L5.md` measured, with the tie that this tree cannot write. **Rust made the opposite trade and the cost is published in the reference:** a pointer to a slice is RUSTDST:11 "twice the size of pointers to sized types, since they also store *metadata*", and RUSTDST:12 "Pointers to slices store the number of elements; pointers to `str` store the length in bytes."

  **7. WHETHER ANYONE RETROFITTED IT, AND WHAT IT COST. THREE DID, AND THE PRICES ARE DIFFERENT BY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE.** **DML retrofitted onto ML and the language half was cheap.** DMLPOPL99:2787 "makes our extension truly conservative in the sense that" DMLPOPL99:2788 "pure ML programs will work exactly as before, not requir-" ing any annotations, and the annotation burden is reported as DMLPOPL99:285 "very little internal change, annotations are usually to the" point. **The published price is at the seam, and DML names it as a loss:** DMLPOPL99:3133 "represent ML types leads to a major loss of information at" DMLPOPL99:3134 "module boundaries. We would like soon to address this issue" by exporting dependent types in signatures. **ATS's price is a doubled API, visible in the shipping prelude.** The unindexed and indexed string types both survive and the name resolves to either, ATSBASICS:532 "stadef string = string1 // 2nd-select" beside a first-select line for the unindexed one. `strlen` is therefore two functions, ATSSTRING:404 "  (x: NSH(string)):<> size_t" for the unindexed carrier and ATSSTRING:407 "  {n:int} (x: NSH(string(n))):<> size_t(n)" for the indexed one returning a singleton, resolved by an overload table: ATSSTRING:411 "overload strlen with string0_length of 0" and ATSSTRING:412 "overload strlen with string1_length of 10". **LiquidHaskell's retrofit is the cheapest measured and it changed the library by zero lines.** `liquid-vector/src/Data/Vector_LHAssumptions.hs` is **47 lines** against the unmodified `Data.Vector` from Hackage: one measure, LHVECTOR:13 "measure vlen    :: forall a. (Data.Vector.Vector a) -> Int", **eight `assume` axioms** including LHVECTOR:17 "assume Data.Vector.!           :: forall a. x:(Data.Vector.Vector a) -> vec:{v:Nat | v < vlen x } -> a", one invariant, and **eleven `qualif` hints** for the inference engine. **The price is trust, and the tutorial says so:** an assume is used LHTUTOR:132 "because we don't have the code" for the function being specified, so the bound is enforced at every call and the library's own body is never checked.

  **8. THE COUNTER-CASE, AND THE ONE SYSTEM THAT GAVE UP.** **Rust chose the runtime check and states it as a property of the language:** RUSTSLICETY:30 "access to a slice is always bounds-checked in safe methods and operators", with the total form RUSTSLICE:183 "    fn get(self, slice: &[T]) -> Option<&T> {" guarded by `slice.len()` at `:184`. The published reason for stopping at const generics is cost: RUSTCONSTGEN:279 "This feature adds a significant amount of complexity to the type system," and it requires rules RUSTCONSTGEN:281 "around abstract const equality, which result in surprising edge cases." **Cogent, the closest published relative of this tree's lane, has no array type in its own language at all.** COGENTFFI:127 "Cogent provides an escape hatch in the form of a" foreign function interface, arrays come from there, COGENTFFI:147 "engineers provide data structures and their associated operations, including iterators," COGENTFFI:148 "in a special dialect of C, and import them into Cogent, including in formal reasoning." The type system does not see the bound: the signature is COGENTFFI:233 ")!, U32, a!)", an unrefined `U32` index with a caller-supplied default returned on failure, COGENTFFI:251 "where array indices and length are unsigned 32-bit integers", and the consequence is stated as the paper's problem: COGENTFFI:129 "This poses a problem when verifying Cogent programs, as imported C components do not enjoy the same level of static guarantees" that Cogent does.

  **9. WHETHER THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS THE FRAMING, SAID PLAINLY.** **The framing's first half holds and is not controversial.** Every surveyed system except Rust and Cogent refuses the out-of-range call at check time, and in ATS it is refused over a C `char*` with the index erased, which is this tree's exact target. **The framing's second half, that the move is a length-indexed carrier, is one of two routes and the sources price it as the more expensive.** The length-indexed route costs a dependent pair at every boundary, a doubled API where an unindexed carrier survives, index arithmetic that Rust declined to build, and a kept `Nat` wherever the pair is consumed. The refinement-over-a-measure route costs one language capability. **This tree already pays most of the length-indexed route's fixed cost for its linear resources** (33 seats), so the marginal cost of extending it to `Str` is smaller here than the literature's average. **This tree has zero of the other route**, and it is the route four of the surveyed systems took, including both whose output is C. **⚑ The two are not exclusive.** ATS ships an indexed string AND a `strlen` returning a singleton; F* ships a `length` function AND refinements that call it. A refinement that can name a preceding value binder is a prerequisite for the Family B route and is also what makes a Family A index usable at a boundary, because that is how `(refine I64 (<= n))` gets tied to the string rather than threaded by hand. **On the evidence the binder-scope defect is the load-bearing one and the index is a separable second question.** The ruling is the author's.

  **10. WHAT THE SOURCES DO NOT SETTLE, AND WHAT WAS NOT REACHED.** **No source gives a measured annotation burden for retrofitting a length index onto an existing string type in a self-hosting compiler.** DML's "very little internal change" is a claim without a count, ATS's doubled prelude is visible but unpriced, and LiquidHaskell's 47 lines are for a route that adds no index. **Xi and Pfenning's PLDI 1998 paper, which carries the array-bound-check elimination benchmarks, was not reached:** `https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~fp/papers/pldi98.pdf` returns 404, as do three mirrors tried at `cs.bu.edu` and `ats-lang.org`, and the ACM DL copy is paywalled. ## Binding a build-state claim to evidence

### FD-27 every surveyed binding keys a claim to a declared artifact identity and fails by a lookup that cannot resolve, only one surveyed field fires when the RULE moves instead of the artifact, and this tree's resolver is the exact inverse of the rule that would have caught E76

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question: how do comparable systems bind a recorded build-state claim to evidence, so that the claim goes stale loudly rather than silently when the artifact moves underneath it? **Nine systems were read at their own sources, eighteen pins, every one raw.** **Every surveyed binding has one shape. A claim carries a key over an artifact identity. The loudness is a lookup that fails, and no comparison of two statements is involved.** The families differ in what the key is over. **NAME** (a Nix store path, in-toto's `REQUIRE`). **BYTES** (in-toto's subject digest, SLSA's subject match, Bazel's external-dependency hash manifest). **THE RULE THE VERDICT WAS TAKEN AGAINST** (SLSA's Verification Summary Attestation carries `policy.digest`). **THE CLOCK** (in-toto layout `expires`, TUF `EXPIRES`). **COVERAGE**, where an artifact that no rule consumed fails the run outright (in-toto `DISALLOW *`, cargo-vet's exemptions table, rebuilderd's `UNKWN`). **Applied to E76 the families split cleanly.** Name keys and coverage keys fire. Byte keys MISS a pure rename, and in-toto states that property in its own words. Input-addressed build keys, the Nix derivation and the Bazel action, MISS entirely: their reach is the declared input set, and both projects state that the enumeration is a human's responsibility whose completeness is best effort. **The one surveyed field that fires on E76's actual defect, where the artifact held still and the design moved over it, is the VSA's policy digest, and no state column in this tree records which rule a `built` verdict was taken against.** **The measured local cause is sharper than the survey: `MAP.md:20` declares three extensions importable and `MAP.md:27` has the resolver probe all three, so `target-linux.chiral` becoming `target-linux.manifest` is invisible to every consumer by construction.** Nix makes the name part of the identity so that a rename breaks every reference. This tree makes the extension the file's declared KIND and then resolves across kinds, so a change of kind breaks nothing and announces nothing. **The cheapest catch needs no new mechanism: `ledger-lint` check AI already fails a row whose cited files changed after its `checked:` date, and it cannot reach a `State` column because that column carries neither a `checked:` date nor an `evidence:` field.**
- measured: **1. THE E76 CASE, MEASURED IN THE TREE TODAY, AND THE CLAIM NAMES TWO PATHS THAT DO NOT EXIST.** The ledger row is `docs/elements/ledger.md:194`, State `built (ENFORCED)`. It names "the swappable 40-row `SysReg` in `target-linux.chiral`" and closes with "Gate: `test-syscall-manifest.sh` 12/12". **`find . -name 'target-linux*'` returns exactly one file, `lib/lowering/tal/target-linux.manifest`, and `find . -name 'test-syscall-manifest*'` returns nothing.** The gate that exists is `tools/test/syscall-manifest.sh`, wired as phase 5 at `tools/test/run-tests.sh:146`. **Seven further live spans across four files name the file by its dead name**: `lib/lowering/tal/sys-check.chiral:11` and `:13`, `lib/lowering/tal/sys.chiral:785` and `:1003`, `lib/module/loader.chiral:263`, plus `tools/test/syscall-manifest.sh:14` and `:73`. The one span that resolves is the extensionless module import at `lib/lowering/tal/sys-linkage.chiral:23`, `(import "lowering/tal/target-linux")`. **The file was added already carrying `.manifest` at `9a206fe` dated 2026-08-30, whose message is "migrate slice 1: move the source, rename the language, compile nothing".** It holds 40 `(sys-row ...)` entries, which is the row's "40-row" figure. **Seven carry the syscall number `16`, at `:30`, `:31`, `:32`, `:33`, `:34`, `:35` and `:60`, and three of the seven (`:30`, `:31`, `:32`) carry no comment at all**, so the ioctl request that distinguishes them is nowhere in the file. `.planning/MANIFEST-DESIGN-MAP.md:118` is requirement 3, "Constructors have named fields", and `:119` is requirement 4, "Anything distinguishing two rows is a field", whose stated justification is "7 rows carry `16`; only comments tell them apart, and `sexp.chiral` drops comments at the lexer". The file satisfies neither. **`records/conformance-map.md` has no E76 row**, and `docs/elements/ledger.md:17-18` names that file as the per-element build-state authority, with `:20` making it win when the two disagree. **That same header carries a third dead path**: `docs/elements/ledger.md:17` sends a reader to `SELF-IMPLEMENT-CATALOG.md` for the detail, and `find . -name 'SELF-IMPLEMENT-CATALOG*'` returns nothing. The file is `docs/elements/catalog.md`.

  **2. FAMILY NAME: THE ARTIFACT'S NAME IS PART OF ITS IDENTITY, SO A RENAME BREAKS EVERY REFERENCE.** Nix puts the name inside the key. A store path base name is NIXPATH:27 "Store path base names are pairs of" a digest and NIXPATH:30 "A symbolic [name]{#name} for people to read", and NIXPATH:22 "A store path base name will always reference exactly one store object." A reference that names the old path finds nothing, which is a failure with no comparison in it. in-toto spells the same key as a rule rather than a path: INTOTOSPEC:880 "**REQUIRE**: indicates that the specified artifact must appear as a material" or product of the step, and INTOTOSPEC:999 "artifact name is not present in the queue of remaining artifacts, rule" processing errors out. **Cost: every reference must carry the full key, and every rename is a tree-wide edit.** Nix pays it with a store nobody edits by hand. in-toto pays it with a layout that enumerates the artifacts by name.

  **3. FAMILY BYTES: THE DIGEST IS THE IDENTITY, AND IN-TOTO STATES THAT THIS MAKES A RENAME INVISIBLE.** in-toto's statement type says INTOTOSTMT:39 "Subjects are assumed to be _immutable_" and then says how matching works: INTOTOSTMT:54 "Subject artifacts are matched purely by digest, regardless of" name or URI. SLSA's verification procedure is the same step, SLSAVERIFY:98 "that statement's `subject` matches the digest of" the artifact in question, and it names what that buys: SLSAVERIFY:116 "covers tampering of the artifact or provenance" after the build. **Bazel carries the same key in a tracked file, which is the surveyed shape closest to a ledger row.** External dependencies go in a BAZELARTIFACT:254 "workspacewide manifest file that lists a _cryptographic hash_ for every external" dependency, and the consequence is stated plainly: BAZELARTIFACT:262 "If the artifact we download has a different hash than the one declared in the" manifest, BAZELARTIFACT:263 "manifest, the build will fail unless the hash in the manifest is updated." The update is a reviewable change, because it must be approved and checked into BAZELARTIFACT:265 "source control before the build will accept the new dependency." **Cost: the claim must be re-signed or re-hashed on every legitimate edit, and a digest says that something changed without saying what obligation broke.**

  **4. FAMILY RULE: THE VERDICT RECORDS WHICH POLICY IT WAS TAKEN AGAINST, AT WHICH VERSION.** SLSA's Verification Summary Attestation is a verifier's recorded claim that an artifact passed, so a consumer need not re-run the check. Its `policy` field is required, and the spec says what it must carry: SLSAVSA:171 "The entry MUST contain a `uri` identifying which policy was applied and" SLSAVSA:172 "SHOULD contain a `digest` to indicate the exact version of that policy." It also carries a clock on the verdict itself, SLSAVSA:152 "Timestamp indicating what time the verification occurred." **This is the only surveyed field that fires when the artifact holds still and the rule moves over it.** Every other mechanism in the survey keys on the thing judged. **Cost: the policy must be a citable object with a stable identity, and every amendment to it invalidates every verdict taken under the old digest, which is loud on purpose and expensive where the policy is churning.**

  **5. FAMILY CLOCK: A CLAIM WITH NO EXPIRY CANNOT BE DISTINGUISHED FROM A CLAIM NOBODY RECHECKED.** in-toto puts the date in the layout: INTOTOSPEC:707 "EXPIRES determines when layout metadata should be considered expired and no" INTOTOSPEC:708 "longer trusted by clients. Clients MUST NOT trust an expired file." and verification checks it first, INTOTOSPEC:1232 "The expiration time is verified to ensure that this layout is still fresh." TUF spells the same field, TUFSPEC:732 "A <a>date-time</a> string indicating when metadata should be considered" expired, and it is the only surveyed source that names the threat the field exists to stop: TUFSPEC:178 "**Indefinite freeze attacks.**  An attacker cannot respond to client" TUFSPEC:179 "requests with the same, outdated metadata without the client being aware" of the problem. TUF's update workflow makes the check a step with a named failure, TUFSPEC:1364 "trusted root metadata file MUST be higher than the fixed update start time." and TUFSPEC:1365 "If the trusted root metadata file has expired, abort the update cycle," and report the potential freeze attack. **Cost: renewal churn, and the signal says a date passed without saying which obligation broke.** **This is the only family that fires on a population of claims nothing has touched, which is the shape of the 56 elements in item 9.**

  **6. FAMILY COVERAGE: AN ARTIFACT NO RULE ACCOUNTED FOR FAILS THE RUN, AND AN UNMEASURED ARTIFACT GETS A STATE OF ITS OWN.** in-toto makes coverage opt-in and states the consequence of taking it. With the catch-all disallow rule at the end of a rule list, INTOTOSPEC:899 "in-toto verification fails if an artifact" INTOTOSPEC:900 "was not consumed by an earlier rule." without it, artifacts can enter a step undetected. Its rule vocabulary also carries a positive drift check, INTOTOSPEC:887 "materials of this step, and their hashes must not be the same." for `MODIFY`. **cargo-vet turns the same idea into a tracked backlog.** A claim is keyed to a version, CARGOVETAUDIT:8 "Specifies that this audit entry corresponds to an absolute version that was" audited in its entirety, an uncovered version is refused in CI, CARGOVETHOW:43 "verify that the new code has been audited by a trusted organization. If not," the patch is refused, and a counter-claim overrides a covering one, CARGOVETAUDIT:33 "If a `violation` entry exists for a given crate version, `cargo vet` will reject" the dependency even when it is exempted. **The backlog is a tracked table.** CARGOVETCONF:207 "This table enumerates the set of crates which are being used despite missing the" required audits, each entry pinned to a version, CARGOVETCONF:213 "Specifies the exact version which should be exempted." The bootstrap move is to enter the discipline from an approved state, CARGOVETHOW:28 "These are automatically added to the exemptions list" at init. **rebuilderd gives the third-party version.** It recomputes rather than records, REBUILDERD:25 "rebuilder backends like [archlinux-repro][1] to verify the provided binary" packages can be reproduced from the given source, REBUILDERD:30 "It tracks the state of successfully verified packages", and a package that has not been measured yet holds a distinct state rather than a stale verdict, REBUILDERD:167 "Check the package was successfully added to the database with status `UNKWN`". Its own docs treat an unknown as a queue question, REBUILDERD:96 "If the rebuilder seems to have outdated data or lists a package as unknown the" update may still be in the build queue. **Cost: the coverage rule must enumerate the domain, and the exemptions table is a permanent visible debt that someone has to keep from growing.**

  **7. FAMILY GENERATED: THE DOCUMENT HOLDS A POINTER OR A CHECKSUM, NEVER AN AUTHORED VERDICT.** Cog writes generated text into a hand-edited file and guards the region with a checksum, COGRUN:43 "Checksum the output to protect it against accidental" edits, and the failure is refusal rather than a silent overwrite: COGRUN:207 "If the generated code is edited by a misguided developer, the next time cog" COGRUN:208 "is run, the checksum won't match, and cog will stop to avoid overwriting the" edited output. The gate half is a separate flag, COGRUN:224 "You can use the ``--check`` option to run cog just to check that the files" would not change if run again, with COGRUN:228 "The ``--diff`` option will show a unified diff of the change that caused" the failure. **Scorecard takes the stronger position of storing no verdict at all.** The README holds a badge URL whose value is computed elsewhere, SCORECARD:207 "This badge also auto-updates for every change made to the repository." over a recomputation on a fixed cadence, SCORECARD:139 "We run a weekly Scorecard scan of the 1 million most critical open source" projects. **A document that holds a pointer cannot hold a stale claim, because it holds no claim.** **Cost: the measurement has to be cheap enough to re-run on the cadence, and a pointer is unreadable in a diff and in a fresh clone with no network.**

  **8. FAMILY ONE-ARTIFACT: THE CLAIM AND THE CHECK ARE THE SAME TEXT, AND THE CONFORMANCE-PACKAGE VARIANT SHIPS THE RAW LOGS AND THE CHECKER'S OWN GIT STATE.** doctest states the purpose as keeping prose honest, PYDOCTEST:15 "To check that a module's docstrings are up-to-date by verifying that all" PYDOCTEST:16 "interactive examples still work as documented." and its author names the loudness property from experience, PYDOCTEST:1946 "examples stops working after a" harmless change. **The Vulkan CTS submission is the same idea at industrial scale, and it is the only surveyed mechanism that pins the CHECKER's identity as hard as the artifact's.** The package is enumerated at VKCTS:496 "The conformance submission package must contain the following:" and the first two items are the raw evidence and the checker's provenance: VKCTS:498 "1. Full test logs (`TestResults.qpa`) from CTS runs against all driver builds and all fractions" and VKCTS:499 "2. Result of `git status` and `git log` from CTS source directory". The checker must be unmodified or the modification must be exhibited, VKCTS:517 "The CTS build must always be done from clean git repository that doesn't have any" uncommitted changes, and VKCTS:524 "Any changes made to CTS must be committed to the local repository, and provided" as patches. The claim itself names the checker version, VKCTS:552 "CONFORM_VERSION:         <git tag of CTS release>". **Cost: the package is large, the discipline is per-submission rather than continuous, and a product that changes after the submission is unexamined until the next one.**

THE E76 TEST, MECHANISM BY MECHANISM, AND FOUR OF THE NINE MISS.** **FIRES, and most cheaply: a name key.** The ledger row at `docs/elements/ledger.md:194` names `target-linux.chiral` and `test-syscall-manifest.sh`, and neither resolves. A VSA-shaped row recording which rule the verdict was taken against, at which version, shows the verdict predating its own policy. **FIRES: expiry.** The row would have gone stale on the clock whatever moved. **MISSES: a byte digest alone.** in-toto matches INTOTOSTMT:54 "Subject artifacts are matched purely by digest, regardless of" name, so a pure rename is invisible to it, and this rename was a `git mv` plus a compile-nothing commit. **MISSES: the input-addressed build key.** Nix requires that the input set be enumerated by hand, NIXDRV:101 "Nix requires that all inputs be explicitly collected in the inputs field", and states whose job that is: the "responsibility of the creator of a derivation" to include everything referenced. Bazel's key is over declared inputs too, BAZELHERM:28 "**Source identity**: Hermetic build systems try to ensure the sameness of" inputs, BAZELHERM:30 "unique hash code. Hermetic build systems use this hash to identify changes to" the build's input, enforced by a sandbox where BAZELARTIFACT:220 "they are unable to read any files they don’t declare". SLSA says the same about its own enumeration, SLSAPROVB:222 "Unordered collection of artifacts needed at build time. WHAT IS TRANSFERABLE HERE, WITH ITS PRICE, AND ONE PIECE IS ALREADY BUILT.** **The already-built piece is `ledger-lint` check AI.** Its docstring quotes the rule it enforces, "A row whose `checked:` date predates the last change to the files it cites is unverified", at `tools/ledger-lint/ledger-lint.py:2120-2122`, and it implements it by `git log -1 --format=%cs` per cited path, `:2129-2134`. **That is the clock family and the name family in one check, and it is scoped by field presence.** It reaches a row that carries `evidence:` and `checked:`. `docs/elements/ledger.md`'s `State` column carries the evidence as prose (E76's row names a gate, a commit `612a2d9`, and two dates) and carries no `checked:` field, so nothing parses it and AI cannot see it. **Price: two fields per built row, and the 109 rows in item 9's population would each need one date.** **The cheapest new check is the name key, and it needs nothing the tree lacks**: every path and gate name a `built` row cites must exist. WHAT THE SOURCES DO NOT SETTLE, AND WHAT WAS NOT REACHED.** **No surveyed mechanism catches an uncited paraphrase, and none of the fifteen claims to.** The three that fire all require a declared key, so the honest statement of the finding is that single-sourcing a rule is enforced by making a second copy impossible or by making every carrier declare itself, and neither is detection. **No source prices the retrofit.** Doorstop assumes items authored as YAML from the start and says nothing about converting an existing prose corpus; test262's own migration off section numbers is described as unfinished at TEST262CON:44 with no cost attached. **No source measures the false-alarm rate of a suspect link**, and Doorstop's own wording at DOORSTOPITEM:222-224 calls it a convenience to the writer, which is advisory language. ## Keeping one register of what a human still owes

### FD-29 no surveyed project runs one register, all eight reconcile several by a shared id, the only family that reaches a ruling given out of band is a procedural MUST with no check behind it, and this tree's own register file holds three settled rulings its own check cannot see

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question: how does a project keep one register of decisions owed by a human, so that a question needing an answer never lives only where no tool looks, and so that an answer once given reaches every carrier that was waiting on it? **Eight mechanisms were read at their own sources. Fourteen pins added, every one raw, four earlier pins reused.** **No surveyed project keeps one register.** Every one runs several at different granularities and binds them with a shared identifier plus a validated or generated view, so the cost of collapsing registers is a price no surveyed project pays. **The families are eight.** **CLOSED TOKEN VALIDATED BY A TOOL**: Kubernetes `kep.yaml` `status:` against a Go enum, PEP `Status` against `ALL_STATUSES`, MADR's status field, and this tree's check AK. **KEYED PROSE MARK**: ruff's flake8-todos, where a `TODO` must carry an author and an issue link, beside Kubernetes' `<<[UNRESOLVED]>>` delimiter, which ships the marker with no checker behind it. **CONFIRM AN OUT-OF-BAND DECISION IN THE DURABLE MEDIUM**: RFC 2418's MUST, and Rust's meeting summary posted back to the pull request. **PERMALINK INTO THE EPHEMERAL MEDIUM**: PEP's `Resolution:` header, a URL at the post that made the decision, form-checked. **NAMED BLOCKING CONCERN**: rfcbot, where a concern is an object with a name, blocks the gate, and is resolvable only by whoever raised it. **WRITE BOTH DIRECTIONS AT THE MOMENT OF THE ANSWER**: adr-tools' `adr link` and `adr new -s`, and PEP's `Superseded-By`/`Replaces` pair. **FINGERPRINT**: Doorstop, reused from FD-28. **ERRATUM STATE MACHINE**: the IESG's three states, whose middle state records a ruling and defers its propagation deliberately. **Applied to the two local cases the split is one-sided.** **§UNSORTED, a question stated in a document's prose where the register's check could not see it, is caught by two of the eight.** The keyed prose mark fires when the mark is a directive the linter enumerates, and Doorstop's coverage rule fires on a normative item that declares no parent. Six miss. **The unrecorded in-session ruling is caught by no surveyed check and by one surveyed obligation.** RFC 2418 and the Rust RFC README both say a decision taken off the record MUST be brought back onto it; neither ships anything that fires when it is not, and neither states a consequence. **That asymmetry is the finding.** Discovery and propagation both reduce to the carrier emitting a key a tool indexes, which is FD-28's result unchanged, and the moment a human speaks emits no key at all, so every surveyed defence there is a rule addressed to a person. **The tiered-repository question has a surveyed answer, and this tree's premise for asking it is false.** The `.planning/` files holding dated author rulings are tracked, `docs/decisions/decision-ai-tier.md:28` heads a section reading `Both tiers are tracked`, and two arcs cite `.planning/DISPLAY-LAYER-GAP.md` already. **The measured defect is one register file carrying two row shapes.** `records/author-calls.md:401-405` records the three display directives of 2026-09-04 as a two-column table with no state cell, and the file says at `:396-399` that they are settled, that none of them holds a row in the table above, and that a directive kept only in a session transcript is lost; check AK's regex reads the token in the first cell, so it sees 40 of the file's 73 body rows and none of those three. **A ruling filed in the register, inside the register's own file, is invisible to the register's own check.** The surveyed answer to a tiered repository is PEP's: leave the ruling where it was made, require the tracked row to carry a form-checked pointer at a permanent copy, and make the pointer a required header. **The measured price of that answer sits inside the same pin.** PEP 1 requires `Resolution` for Standards Track PEPs, `check-peps.py` omits it from `REQUIRED_HEADERS`, and the validator it does run checks the pointer's shape and never its content.

## Where an editor's model stops and its presentation begins

### FD-30 one surveyed editor serves a terminal and a graphical surface from a single model, and it does so by carrying pixel fields that collapse to unit values on the cell lane

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question, aimed at the cut the author is choosing in `prog/scriba/`: in editors that drive both a terminal and a graphical surface, where does the boundary between the editor model and the presentation layer fall, what value crosses it, and does one model genuinely serve both surface kinds? **Ten systems were read at their own sources: GNU Emacs, sam, Acme, xi-editor, Kakoune, Neovim, Vim, Helix, vis, Project Oberon, with Zed's GPUI read for its platform list. The answer has three parts. (a) Exactly one surveyed system serves a text terminal and a graphical window from one model, and that is GNU Emacs; its seam is a glyph matrix, and the same `struct glyph` carries `pixel_width`, `ascent`, `descent` and `voffset` on both lanes, with the row's ascent forced to zero and its height to 1 on a terminal frame. (b) Every other seam takes one of two shapes. A byte-offset edit stream carrying zero presentation property (sam, Acme), or a grid or line list carrying a closed face vocabulary in cell units (Vim, Kakoune, Neovim, vis, xi-editor). (c) The two systems that declared a model-to-presentation boundary in order to serve structurally different surfaces both recorded its failure in their own documents: xi-editor's author wrote that the front-end/core process separation was a mistake, and Helix's architecture doc says the view layer meant to be frontend-agnostic is tied to the terminal UI.**
- measured: **1. THE TWO AXES, NAMED PER SYSTEM.** A client/server split multiplexes one editing session across several attached clients. A model/presentation split serves surfaces of different kinds. Kakoune is client/server only, and its design document says so in the multiplexing terms: KAKDESIGN:37 "multiple windows by supporting many clients on the same editing session," with the surrounding sentence naming the graphical environment it wants to exploit KAKDESIGN:36 "of that without hindering text mode support." Neovim is both axes at once: the UI protocol admits many simultaneous UIs and resolves capabilities across all of them, NVIMUI:35 "			  supported by all connected UIs (including |TUI|)." sam is both: one host part with one terminal part over a stream, and the stream exists to cross a machine boundary. Emacs is model/presentation with a multiplexing side effect, since one process owns many terminals. xi-editor, Helix, vis and Oberon are model/presentation only. Acme inverts the axis: the editor is the display program and the split faces outward at its clients. **A thin terminal client answers the multiplexing question and answers nothing about a pixel surface.** **2. GNU EMACS: one model, two seams, one glyph vocabulary.** Model side: buffers, windows, and the display iterator that produces glyphs. Presentation side: a per-terminal hook table. The terminal object is typed by output method, EMACSTERMH:55 "/* Output method of a terminal (and frames on this terminal, respectively).  */", and the graphical seam hangs off it as a function-pointer record that the terminal lane does not receive at all, EMACSTERMH:556 "  /* Window-based redisplay interface for this device (0 for tty". The tty lane instead gets frame-level hooks on the same terminal object, EMACSTERMH:574 "  void (*write_glyphs_hook) (struct frame *f, struct glyph *s, int n);", and the window lane gets the metric producer, EMACSDISPX:3075 "  void (*produce_glyphs) (struct it *it);". So Emacs has two seams of different shape over one model. **The value crossing both is the same glyph matrix**, and the matrices are distinguished by capability rather than by vocabulary, EMACSDISPX:773 "   1. Frame glyph matrices.  These are used for terminal frames whose" and EMACSDISPX:785 "   3. Free-standing window glyph matrices managing their own glyph" whose purpose is stated as EMACSDISPX:786 "   storage.  This form is used in window-based redisplay which" variable width and height fonts. **That one vocabulary is a pixel vocabulary, and the cell lane degenerates its fields.** A glyph carries EMACSDISPX:502 "  /* Width in pixels.  */", EMACSDISPX:505 "  /* Ascent and descent in pixels.  */" and a sub-cell vertical displacement, EMACSDISPX:508 "  /* Vertical offset.  If < 0, the glyph is displayed raised, if > 0". The degeneration is written into the row struct, EMACSDISPX:958 "     and height is 1 on terminal frames.  */". Emacs displays both kinds at once in one session, EMACSFRAME:54 "There are two classes of terminals" and EMACSFRAME:72 "both, graphical and text terminals, simultaneously." **The lesson is directional: Emacs generalized the cell lane up into pixels, and paid by making every cell-lane glyph carry three fields whose only legal value there is a constant.** **3. SAM: the seam carries byte offsets and nothing else.** Model side: the file as a string, the command language, the transaction log. Presentation side: proportional-font layout, tiled boxes, a bitmap. The split is two programs over a stream, SAMPAPER:163 "is implemented as two processes connected by a low-bandwidth stream," and it exists for bandwidth, SAMPAPER:2665 "The low bandwidth of an RS-232 link". **The protocol is typed as data edits at character positions**, SAMPAPER:2707 "popping up menus and interpreting the responses, the messages are about" data and SAMPAPER:2709 "For example, the host knows nothing about what is displayed on the screen," with the example given as an insert of one byte at location 123 in file 7. The wire type is a two-enum message set with one length-prefixed header, SAMMESG:17 "	Trequest,	/* request data to fill a hole */" and SAMMESG:49 "	Hgrow,		/* insert space in rasp */", and its only size constant is a text block bound, SAMMESG:6 "#define	TBLOCKSIZE 512		  /* largest piece of text sent to terminal */". **sam does not serve two surface kinds from one presentation.** Its terminal answer is to drop the display program and use the command language alone, SAMPAPER:2640 "part&rsquo;s command language to edit text on an ordinary terminal." All layout lives on the graphical side, where text is tiled as boxes over a bitmap, SAMPAPER:3142 "The update algorithms always use the" bitmap image. Pike priced the split in the same paper, SAMPAPER:2669 "a program in two parts is much harder to write and to debug". **4. ACME: the seam is a file namespace and the editor is the display program.** Presentation, input and text all live in one program that exports files, ACMEPAPER:162 "Acme is in part a file server that exports device-like files that may be" manipulated. What crosses is a character position and the bytes at it, ACMEPAPER:789 "file is written to set a character position within the body; the" data file is then read or written. Six files per window: `addr`, `body`, `ctl`, `data`, `event`, `tag`. **Acme has no terminal surface and no presentation vocabulary on its seam.** It answers the plugin question and leaves the surface question untouched. **5. XI-EDITOR: the seam was a line list with style spans, and its author reversed the decision.** Model side: a rope, CRDT edits, syntax highlighting in a third process. Presentation side: a native GUI per platform. The value crossing is a cached array of lines, XIPROTO:448 "considered an array of lines. Each line consists of the *text* (a string), a set" of cursor locations and style information, with styles interned by id, XIPROTO:479 "(It's not hard to imagine more style properties such as typeface, size, OpenType" features. **The viewport crossed in pixels**, XIPROTO:154 "in px units / points" rather than device pixels. **The core could not compute line breaks from that, so the protocol grew a synchronous reverse call into the presentation layer**, XIPROTO:618 "Asks the frontend to measure the display widths" of a group of strings, and XIPROTO:620 "These widths are used to determine how to" calculate line breaks. **That is the cell-to-pixel question answered by giving up: font metrics stayed on the presentation side and the model had to ask.** The retrospective names word wrap as the hardest consequence, XIRETRO:93 "live-resizing the window causes text to rewrap continuously" and, on the same line, "tearing-style artifacts" as what the async seam made hard to avoid. Scrolling took months where a shared data structure would have been direct, XIRETRO:95 "in-process data structure for the UI to query, it would have been quite straightforward". The verdict is explicit, XIRETRO:99 "I now firmly believe that the process separation between front-end and core" was a mistake, and the plugin split is kept as supportable in the same sentence. The motivation for the split collapsed too, XIRETRO:123 "There is no such thing as native GUI". One further cost was social, XIRETRO:157 "monolithic architectures, perhaps ironically, are *better* for community". **6. KAKOUNE: a typed presentation interface in cell units, terminal lane only in tree.** The seam is one abstract class whose draw call takes a computed display buffer, KAKUI:68 "  virtual void draw(const DisplayBuffer& display_buffer," with the width argument typed in columns, KAKUI:72 "                      ColumnCount widget_columns) = 0;" and the size query returning a cell coordinate, KAKUI:81 "  virtual DisplayCoord dimensions() = 0;". A `DisplayBuffer` is lines of atoms each carrying a `Face` of foreground, background, underline colour and a thirteen-bit attribute set. **The unit is the column and it is in the type**, so a pixel client inherits a monospace advance assumption from the interface itself. **7. NEOVIM: the seam is a cell grid, declared as such, and the pixel knowledge is pushed to the client as opaque strings.** NVIMUI:15 "The default UI model is a terminal-like grid with a single," NVIMUI:16 "monospace font. The UI can opt-in to have windows drawn on separate grids, and" have elements externalized. The redraw event is a run-length encoded cell span, NVIMUI:366 "	Redraw a continuous part of a `row` on a `grid`, starting at the column" given as NVIMUI:368 "	`[text(, hl_id, repeat)]` . `text` is the UTF-8 text that should be put in" a cell, against a highlight table defined by id. **Two entries in that closed face vocabulary have no cell-lane meaning and shipped anyway.** NVIMUI:327 "	`altfont`:		alternative font." and NVIMUI:328 "	`blend`:		blend level (0-100). Could be used by UIs to" support blending floating windows. The permission is advisory, so a terminal client ignores them and a pixel client honours them. **Font choice and cell metrics never enter the grid vocabulary at all**, and travel instead as option strings the model does not interpret, NVIMUI:206 "	- 'guifont'" alongside `guifontwide` and `linespace`. Per-window grids were added so a client could vary metrics, NVIMUI:591 "  occupies on the global layout. So the UI could use a different font size" per window. **The price of one vocabulary across clients of unequal capability is a downgrade to the intersection**, NVIMUI:35 "			  supported by all connected UIs (including |TUI|)." **8. VIM: the split was refused, and the graphical surface is modelled as a terminal type.** One global cell grid backs both lanes, VIMGLOBALS:32 " * The characters that are currently on the screen are kept in ScreenLines[]." with attributes in a parallel array and dimensions in rows and columns, VIMGLOBALS:29 "EXTERN long	Columns INIT(= 80);	// nr of columns in the screen". The GUI announces itself by naming a fake terminal, VIMGUIDOC:44 "- The 'term' option is set to " a pseudo-terminal named builtin_gui, VIMGUIDOC:44 " and terminal options are reset to" their GUI defaults. **Vim's answer to the graphical surface is to make the graphical surface pretend to be a terminal.** It ships, and the cell grid is the whole model of the screen. **9. HELIX AND VIS: a declared boundary that did not hold, and a boundary typed in cells from the start.** Helix names the intent and the outcome in consecutive lines, HELIXARCH:52 "The `view` layer was supposed to be a frontend-agnostic imperative library that" HELIXARCH:53 "would build on top of `core` to provide the common editor logic. Currently it's" tied to the terminal UI. **A frontend-agnostic layer with one frontend drifts into that frontend.** vis draws the boundary at a cell buffer and says so in the field comment, VISUI:141 "	VisCellBuffer cell_buffer; /* 2D grid of cells, at least as large as current terminal size */", where a cell is an eight-byte record with a width in terminal columns and a per-cell style, VISUI:98 "typedef alignas(16) struct {" and VISUI:108 "	VisCellStyle style;". vis has one surface kind. **10. PROJECT OBERON: presentation properties live inside the text value, and there is no cell lane.** The typed text is a piece list, and each piece carries a font, a colour and a vertical offset, OBTEXTS:23 "      fnt: Fonts.Font;" with the on-disk encoding naming the same three, OBTEXTS:13 "      run = fnt [name] col voff len. *)". **A minimal-by-construction system put font, colour and a sub-cell vertical displacement in the model.** The presentation side is a frame tree with a single dispatching procedure variable over extensible message records, OBDISPLAY:10 "    Handler* = PROCEDURE (F: Frame; VAR M: FrameMsg);" over a memory-mapped bitmap, OBDISPLAY:6 "    base = 0E7F00H;  (*adr of 1024 x 768 pixel, monocolor display frame*)". Layout advances per glyph, OBTEXTFRM:99 "  PROCEDURE Width (VAR R: Texts.Reader; len: LONGINT): INTEGER;" summing per-character advances, OBTEXTFRM:104 "      ox := ox + dx; INC(pos); Texts.Read(R, nextCh)". **Oberon's seam type is an open message sum extended by record subtyping, and its coordinates are pixels throughout.** **11. ZED AND GPUI: the terminal surface was declined.** GPUIREADME:3 "GPUI is a hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU accelerated, UI framework" for Rust. Its platform feature list names Metal, Wayland, X11, Win32 and DirectWrite, with glyph rasterization gated on a font backend. **No terminal backend appears in that list.** Reading the absence as a deliberate refusal is inference from the platform list rather than a statement by the project. **12. WHAT THE CELL VOCABULARY COST THE SYSTEMS THAT FACED IT.** Four of them carried a cell-shaped value into a pixel surface and each paid differently. Emacs paid by making the vocabulary pixel-shaped and pinning three fields to constants on the cell lane. Vim paid by declaring the GUI a terminal type. Neovim paid by shipping two attributes with no cell meaning under an advisory rule, by moving font identity off the seam entirely, and by intersecting capabilities down to the weakest attached client. xi paid by discovering that line breaking cannot be computed on the model side and adding a synchronous callback to the presentation layer for string widths. **Nobody carried a cell vocabulary into pixels and kept one meaning for every property.** The two systems that refused the shared vocabulary (sam, Acme) put byte offsets on the seam and accepted that the terminal surface is a different program with a different interaction model. **13. THE LINEAGE CANDIDATES FOR A CUT AT `RendererFn`.** The live plug is `lib/protocol/render.chiral:34-35`, `(-> Str (Pair I64 I64) I64 Rendering)`, and `Rendering` at `:7-31` is a nine-constructor tree with a `Face` of foreground, background and attribute bits at `:37`. Five named lineages, with the match stated: (i) **Emacs**, one model and two seams of different shape, where the shared value is pixel-typed and the cell lane uses constants. This is the only lineage that has actually shipped both surfaces. (ii) **Kakoune and xi**, a per-line list of faced atoms measured in columns. **This is the closest match to `Rendering` as written**, because `rnd-cols` is declared `(-> Rendering I64)` at `lib/protocol/render.chiral:91` and its contract is stated in cell units at `:458` as the number of terminal columns a node advances the cursor by, with the standing precondition at `:465` that nothing in `Rendering` reflows. (iii) **Neovim**, a cell grid on the wire with font identity off-seam and advisory attributes. The tree's `(Pair I64 I64)` dimension argument is this shape, and `Rendering` has a different shape. (iv) **sam and Acme**, byte offsets on the seam and no presentation property at all. (v) **Oberon**, presentation properties inside the text value and an open message sum at the frame boundary. **The measured obstruction to (ii) is one type.** `rnd-cols` returning a single `I64` is a monospace-advance assumption in the value vocabulary; xi's `measure_width` is the same function under a proportional font and it returns a float per string per style and runs on the presentation side. The tree's own comment at `:469` already says that a wrapping constructor makes this signature wrong rather than imprecise. **14. WHETHER THE RECORD SUPPORTS A FULLY ALTERNATE GRAPHICAL VERSION.** The record splits. **It supports the author's position on the seam value and undercuts it on the codebase.** Supporting: no surveyed system carries one property vocabulary across both surface kinds without degeneration or advisory opt-out, which is the tree's standing ruling holding in four independent codebases; sam and Acme treat the terminal surface as a different interaction model reached by a different program; xi's retrospective and Helix's architecture doc are two recorded failures of a declared model-to-presentation boundary. Undercutting: **the one system that actually ships a terminal and a graphical surface kept one codebase and one model**, and its cost was three degenerate fields on a struct rather than a fork; xi's failure was a process and async boundary, which is a different decision from a second renderer in one program, and Levien's reversal was toward one process; Helix's drift argues that a second surface built outside the shared layer pulls the shared layer with it. **The supported reading of the survey is one model with two presentation seams of different shape and two property vocabularies, which is Emacs's shape, and the unsupported reading is a second copy of the model.** The 3,487 lines already free of `Rendering`, `ansi-` and `read-key` are the model side by this reading. **15. WHAT THE SOURCES DO NOT SETTLE.** **No source prices a second renderer registered against an existing typed plug.** Every surveyed boundary is either a process boundary or a vtable over one surface family, so the tree's actual question, a third registration against `RendererFn` that emits pixels, has no occupant in the survey. **No surveyed system states a rule for which property belongs to which lane.** Neovim's `blend` and `altfont` are the closest thing to one and they are permissions rather than a rule. **Neither the Emacs internals manual nor `xdisp.c` carries a pin here.** The redisplay seam here is quoted from `dispextern.h` and `termhooks.h` only, so this row makes no claim about the ordering of the two redisplay phases. **Kakoune's and vis's GUI story is absent rather than negative.** Only in-tree sources were read, the in-tree `UserInterface` implementation is the terminal one, and no source was pinned that says a pixel client exists or cannot. **Zed's refusal of a terminal frontend is inference.** **Project Oberon's book carries no pin**, because `PO.System.pdf` is a PDF and a line-addressed pin over it would carry a transcriber's reading; the module sources were pinned instead, so this row quotes Oberon's code and none of Wirth's prose. **Two fetches failed and are named**: `neovim/neovim/master/runtime/doc/ui.txt` returned HTTP 404 on 2026-09-15 and the protocol is pinned from the `release-0.11` branch at that path; `projectoberon.net/wirth/ProjectOberon/Sources/*.Mod.txt` returned HTTP 404 and the ETH mirror at `people.inf.ethz.ch` served the same files.
- evidence: **Nineteen pins added 2026-09-15 in `.planning/sources/`, every one origin `raw`.** `EMACSDISPX` (`git.savannah.gnu.org/cgit/emacs.git/plain/src/dispextern.h`, 4,023 lines), `EMACSTERMH` (same tree, `src/termhooks.h`, 993), `EMACSFRAME` (`gnu.org/software/emacs/manual/html_node/elisp/Frames.html`, 226, served as HTML and pinned as the bytes served), `SAMPAPER` (`doc.cat-v.org/plan_9/4th_edition/papers/sam/`, 3,829, Pike's 1987 Software-Practice and Experience paper as mirrored, served as HTML), `SAMMESG` (`9fans/plan9port/master/src/cmd/sam/mesg.h`, 131), `ACMEPAPER` (`doc.cat-v.org/plan_9/4th_edition/papers/acme/`, 1,590, served as HTML), `XIRETRO` (`raphlinus/raphlinus.github.io/master/_posts/2020-06-21-xi-retrospective.md`, 198, the authored Markdown behind the published post; the rendered HTML at `raphlinus.github.io` was fetched first and rejected as a pin because three metadata tags repeat the whole article and every span in it resolves four times), `XIPROTO` (`xi-editor/xi-editor/master/docs/docs/frontend-protocol.md`, 797), `KAKDESIGN` (`mawww/kakoune/master/doc/design.asciidoc`, 152), `KAKUI` (`mawww/kakoune/master/src/user_interface.hh`, 94), `NVIMUI` (`neovim/neovim/release-0.11/runtime/doc/ui.txt`, 865), `HELIXARCH` (`helix-editor/helix/master/docs/architecture.md`, 128), `VISUI` (`martanne/vis/master/ui.h`, 202), `VIMGUIDOC` (`vim/vim/master/runtime/doc/gui.txt`, 1,298), `VIMGLOBALS` (`vim/vim/master/src/globals.h`, 2,191), `OBTEXTS` (`people.inf.ethz.ch/wirth/ProjectOberon/Sources/Texts.Mod.txt`, 537), `OBDISPLAY` (same directory, `Display.Mod.txt`, 190), `OBTEXTFRM` (same directory, `TextFrames.Mod.txt`, 856), `GPUIREADME` (`zed-industries/zed/main/crates/gpui/README.md`, 98). `xlat pin` stamps a UTC clock, so each `.meta` reads `pinned: 2026-09-15`. Live tree spans, measured 2026-09-15 at `7e0eb24`: `lib/protocol/render.chiral:7-31` (the nine `Rendering` constructors), `:34-35` (`RendererFn`), `:37` (`Face`), `:41-42` (`Mode`), `:91` (the `rnd-cols` declaration), `:451-475` (its contract, with the cell-unit statement at `:458` and the no-reflow precondition at `:465-470`). The per-file presentation-coupling counts over `prog/scriba/` were supplied to this run and this run re-measured none of them. `ledger-lint` measured after this row at the figure in the report.
