It omits `abvm` and `blwm`, which are the two HarfBuzz applies globally for scripts with above and below marks. Ordering is load-bearing in the standard's own words, OTGSUB:847 "Thus, the ordering of lookups in the LookupList can be very significant.", and the advance-cursor rule is stated per lookup at OTGSUB:848 "To move to the" next glyph the client skips the whole matched input sequence, with one exception for kerning at OTGPOS:869 "if the ValueRecord for the second glyph is null, that glyph is treated as the" next glyph. **4. WHAT THE SAFE-BREAK WORKFLOW COSTS PER CANDIDATE BREAK.** HarfBuzz prescribes an unbounded search. The documented procedure is HBBUF:108 "1. Iterate back from the line-break position" until HBBUF:109 "until the first cluster start position that is" clear of unsafe-to-concat, then HBBUF:111 "there till the end of line, 3. check whether the" result is itself clear at its start, and if it is not, move further back and HBBUF:117 "from there, and repeat.". **No bound is stated on the number of retries**, and the header names an API gap that forces over-shaping, HBBUF:135 "can be alleviated by shaping more text than needed". The flag also needs a buffer flag to be produced at all, HBBUF:140 "To use this flag, you must enable the buffer flag", and HBBUF:138 "The #HB_GLYPH_FLAG_UNSAFE_TO_BREAK flag will" always imply it, so the two flags are nested rather than independent. Only a pair of runs both clear of the concat flag may be joined, HBBUF:96 "Only two pieces of text both of which clear of" it. **The shipped arrangement is cheaper and departs from that procedure.** Chromium shapes the paragraph once and stores one bit per character, BLINKSHAPE:101 "unsigned safe_to_break_before : 1 = false;". The per-candidate query is a lookup over a precomputed array, BLINKSHAPE:262 "unsigned CachedNextSafeToBreakOffset(unsigned offset) const;" documented at BLINKSHAPE:258 "break without reshaping. Operates on a cache (that needs to be pre-computed", beside the uncached form at BLINKSHAPE:208 "unsigned NextSafeToBreakOffset(unsigned offset) const;". The policy is stated in the breaker's own header: BLINKSLB:30 "is at a safe-to-break boundary (as identified by HarfBuzz) the beginning and/" plus BLINKSLB:31 "or end of the line is reshaped to account for differences caused by breaking.", justified at BLINKSLB:33 "This allows for significantly faster and more efficient line breaking by only" plus BLINKSLB:34 "reshaping when absolutely necessarily and by only evaluating likely candidate". **The line it emits is exactly three segments**, BLINKSLBCC:620 "std::array<ShapeResultView::Segment, 3> segments;": an optionally re-shaped head, a by-reference slice of the paragraph-wide result, and an optionally re-shaped tail. **So the measured cost is a bit test per candidate break and at most two partial re-shapes per accepted line, each covering the span between the break and the nearest safe boundary.** For `FD-36`'s bound of breakpoints times active-list size, the multiplier on the candidate term is therefore one array read, and the re-shaping attaches to the line count instead. **The limit of that result**: Blink is greedy and says so, BLINKSLB:35 "break opportunities instead of measuring and evaluating all possible options.". No surveyed optimal breaker shapes at all, so the record does not price total-fit against re-shaping. **5. WHERE UNSAFE-TO-BREAK IS ACTUALLY SET.** Three sites, each on a successful multi-cluster match. Context and chained-context lookups, HBGSUBGPOS:3025 "c->buffer->unsafe_to_break (c->buffer->idx, match_end);", against the failure path at HBGSUBGPOS:3034 "c->buffer->unsafe_to_concat (c->buffer->idx, match_end);". GPOS pair positioning, and only in the branch where an adjustment was applied, HBPAIRSET:135 "bool applied_first = len1 && valueFormats[0].apply_value" guarding it, while the zero-valued case falls through to the weaker flag, HBPAIRSET:156 "Even a zero-valued pair record is a concat hazard.". The legacy kern machine, per kerned pair, HBKERNHH:127 "buffer->unsafe_to_break (i, j + 1);", and **that path marks the entire buffer unsafe to concatenate up front**, HBKERNHH:54 "buffer->unsafe_to_concat ();", which removes the concat optimisation for a legacy-kern font altogether. Fallback mark positioning marks the base-and-marks run, HBFALLBACK:334 "buffer->unsafe_to_break (base, end);". Cluster merging routes to the same setter under a non-monotone level, HBBUFHH:396 "void merge_clusters (unsigned int start, unsigned int end)". **The flag lands on the span's interior and spares its first cluster**, HBBUFHH:444 "If interior is true, then the cluster having the minimum value is skipped.", which HBBUFHH:506 "void unsafe_to_break (unsigned int start = 0, unsigned int end = -1)" passes true and HBBUFHH:526 "void unsafe_to_concat (unsigned int start = 0, unsigned int end = -1)" passes false. Flags are then made uniform across each cluster, HBOTSHAPE:1111 "Propagate cluster-level glyph flags to be the same on all cluster glyphs.". **Two bounds on the mechanism itself.** HBBUFHH:494 "if (unlikely (end != (unsigned) -1 && end - start > 255))" returns without setting anything, and HBBUFHH:499 "if (interior && !from_out_buffer && end - start < 2)" does the same below two. The second is a tautology. **The first means a match wider than 255 glyphs gets no flag at all, which under-marks rather than over-marks; that reading is inference and the record states no rationale for 255.** **Frequency.** No surveyed source gives a proportion, and a search for one returned only derivative wikis. What the record supports structurally: at tier (a) no lookup runs, so nothing is ever marked and the shaped run is invariant under breaking with no precondition, which makes `T6`'s chirality column hold outright at the floor; at tier (b) the unsafe positions are exactly the applied kern pairs; at tiers (c) and (d) ligature and contextual spans join them. The only evidence that those positions are sparse is the two implementers' design statements, HBBUF:100 "after line-breaking, by limiting the" reshaping to a small piece around the break, and BLINKSLB:34's "only reshaping when absolutely necessarily". **6. CLUSTER LEVELS AND THE ADDRESS.** Four levels. HBBUF:419 "Return cluster values grouped by graphemes into" monotone order is the default; HBBUF:421 "Return cluster values grouped into monotone order." keeps per-character values and stays monotone; HBBUF:422 "Don't group cluster values." keeps them and gives up monotonicity; HBBUF:425 "Only group clusters, but don't enforce monotone order." is the fourth. **The guarantee is a character index on every glyph**, HBBUF:47, with the collapse rule at HBBUF:53, so glyph-to-character is a total function and character-to-glyph is a range. The default merges marks into their base and merges again on demand, HBBUF:432 "characters are merged into the cluster of the base character that precedes them." and HBBUF:433 "There is also cluster merging every time the clusters will otherwise become non-monotone.". The granular level trades ordering for resolution, HBBUF:443 "the cluster values are not merged into monotone order. This is the most granular", and HarfBuzz tells new clients to leave the default, HBBUF:457 "instead of the default.". **Bearing on `text-tools/P4`**: the address that survives shaping is a character index into the input, and the shaper returns it on every glyph, so shaping does not destroy an address; what it destroys is one-to-one-ness, and at the default level it destroys the distinction between a base and its marks. Cluster values are recomputed by each call, so they address a position rather than an identity, which is `FD-31`'s finding reached from the shaper's side. A flag is a cluster property after HBOTSHAPE:1111, so a per-character address cannot carry a per-glyph flag. **7. TOTALITY, AND THE FUEL.** Every iteration in HarfBuzz is bounded and the bounds live in one 232-line file. Buffer growth is bounded in the input, HBLIMITS:32 "#define HB_BUFFER_MAX_LEN_FACTOR 256" with a floor at HBLIMITS:35 "#define HB_BUFFER_MAX_LEN_MIN 65536". **Work is bounded in the input**, HBLIMITS:42 "#define HB_BUFFER_MAX_OPS_FACTOR 4096" with the same floor at HBLIMITS:45 "#define HB_BUFFER_MAX_OPS_MIN 65536". Recursion is bounded, HBLIMITS:53 "#define HB_MAX_NESTING_LEVEL 64". Match width is bounded, HBLIMITS:58 "#define HB_MAX_CONTEXT_LENGTH 64", as is a syllable, HBLIMITS:62 "#define HB_MAX_SYLLABLE_LENGTH 64". Repeated application is bounded with the reason stated, HBLIMITS:67 "The maximum number of times a lookup can be applied during shaping." at HBLIMITS:72 "#define HB_CLOSURE_MAX_STAGES 12", and visits are capped at HBLIMITS:92 "#define HB_MAX_LOOKUP_VISIT_COUNT 35000". When the length is unknown the cap is a constant, HBLIMITS:38 "#define HB_BUFFER_MAX_LEN_DEFAULT 0x3FFFFFFF /* Shaping more than a billion chars? Let us know! */". The enforcement sites are two. The shaping apply context initializes from the constant, HBGSUBGPOS:1139 "unsigned int nesting_level_left = HB_MAX_NESTING_LEVEL;", and refuses at zero, HBGSUBGPOS:1103 "if (unlikely (nesting_level_left == 0))". The buffer spends the operation budget on every flag-setting span, HBBUFHH:657 "max_ops -= end - start;", and the exhaustion policy is declared outright, HBLIMITS:168 "Once a budget is exhausted, further work" plus HBLIMITS:169 "is skipped best-effort.". **So shaping over an arbitrary font file is expressible as a total function of the input length: at most 4,096n operations producing at most 256n glyphs at recursion depth at most 64, with a floor of 65,536 for short inputs. That is fuel rather than structure, and it is exactly the shape `PRINCIPLES.md:66` calls an over-approximate bound.** The two Rust ports are stricter on malformed input than the C++ original, RBREADME:31 "Malformed fonts will cause an error. HarfBuzz uses fallback/dummy shaper in this case." and HARFRUST:39 "Malformed fonts will cause an error.". **stb_truetype is at the other end and says so**: STBTT:6 "NO SECURITY GUARANTEE -- DO NOT USE THIS ON UNTRUSTED FONT FILES", STBTT:8 "This library does no range checking of the offsets found in the file," and STBTT:9 "meaning an attacker can use it to read arbitrary memory.", with STBTT:22 "crashproof on bad data" still on its todo list. So the cheapest tier in the survey is also the one with no bound at all, and the tier ladder and the safety ladder run in opposite directions. **8. `T2`'S CLAIM ABOUT RUSTYBUZZ, TESTED. BOTH CLAUSES FAIL.** "an incremental port": RBREADME:9 "is a complete [" harfbuzz shaping algorithm port, RBREADME:75 "Since the port is finished, there is not much to do other than syncing it with" new releases, and RBREADME:1 "This project is not developed further, unmaintained, and archived." recommends HarfRust instead. "strictly an OpenType shaper": the module list declares six Apple Advanced Typography modules, RBMOD:26 "mod aat_layout_kerx_table;" and RBMOD:27 "mod aat_layout_morx_table;" among them, measured at 2,279 lines, beside RBMOD:32 "mod kerning;" for the legacy table and RBMOD:42 "mod ot_shape_fallback;" for the no-GPOS path. **Measured size at commit `9faca96` dated 2026-07-26: 74 `.rs` files under `src/`, 29,232 lines, of which 28,143 sit under `src/hb/`; 23,748 non-blank non-comment lines, which lands on RBREADME:57 "In the end, we still have around 23 KLOC. While harfbuzz is around 80 KLOC.", and 14,141 once the README's own generated-table exclusions are applied against its own RBREADME:71 "Which gives us around 17 KLOC, which is still a lot.".** Conformance and speed as the project states them: RBREADME:21 "rustybuzz passes nearly all of harfbuzz shaping tests (2221 out of 2252 to be more precise)" and RBREADME:41 "We're 1.5-2x slower than harfbuzz." against RBREADME:12 "Matches `harfbuzz` v10.1.0.". **The live successor is HarfRust**, HARFRUST:20 "Matches HarfBuzz [" v14.3.1, HARFRUST:44 "HarfRust is less than 25% slower than HarfBuzz on most common fonts.", measured at 73 `.rs` files and 38,666 lines in `harfrust/src` at commit `41c79c8` dated 2026-09-17 and cloned 2026-09-18, 31,695 non-blank non-comment. So a from-scratch shaper that reaches HarfBuzz parity costs between 23 and 32 thousand lines by two independent measurements, and 28.6% of that is the complex-script tier. **9. SCRIPT COMPLEXITY TIERS. THE RECORD DOES CLASSIFY.** HarfBuzz's own dispatch is the classification. The shaper list is declared in one place and holds eleven entries, HBSHAPERHH:52 "#define HB_OT_SHAPERS_IMPLEMENT_SHAPERS" through HBSHAPERHH:63 "HB_OT_SHAPER_IMPLEMENT (use)" with HBSHAPERHH:64 "Add new shapers here; keep sorted.": nine script-specific shapers, the default, and a degenerate one at HBSHAPERHH:55 "HB_OT_SHAPER_IMPLEMENT (dumber)". The dispatch is a switch over scripts **naming 109 of them and routing them to those nine, with every script it does not name falling to the default shaper**. Of the 109, 91 sit in one arm that forks on the font's own script tag between the default shaper and the Universal Shaping Engine. The comment above that fork states the floor in the implementer's words: HBSHAPERHH:413 "Note that for some simple scripts, there may not be *any*" and HBSHAPERHH:414 "GSUB/GPOS needed, so there may be no scripts found!". The nine non-default buckets are Arabic with Syriac, Thai with Lao, Hangul, Hebrew, nine Indic scripts, Khmer, Myanmar, a Zawgyi variant, and the Universal Shaping Engine. Microsoft draws the same line by definition at MSSTDSCR:740 and MSSTDSCR:752. A third-party specification lists the same nine models plus OTSDINDEX:41 "All non-complex scripts" for the default and OTSDINDEX:38 "All complex scripts that are not handled by a dedicated" model for the engine, **and disclaims itself**, OTSDINDEX:11 "NONE of the documents you currently see here are complete", so it corroborates without carrying weight. Two shipped shapers state their own coverage in the same vocabulary: SWASH:66 "Full support for OpenType advanced typography (GSUB/GPOS)" beside SWASH:71 "Implementation of the Universal Shaping Engine for complex scripts such as Devanagari" and SWASH:73 "Basic shaping support: ligatures, marks, kerning, etc.", with cluster identity preserved at SWASH:78 "Shaper output is structured by cluster including original source ranges"; and Allsorts, which was built beside the specification just quoted, ALLSORTS:33 "The Allsorts shaping engine was developed in conjunction with [a specification", and whose only declared gap is ALLSORTS:71 "Unicode normalisation.". **10. WHAT THE RECORD DOES NOT SETTLE.** Five things. ### FD-39 the record calls the property resolution independence and the family path rendering, no surveyed technique holds a border exact at unbounded zoom, each one publishes its own bound, Skia drops antialiasing outright once a path spans 8192 device pixels, and the single mechanism any surveyed renderer uses to keep a border exact while the zoom changes is re-deriving the flattening tolerance in device pixels each frame

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question was posed from a description with no answer set: the author asked for "those things where you can continuously zoom into a border and it stays ridiculously exact" and added only "its something to do with vectors". Identify what that names in the literature and the practitioner record, then report the set of approaches that deliver it, each one's storage, arithmetic, failure condition, CPU viability and primitive list, against `FD-33`'s two-rectangle surface floor and the closed sixteen-op integer `Op` sum at `lib/prelude/prelude.chiral:37-39`. **Fifteen pins added, nine raw and six transcribed from PDF or from a JSON issue body; six earlier pins reused (`FTGRAYS`, `SKANTIPATH`, `SKSCANPRIV`, `CAIROFIXP`, `CAIROFIXT`, `VELLOARCH`). The answer: the property's name in the record is resolution independence, the family's name is path rendering, the surveyed set splits four ways by when sampling happens and what gets sampled, and every one of the four publishes a condition under which it stops being exact. The tree's border is reachable in the sixteen integer ops with no float type, and the price is an error bound of 1/256 of a pixel in geometry and 1/256 in coverage plus a flattening residual, which is the price FreeType and Skia both already pay in shipped code.**
- measured: **1. WHAT THE AUTHOR IS DESCRIBING, NAMED AS THE RECORD NAMES IT.** The property has one name across the survey and it is **resolution independence**; the technique family that carries it has one name and it is **path rendering**. The name and the family arrive together in the `NV_path_rendering` overview, which introduces path rendering and then says it is NVPATHREND:74 "but rather a standard part of most resolution-independent 2D rendering" systems, listing Flash, PDF, Silverlight, SVG, Java 2D, TrueType fonts, PostScript, Quartz 2D, XPS and OpenVG. The mechanism in one sentence, from the same source: NVPATHREND:95 "rendering also allows path segments to be specified by Bezier (cubic" or quadratic) curves or partial elliptical arcs, which is what lets a border be a curve at every scale instead of a stored picture of a curve. Loop and Blinn name the property in the same words and put the reason in the method: LOOPBLINNGG:183 "rendering these spline curves directly in terms of their mathematical descriptions, so that they are resolution" independent, and their result is LOOPBLINNGG:1024 "footprint, and the resulting image is resolution independent." Lengyel's shipped library uses the phrase as its product claim, SLUGLIB:199 "technology. Complex diagrams and vector drawings can be rendered at blazingly fast speeds directly on the GPU with" total resolution independence. **The author's phrase maps onto the family cleanly: what stays exact under zoom is a border whose description reaches the rasterizer as a curve, and what is re-run at every zoom level is the rasterization.** The unprompted arrival of two texture-side papers under the same phrase is the first warning in the record: NVIDIA's Infinite Resolution Textures claims IRTEX:84 "provides a resolution-independent image representation capable of billions of texels per second on a mid-range graphics card." for a method whose input is a photograph, and Nehab and Hoppe say RAVG:2925 "cell-specialized graphics allow resolution-independent rendering)." for a lattice of cached per-cell encodings. **The phrase is used for both the family that keeps the curve and the family that caches a sampling of it.**

  **2. THE SET, AND THE AXIS THE SOURCES THEMSELVES DRAW.** Searching from the description reached eight approaches. The axis the sources draw between them is **when the shape gets sampled, and what the sample is of**. Chlumský's thesis draws that axis explicitly and puts his own method on the losing side of it: an SDF grid has MSDFTHESIS:205 "with the signed distances specified only at a finite number of discrete points," MSDFTHESIS:206 "and therefore not exact." while his §1.3.1.3 is headed exact vector rendering and describes MSDFTHESIS:381 "ility of using programmable shaders to draw parametric curves exactly. This" method, of which he says MSDFTHESIS:383 "It is an exact method, and therefore provides higher quality than distance" fields. Four positions result. **(a) Sampled at authoring time into a stored field**: signed distance fields, multi-channel SDF, Infinite Resolution Textures, GLyphy's arc encoding, and the RAVG lattice. **(b) Point-sampled at render time on the device grid**: `NV_path_rendering` stencil-and-cover, and the supersampling rasterizers. **(c) Area-integrated at render time in device space**: FreeType `grays`, Skia's analytic antialiasing, `font-rs`, Vello. **(d) Implicit function evaluated at render time**: Loop-Blinn, Slug. Kilgard puts (b) against (c) as a design argument and comes out against (c): the extension NVPATHREND:7375 "does it even attempt, to compute or approximate a path's area" NVPATHREND:7376 "coverage with respect to a pixel.  For practical reasons, such" NVPATHREND:7377 "analytical computations are inevitably approximations for" arbitrary paths and are difficult to make robust, and NVPATHREND:7380 "Point sampling of path object rasterization can offer more" robustness and precision. **Both sides of that argument are in the record and the record does not settle it.**

  **3. PER FAMILY: WHAT IS STORED, WHAT IS COMPUTED, AND THE CONDITION THAT ENDS THE EXACTNESS.**

  **SDF (Green, Valve 2007).** Stores GREENSDF:104 "We chose to implement a simple uniformly-sampled signed-" distance field in an 8-bit channel; the runtime computes a threshold against a bilinear fetch, where GREENSDF:142 "A texel value of 0.5 represents the exact position of the edge and," hence 0.5 is the alpha test. What is reconstructed is stated as an approximation by its own author: the distance between GREENSDF:109 "a sub-texel and a piecewise-linear approximation of the true high-" GREENSDF:110 "resolution image. While this representation is limited in terms of" the topology of features it can represent. The input is a raster and the method GREENSDF:98 "not require that input images be provided in a vector form." **Two failure conditions, both published.** Corners: GREENSDF:227 "edges using a single signed distance" rounds off corners as the GREENSDF:228 "resolution of the distance field decreases". Edge shape under magnification: the alpha-tested result is GREENSDF:151 "resolution (albeit, aliased) linear edges, free of the false curved con-" tours, so the border you zoom into is the piecewise-linear zero set of the interpolant and not the glyph outline. Chlumský adds the resolution condition and the scale at which it bites: the method MSDFTHESIS:349 "cannot capture features smaller than the resolution of the SDF's grid, and" thin strokes are a problem too, and quality holds only if the field is large in proportion to the target size, in which case the result is almost indistin- MSDFTHESIS:339 "guishable from exact methods. Otherwise, a larger SDF can be used."

  **MSDF (Chlumský 2015, `msdfgen`).** Stores three distance channels; the runtime adds one operation, MSDFGEN:147 "The only additional operation is computing the **median** of the three channels inside the fragment shader,". Corners become better and do not become exact: the README claims the ability MSDFGEN:9 "to reproduce sharp corners almost perfectly by utilizing all three color channels." and the thesis says the MSDFTHESIS:5165 "improved method is capable of near-perfect reconstruction of the shape's" corners. **Three published failure conditions.** Field resolution against stroke width: MSDFTHESIS:5211 "If a stroke is thinner than about two cells of the distance field grid across," it cannot be encoded properly and will probably be heavily distorted. A channel-splitting artifact specific to the multi-channel trick: MSDFTHESIS:2256 "Since the distance field representation isn't exact, it can be disturbed by" nearby edges in such a way that the border between the uncorrelated quadrants will be shifted slightly differently for each colour channel. And a minification floor, stated numerically in the shader contract: the screen-pixel range MSDFGEN:198 "must never be lower than 1. If it is lower than 2, there is a high probability that the anti-aliasing will fail" and the field should be regenerated wider. **The 8-bit storage is a modelled loss the generator can simulate**, MSDFGEN:112 "on the distance field beforehand to simulate the standard 8 bits/channel image format."

  **Loop-Blinn.** Stores control points and per-vertex texture coordinates; the shader evaluates an implicit equation for the inside test. The exactness is real, conditional, and confined to the inside test. The condition is the number type: the paper assumes LOOPBLINNGG:397 "simplify curve classification. Our second assumption is that the control point coordinates are exact" LOOPBLINNGG:398 "floating-point numbers. This assumption is not strictly necessary, but we can avoid floating-point round-off" error by making it, and on that assumption, with LOOPBLINNGG:556 "exact floating-point coordinates, the classification given in Table 25-1 can" be done exactly, because the discriminant and all LOOPBLINNGG:558 "intermediate variables can be derived from exact floating representations." **The antialiasing is an approximation and the authors say so**: LOOPBLINNGG:872 "We present an approach to antialiasing in the pixel shader based on a signed distance approximation to a curve" boundary, and where the straight edge LOOPBLINNGG:876 "of a triangle is the boundary, this scheme breaks down. Fortunately, this is exactly the case that is handled by" hardware multisample antialiasing. So Loop-Blinn's border exactness rests on a sampled coverage after all, either from a distance approximation or from MSAA. A second condition is geometric: LOOPBLINNGG:739 "A rendering artifact will occur if one of the double point parameters lies in the interval" of the curve, fixed by subdividing the loop curve at the double point. Derivatives for the distance estimate are exact and cost arithmetic, LOOPBLINNGG:942 "additional math operations, we can get exact derivatives by applying the chain rule to our shader equations".

  **Stencil-and-cover (`NV_path_rendering`, Kilgard).** Stores the path; computes per-sample inside tests into the stencil buffer. Its exactness claim is precise and bounded by the sample count: coverage NVPATHREND:7352 "by stenciling path objects should be accurate to the sample" resolution, and with N samples per pixel that NVPATHREND:7356 "means that there are N+1 possible coverage weightings of a given" NVPATHREND:7357 "path with respect to that pixel, assuming a single "stencil, then" cover step. **The magnification condition is a hardware limit, stated as one**: NVPATHREND:7400 "This extension implicitly assumes that GPUs have some maximum" sample location precision while rasterizing, an artifact of subpixel precision, and developers NVPATHREND:7404 "should not expect any additional sampling precision beyond this" limit, with rendering larger and downsampling given as the only way past it. **Strokes carry a separate, numbered approximation**: exact stroke sweep along cubics and rational quadratics is NVPATHREND:3977 "intractable for real-time rendering so an approximation is required", governed by a stroke approximation bound whose initial value NVPATHREND:3987 "of /sab/ when a path is created is 0.2", meaning samples within 80% of the stroke width are guaranteed and the remaining 20% is implementation licence.

  **Slug (Lengyel).** Stores the outline: SLUGLIB:188 "crisp text at any scale or from any perspective. There are no precomputed texture images or signed distance fields." and SLUGLIB:329 "One texture holds all of the B" ezier curve data. Computes coverage per pixel from that data, SLUGLIB:242 "is covered by the glyph using the original B" ezier curve data stored in the font, so that SLUGLIB:243 "involved, the result is a sharp outline at all resolutions with no faceting or blurring." **The strongest exactness claim in the survey is here and it is a vendor claim with no published method**: it is SLUGLIB:191 "glyphs with no artifacts under both magnification and minification." The algorithm is described on the site as a breakthrough mathematical algorithm and the record reachable from this sandbox does not contain it. **This row does not confirm or refute Slug's claim.**

  **Sampled-field texture methods that arrived unprompted.** Infinite Resolution Textures stores extracted curved silhouettes beside the original raster and IRTEX:82 "silhouette edges from the underlying images. These edges are used to adjust the texture coordinates of the requested samples" during magnification; it IRTEX:80 "We propose a new texture sampling approach that preserves crisp silhouette edges when magnifying during close-up viewing, and" benefits from prefiltering when minifying. Its own limitations section names the condition: IRTEX:2173 "IRT is only as good as the edge detection algorithm it uses. Underde-" tected edges give wrong results, and the honest consequence is that a crisp border carries no new detail, the IRT eye looks better IRTEX:2194 "than the bilinearly interpolated one, but individual eyelashes are not" visible. RAVG stores a lattice in RAVG:26 "which each cell contains a variable-length encoding of the" primitives it overlaps and antialiases by sampling, RAVG:31 "Most importantly, we perform both prefiltering and supersampling" per pixel-shader invocation, with RAVG:95 "(2) supersampling across primitives. Although supersampling" named as its own inter-primitive mechanism. GLyphy is in the record only through Chlumský, who describes it as approximating the MSDFTHESIS:394 "geometry using circular arcs, and also stores their definitions as texture data." and says MSDFTHESIS:395 "All of these methods offer higher quality than distance fields, however," they need complex shader work and are rarely used.

  **Analytic area coverage, which is the CPU lineage.** One family, four shipped members, one shared architecture and one shared limit. FreeType states both halves in its own header: it is FTGRAYS:80 "A perfect anti-aliaser, i.e., it computes the _exact_ coverage on" each pixel cell by straight segments, and FTGRAYS:61 "Bézier segments are flattened by splitting them until their deviation" FTGRAYS:62 "from straight line becomes much smaller than a pixel.  Therefore, the" FTGRAYS:63 "pixel coverage by a Bézier curve is calculated approximately." Skia's analytic path states the same two halves in its own header comment: SKAAAPATH:36 "algorithm. We consider a path as a collection of line segments, as" SKAAAPATH:37 "quadratic/cubic curves are converted to small line segments." is the first, and it generates ground- SKAAAPATH:84 "truth coverages analytically. It is also faster because it has much fewer" unnecessary scan lines is the second, by computing SKAAAPATH:56 "the coverage of this horizontal strip of our path on each pixel. This can be" done from trapezoids. `font-rs` and Vello accumulate signed area per cell and prefix-sum the row; Vello states the integral outright, VELLOSTRIP:589 "        // The fractional area coverage of a pixel is the integral of the winding within it." with the per-pixel shape being a trapezoid, VELLOSTRIP:594 "        // itself, the area to the right of the line segment forms a trapezoid (or a triangle in" the degenerate case, and the carry to the right being VELLOSTRIP:593 "        // accumulated and added to the area coverage of pixels to the right. Within the pixel". **The condition that ends the exactness in this family is the flattening tolerance, and it is a number.** Vello: VELLOFLAT:15 "// The current tolerance is set to 0.25. Since `sqrt` doesn't work in const contexts, we instead" hardcode the square, VELLOFLAT:17 "pub(crate) const SQRT_TOL: f64 = 0.5;". `font-rs`: a quad is drawn as a line when FONTRSRAST:111 "        if devsq < 0.333 {" and otherwise subdivided FONTRSRAST:116 "        let n = 1 + (tol * (devx * devx + devy * devy)).sqrt().sqrt().floor() as usize;" times. FreeType: conics split while FTGRAYS:1073 "} while ( dx > ONE_PIXEL / 4 );" holds, with FTGRAYS:1064 "/* We can calculate the number of necessary segments because    */" each bisection reducing deviation four-fold and the count taken as FTGRAYS:1074 "count = 0x10000U >> shift;", and cubics split while FTGRAYS:1319 "if ( FT_ABS( 2 * arc[0].x - 3 * arc[1].x + arc[3].x ) > ONE_PIXEL / 2 ||" any of four trisection distances exceeds half a pixel, because FTGRAYS:1317 "chord trisection points and the vanishing distances below" indicate flatness.

  **4. THE MECHANISM THAT ACTUALLY DELIVERS THE AUTHOR'S PROPERTY, AND IT IS ONE LINE OF CODE.** A flattening tolerance is only a resolution-independence mechanism if it is expressed in the pixels you are about to draw. Vello divides it by the transform scale before flattening: VELLOFLAT:231 "    // TODO: Temporary hack to ensure that strokes are scaled properly by the transform." then VELLOFLAT:232 "    let tolerance = TOL" VELLOFLAT:233 "        / affine.as_coeffs()[0]" `.abs().max(affine.as_coeffs()[3].abs()).max(1.)`. **That is the whole answer to "why does it stay exact as I zoom": the polyline is regenerated at every zoom level against a device-pixel error budget, so the residual stays a quarter of a pixel at 1x and at 10,000x.** Every family in the survey that caches a scale-dependent intermediate loses the property at a computable zoom, and the four positions in §2 are exactly the four choices of what to cache: a field (a), a sample grid (b), nothing (c), nothing (d).

  **5. THE ARITHMETIC, THE PRECISION, AND WHERE FIXED POINT SHIPS.** **Float is required by (a) and (d) and by one of the two CPU implementations of (c), and (c) in general does without it, because two shipped rasterizers do (c) in integers.** SDF and MSDF need a float shader: `smoothstep`, screen-space derivatives, `median`, `clamp` and `mix`, with generation into a floating-point bitmap. Loop-Blinn's exactness is *defined* on IEEE floats, LOOPBLINNGG:398, and the chain-rule derivatives at LOOPBLINNGG:942 are float multiplies and divides. `NV_path_rendering` needs no application arithmetic at all and pushes everything into fixed-function sample tests. **`font-rs` is float**: the accumulation buffer is FONTRSRAST:27 "    a: Vec<f32>," fed by a slope FONTRSRAST:54 "        let dxdy = (p1.x - p0.x) / (p1.y - p0.y);" and per-pixel areas FONTRSRAST:81 "        let a0 = 0.5 * s * (1.0 - x0f) * (1.0 - x0f);", closed by FONTRSRAST:143 "        accumulate(&self.a[0..self.w * self.h])" whose scalar body at FONTRSACC:69 "#[cfg(not(feature = "sse"))]" is a running f32 sum clamped to 1.0 and truncated to `u8`, and whose fast path at FONTRSACC:29 "#[cfg(feature = "sse")]" is a hand-written SSE prefix sum starting FONTRSACC:42 "        let mut offset = _mm_setzero_ps();". **Vello CPU is float and depends on IEEE special values**: coverage is accumulated in `f32x4` against VELLOSTRIP:455 "                    let p2 = f32x4::splat(s, 255.0);", it re-seeds the accumulator because of VELLOSTRIP:556 "                // Note: this fill is mathematically not necessary. It provides a way to reduce" VELLOSTRIP:557 "                // accumulation of float rounding errors.", its slope path relies on the platform-specific NaN behaviour of `max`, VELLOSTRIP:670 "            // use the relaxed version. If this ever breaks, tests should fail loudly, because NaNs" happen a lot here, and a NaN in a path is handled by discarding the path, VELLOFLAT:211 "    // A path that contains NaN is ill-defined, so ignore it." **FreeType `grays` is integer and says so**: it is a different implementation from Levien's libart, which FTGRAYS:50 "It is based on ideas that I initially found in Raph Levien's" excellent library, and unlike it, FTGRAYS:59 "use floating point values." is what it does not do. **Skia's analytic antialiasing is integer too, in `SkFixed` 16.16**, and this is the finding the record did not previously carry: SKAAAPATH:535 "static SkAlpha trapezoid_to_alpha(SkFixed l1, SkFixed l2) {" computes SKAAAPATH:537 "    SkFixed area = (l1 + l2) / 2;" and returns `area >> 8`, one add and two shifts. **Skia names two of its own approximations inside the analytic path.** The triangle case is SKAAAPATH:549 "    // Approximating..." and replaces a wide multiply with SKAAAPATH:551 "    SkFixed area = (a >> 11) * (a >> 11) * (b >> 11);", discarding eleven low bits of each operand. Edge crossings are resolved by a routine that SKAAAPATH:578 "approximate (very coarsely) the x coordinate of the intersection." **So fixed point carries coverage in two shipped renderers, and what it gives up is stated by both: a quantised geometry grid, a quantised coverage byte, and in Skia's case a five-bit-per-operand product for one of four cases.** Cairo's coordinate side is the third fixed-point data point already pinned: CAIROFIXT:56 "#define CAIRO_FIXED_BITS	32" with CAIROFIXT:62 "#define CAIRO_FIXED_FRAC_BITS	8", a 24.8 grid whose quantisation is stated as CAIROFIXP:61 "#define CAIRO_FIXED_ERROR_DOUBLE (1. / (2 * CAIRO_FIXED_ONE_DOUBLE))", one half of 1/256.

  **6. `FTGRAYS` AT `PIXEL_BITS 8`, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL BOUND `FD-34` LEFT OPEN.** The subpixel grid is FTGRAYS:332 "#define PIXEL_BITS  8" giving FTGRAYS:334 "#define ONE_PIXEL       ( 1 << PIXEL_BITS )", so geometry is quantised to 1/256 of a pixel per axis. Coverage is derived from the accumulated cell area by FTGRAYS:410 "coverage = (int)( area >> ( PIXEL_BITS * 2 + 1 - 8 ) ); \" which is `area >> 9`; a fully covered cell holds `2 * 256 * 256` = 131,072, and 131,072 >> 9 is 256, clamped to 255, so **the coverage quantum is 1/256 of a pixel's area and the rounding is truncation toward zero**. Accumulation is two integer updates, FTGRAYS:533 "ras.cell->area  = ADD_INT( ras.cell->area, (a) * (TArea)(b) )" beside the winding delta. **Three error sources, each with its own character.** (i) The 1/256 geometry grid and the 1/256 coverage quantum, both exact-by-construction quantisations. (ii) Division replaced by reciprocal multiply-shift, where the source states the requirement and no residual: FTGRAYS:393 "the shift magnitude should be at least PIXEL_BITS wider than the  */" divisors to provide sufficient accuracy. (iii) Per-scanline division remainders, which are **compensated rather than dropped**: FTGRAYS:351 "the remainder is always positive.  We use the remainder to keep   */" track of accumulating errors and compensate for them, so error along a slanted edge does not accumulate. **Curve residual is separate and larger than any of the three**: the conic threshold at FTGRAYS:1073 is a second difference of `ONE_PIXEL / 4` = 64 subpixel units and the cubic threshold at FTGRAYS:1319 is `ONE_PIXEL / 2` = 128, both stated as subpixel thresholds and neither converted to a proven deviation bound in the source. **`FD-34`'s open question is therefore answered from the opposite direction: `grays` does not argue for 1/256 as a denominator, it argues that a coverage rasterizer can be built with no float type at all, and 1/256 is the resolution at which it chose to stop.** The 7% figure elsewhere in that file belongs to `FT_HYPOT`, which is defined once at FTGRAYS:130 and used nowhere in the file; **it does not bear on coverage and must not be cited as though it did.**

  **7. CPU OR GPU, AND THE CPU COST.** GPU-only, with no CPU meaning: SDF and MSDF shading (a fragment shader with derivatives is the method), Loop-Blinn (a pixel shader per control triangle), stencil-and-cover (a stencil buffer with multisample resolution), Slug (two textures bound to a glyph shader), RAVG (per-cell streams interpreted in a pixel shader), IRT (a texture-coordinate adjustment inside a sampler). SDF and MSDF *generation* is CPU work and it is the expensive half: Green's generator brute-force searches a neighbourhood per output texel from a 4096x4096 input for a 64x64 field. **CPU-viable, and shipping on CPUs today: the whole of family (c).** Cost per family member, as the sources describe it: `grays` walks the outline once and keeps a linked list of touched cells, needing no intermediate bitmap; Skia's analytic path uses non-uniform scanlines at path vertices and crossings, about `3 + H` scanlines for a triangle against `4H` for its 16x supersampling predecessor; `font-rs` writes into a dense `w * h + 4` float buffer and closes with one prefix sum; Vello's CPU path does the same over 4-wide SIMD strips. **The tree has neither a GPU path nor SIMD**: zero hits for SIMD or xmm across the prelude and the x64 backend, re-verified 2026-09-18, so the SIMD prefix sums in `FONTRSACC` and `VELLOSTRIP` are performance variants of a scalar loop the tree can write.

  **8. AGAINST `FD-33`'s TWO RECTANGLE PRIMITIVES.** `FD-33` measured the floor as fill-a-rectangle-with-one-colour and composite-a-coverage-rectangle-against-one-colour. **Family (c) fits that floor exactly and needs no third primitive.** The coverage rectangle is one pixel wide for an edge span and arbitrarily wide for an interior span, which is what every member emits: `grays` calls a span callback, Skia blits alpha runs, `font-rs` and Vello hand out a byte per pixel. `FD-37` already established that source-over with a coverage mask is integer-reachable at ±1 LSB in the sixteen ops, so **the composite half of the floor is priced and the fill half is trivial.** Families (a), (b) and (d) do not fit: (a) needs a bilinear sample of a stored field, which is a third primitive (sample-a-two-dimensional-field-with-bilinear-interpolation) plus a float multiply-add chain; (b) needs a per-sample stencil buffer, which is a fourth (test-and-update-a-per-sample-mask); (d) needs per-pixel evaluation of an implicit polynomial over interpolated coordinates, which is a fifth (evaluate-an-implicit-function-at-a-pixel-centre) and is the one that hard-requires a float type. **What family (c) adds above the two rectangle primitives never writes a pixel.** It needs: a signed-area accumulation buffer of one integer per pixel of the current band; a prefix sum along each row; curve subdivision, which in `grays` is integer midpoint splitting with a shift-based counter; and a fixed-point coordinate type. All four stay off the surface, and all four are expressible in the sixteen ops.

  **9. CONFLATION, WHICH IS THE ONE FAILURE FAMILY (c) HAS AND (b) DOES NOT.** Exact per-shape coverage composited with Porter-Duff leaves a visible seam where two shapes abut. Vello's own issue states the architecture and the consequence in one sentence: VELLOCONF:1 "The current piet-gpu rendering strategy uses exact-area pixel coverage calculations to derive an antialiased alpha mask" followed by Porter-Duff compositing, susceptible to conflation artifacts, quoting Kilgard: VELLOCONF:1 "Conflation is particularly noticeable when two opaque paths exactly seam at a shared boundary." **It happens inside one path too, with a reproducing input**: the SVG path `M0 0L0 4 4 4 0 0 4 0 4 4z` VELLOCONF:3 "can render with a gap along the diagonal, as the winding number is of opposite signs on the lower and upper triangles". Kilgard's spec states the same mechanism from the other side and uses it to justify separating coverage from opacity: NVPATHREND:7364 "Conflating the two leads to coverage" bleeding at what should be sharp, though transparent, edges and corners. **The surveyed cure is to give up exactness**: academic renderers VELLOCONF:7 "deal with conflation artifacts by doing some form of supersampling", and `NV_path_rendering` uses hardware MSAA and so is VELLOCONF:7 "limited by the sampling factor provided by the hardware". Levien records that the alpha-mask model is kept anyway because the web mandates it, the artifacts being LEVIENCLIP:152 "which are not fully addressed by the alpha-channel compositing approach to clipping" and the approach remaining standard because the W3C compositing spec and the canvas drawing model require it.

  **10. THE HARDEST NUMBER IN THE SURVEY, AND IT IS A ZOOM THRESHOLD IN SHIPPED CODE.** SKANTIPATH:59 "void SkScan::AntiFillPath(const SkPathRaw& path, const SkRegion& origClip," is Skia's antialiased fill entry point, and its body ends by calling the analytic rasterizer of §3, SKANTIPATH:130 "    SkScan::AAAFillPath(path, blitter, ir, clipRgn->getBounds(), forceRLE);". **Before it gets there it passes a size guard, and the guard drops antialiasing entirely.** SKANTIPATH:74 "    // If the intersection of the path bounds and the clip bounds" SKANTIPATH:75 "will overflow 32767 when << by SHIFT, we can't supersample," is the comment, SKANTIPATH:87 "    if (rect_overflows_short_shift(clippedIR, SK_SUPERSAMPLE_SHIFT)) {" is the test, and SKANTIPATH:88 "        SkScan::FillPath(path, origClip, blitter);" is the non-antialiased fallback it takes. The shift is SKSCANPRIV:16 "#define SK_SUPERSAMPLE_SHIFT    2" under a comment that already hedges, SKSCANPRIV:15 "// controls how much we super-sample (when we use that scan convertion)". The threshold is asserted twice: SKANTIPATH:41 "static_assert(!overflows_short_shift(8191, SK_SUPERSAMPLE_SHIFT));" and SKANTIPATH:42 "static_assert(overflows_short_shift(8192, SK_SUPERSAMPLE_SHIFT));" **So in Skia, a path whose device-space extent reaches 8192 pixels loses its antialiased border outright, and the guard that does it is named after a supersampling rasterizer while the code past it calls the analytic one.** A second limit sits below it and clamps the clip instead of the path, SKANTIPATH:101 "        static const int32_t kMaxClipCoord = 32767;". **That is the concrete shape of the answer to the author's question: the border does not degrade gradually, it reaches a coded limit and changes behaviour.** Nothing in the survey suggests the limit is inherent to analytic coverage; it is a 16-bit run index, stated as one at SKANTIPATH:75.

  **11. TEXT AND GENERAL PATHS.** Glyph-only in the survey: Slug's core product, and the MSDF atlas workflow. Both, and stated as both: `NV_path_rendering` covers glyph ranges beside arbitrary paths; Loop-Blinn's chapter renders text and vector art from the same triangles; Slug says it was originally designed only to render text and SLUGLIB:199 "technology. Complex diagrams and vector drawings can be rendered at blazingly fast speeds directly on the GPU with" total resolution independence. Family (c) is path-general throughout: `grays` rasterizes `FT_Outline`, Skia's analytic path takes an `SkPath`, Vello and `font-rs` take a path. **Text is a path in family (c), and glyph outlines are already quadratics in the font file, so the tree gains no separate text rasterizer from this.**

  **WHAT THE RECORD DOES NOT SETTLE.** Six things. **(i) Slug's exactness claim cannot be checked.** The claim is published, SLUGLIB:191, and the method stays unpublished; this row neither confirms nor refutes it. **(ii) No surveyed source gives a proven deviation bound for a flattening threshold.** FreeType states thresholds in subpixel units, Vello states a tolerance of 0.25, `font-rs` states `0.333` and a fourth-root subdivision count, and no source in the survey derives the resulting maximum distance from the true curve. **(iii) `FT_UDIV`'s error is unquantified.** The source states the shift requirement, FTGRAYS:393, and states no residual bound; this run left unmeasured whether a 32-bit truncated reciprocal introduces a coverage LSB. **(iv) Kilgard's claim that analytic coverage is inevitably approximate for arbitrary paths, NVPATHREND:7377, is asserted without a counter-example in the spec, and no surveyed source rebuts it.** Family (c) exists and ships, which makes the claim narrower than it reads, and the record does not say which paths he meant. **(v) The Chlumský thesis is pinned from a GitHub mirror of the PDF**; the CTU `dspace` original was reachable at roughly 200 KB per 100 s and could not be pulled inside this run. **(vi) No surveyed source states an integer coverage width above 8 bits for a CPU rasterizer**, so whether 1/65536 coverage buys anything measurable over 1/256 is unanswered, matching `FD-34`'s finding that three projects made the denominator a type parameter and none argued a value.

  **WHAT THE RECORD SUPPORTS FOR THE AUTHOR'S PROPERTY, AND THE COMPLETE BUILD LIST.** **Analytic area coverage in fixed point, over a path re-flattened per frame against a device-pixel tolerance.** It is the only family in the survey that is CPU-viable with no GPU, fits `FD-33`'s two rectangle primitives with no third drawing primitive, needs no float type, and has two independent shipped proofs in integers, FreeType `grays` and Skia's `SkScan_AAAPath`. The build list, in full: **(1)** a fixed-point coordinate type, 24.8 following cairo or 26.6 following FreeType's input, with the subpixel denominator a type parameter per `FD-34`; **(2)** a signed-area cell accumulator, one integer per pixel of the active band, updated by the two adds at FTGRAYS:533; **(3)** a row prefix sum with a truncating clamp to the coverage byte; **(4)** integer curve subdivision by midpoint splitting with a shift-derived segment count, FTGRAYS:1073 to FTGRAYS:1074; **(5)** the two rectangle primitives `FD-33` already named, with the composite half priced by `FD-37` at ±1 LSB; **(6)** a coverage-span emitter, which is a loop over `(3)` and not a new primitive. **No float type is required, and this row states that positively rather than as an absence: every arithmetic operation in (1) through (6) is one of add, sub, mul, div, mod, mulhi, mulhu, sar, shr, band, bor, bxor, shl, eqi, lti, lei.** What the tree gives up by choosing this over family (d) is corner-exact curve boundaries; what it gives up by choosing it over family (b) is freedom from conflation artifacts at abutting edges, and §9 records that the seam is a real defect in a shipped renderer that Levien has not closed.

It hands the author five things. **A correction to the brief this run was dispatched with**: the exact-by-construction against exact-until-you-zoom axis does not survive contact with the sources, because the axis the sources draw is when sampling happens and what is sampled, and on that axis Loop-Blinn's inside test is exact while its coverage is a distance approximation with MSAA underneath, which the imposed axis cannot represent. **A number the author can act on**: 8192 device pixels, the extent at which Skia stops antialiasing, SKANTIPATH:42. **A mechanism the author can copy in one line**: dividing the flattening tolerance by the transform scale, VELLOFLAT:233. **An answer to the float question**: no float type is required for the recommended family, and two shipped renderers prove it. **One open defect to decide about before building**: conflation at abutting edges, §9, which family (c) has and family (b) does not, and which no surveyed project has closed while keeping exact coverage.

## What a field does with an out-of-range slice

### FD-40 the field splits three ways and the line is observability rather than clamp against halt, every surveyed clamp that the field treats as safe hands the caller a value that reports the truncation, the two clamps that report nothing are the two with no published rationale, and the one standard that moved in the last two years moved from undefined behaviour to a terminating check

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question: when a slice or substring is called with out-of-range indices, does the field clamp, trap, or make the call unrepresentable, and what does it say its reason is. **Twenty-five sources were pinned and the consensus SPLITS, but not along the axis the question assumed.** Clamping and halting are both live and both shipping. **The axis the sources actually divide on is whether the out-of-range condition survives the call in a form the caller can test.** Six surveyed clamps exist; the three the field endorses in print (`copy` in Go, `strlcpy`, `snprintf`) all return the untruncated length so the caller can detect the clamp, and GCC's default diagnostic fires precisely when that return value is discarded. **The two clamps that report nothing, Python's slice and Lua's `string.sub`, are also the two for which no surveyed source states any reason at all**, including the language author's own published account of the design. **The trap camp states its reason and states it in one sentence**: the caller is wrong, and the only correct repair is to the caller. **No surveyed source argues that totality at this site is worth the lost detection.** Swift alone records the counterargument, in its own words, and calls it unresolved. **On this tree's question the outside world agrees with halting over a silent clamp, and it disagrees with halting over a reporting clamp.** A clamp with no signal is the one shape nothing in the survey defends.
- measured: **1. THE CLAMP CAMP HAS SIX MEMBERS AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME SHAPE.** **Python's sequence slice clamps both bounds and the library reference is where it is written**, PYSTDTYPES:1062 "*k* such that ``i <= k < j``.  If *i* or *j* is greater than ``len(s)``, use" continued at `:1063` "``len(s)``.". The implementation is the two-branch saturation at CPYSLICEOBJ:271 "    else if (*start >= length) {" and CPYSLICEOBJ:272 "        *start = (step < 0) ? length - 1 : length;". **Python splits within itself at the same site**: PYTUTORIAL:321 "Attempting to use an index that is too large will result in an error::" against PYTUTORIAL:328 "However, out of range slice indexes are handled gracefully when used for" slicing. **Lua clamps and says so in two sentences with no reason given**, LUAMANUAL:9464 "it is corrected to 1." and LUAMANUAL:9466 "it is corrected to that length.". **ECMAScript is the only surveyed language that names the clamp as a first-class specification primitive**, ECMA262:5850 "<dd>It converts _value_ to an integer (interpreting negative values relative to _length_) and clamps the result to the inclusive interval from 0 to _length_.</dd>", used by `String.prototype.slice`. `substring` goes further and repairs the argument order, ECMA262:36925 "If either argument is *NaN* or negative, it is replaced with zero; if either argument is strictly greater than the length of the String, it is replaced with the length of the String." and ECMA262:36926 "If _start_ is strictly greater than _end_, they are swapped.". **JavaScript never traps at this site at all**: an out-of-range string index is a missing property, ECMA262:14906 "1. If ℝ(_numericIndex_) ≥ _length_, return *undefined*.". **C++ `substr` is half a clamp and half a throw, in one function.** `basic_string::substr` is CPPSTRINGS:4479 "Equivalent to: \tcode{return basic_string(*this, pos, n);}" and that constructor clamps the length, CPPSTRINGS:2486 "\tcode{rlen} be \tcode{pos + min(n, s.size() - pos)}", while checking the start, CPPSTRINGS:2498 "\tcode{out_of_range} if \tcode{pos > s.size()}.". **The remaining two clamps both return the untruncated length.** Go's `copy` is GOSPEC:7483 "The number of elements copied is the minimum of" `len(src)` and `len(dst)`, and it returns the count. `strlcpy` states the contract outright, STRLCPY:228 "<var class=\"Va\">dstsize</var>, the output string has been truncated. It is" and STRLCPY:229 "    the caller's responsibility to handle this.</p>".

  **2. THE TRAP CAMP IS LARGER, IT IS UNANIMOUS ON MECHANISM, AND TWO OF ITS MEMBERS STATE THE REASON.** **Go panics on every out-of-range slice expression and clamps nowhere in one.** The in-range condition is GOSPEC:4076 "For arrays or strings, the indices are <i>in range</i> if" `0 <= low <= high <= len(a)`, widened for slices by GOSPEC:4079 "For slices, the upper index bound is the slice capacity <code>cap(a)</code> rather than the length.", and the general rule is GOSPEC:8471 "Execution errors such as attempting to index an array out" GOSPEC:8472 "of bounds trigger a <i>run-time panic</i> equivalent to a call of" `panic`. **The word `clamp` occurs zero times in the 8,997-line Go specification.** **Rust panics on `&s[a..b]` and ships the total form beside it under a different name**, RUSTSTRIDX:163 "/// Panics if `begin` or `end` does not point to the starting byte offset of" a character, `begin > end`, or `end > len`, against the checked form RUSTSTRIDX:369 "    fn get(self, slice: &str) -> Option<&str> {" and the slice equivalent RUSTSLICE:183 "    fn get(self, slice: &[T]) -> Option<&T> {". **Java throws for a substring and clamps for a search, in the same class.** The substring is JAVASTRING:3259 "     *             {@code endIndex} is larger than the length of" this string, enforced at JAVASTRING:3266 "        checkBoundsBeginEnd(beginIndex, endIndex, length);", while the search clamps at JAVASTRING:3115 "        fromIndex = Math.clamp(fromIndex, 0, srcCount);" inside `indexOf`. **Ada raises**, ADARMSLICE:83 "<A NAME=\"I2523\"></A>Constraint_Error is raised if this check fails.</div>". **Standard ML raises at exactly this tree's function**, SMLSTRING:99 "or |<VAR>s</VAR>| &lt; <VAR>i</VAR> + <VAR>j</VAR>" is the condition under which `String.substring` raises `Subscript`, and the same line records that `extract` returns the empty string when `i` equals the length, so the boundary case is total and the overrun is fatal.

  **3. THE STATED REASON, WHICH IS ONE SENTENCE AND THE SAME SENTENCE TWICE.** **Swift's design document classifies this exact call and rules on it.** SWIFTERRRAT:263 "The final category is logic failures, including out of bounds array" accesses, forced unwrap of nil, and other assertions, and SWIFTERRRAT:266 "handled by fixing the code, not by attempting to recover dynamically." because SWIFTERRRAT:265 says the programmer has made a mistake. Swift also names the counterargument and refuses to settle it: SWIFTERRRAT:269 "assertion failure. Tearing down the process can be viewed as a vector" for denial of service, against the reply that the process may be under attack, and SWIFTERRRAT:275 "The correct handling of these error conditions is an open question". **Rust states the same reasoning at the adjacent site and states it as a change of mind.** RFC 560 changed integer overflow RUSTOVERFLOW:9 "program error (but *not* undefined behavior in the C" sense) away from defined wrapping, because RUSTOVERFLOW:96 "failure to do so can be considered a bug, and hence can be flagged by" analysis tools, and its first listed goal is RUSTOVERFLOW:35 "1. Ensure that code which intentionally uses wrapping semantics is" clearly identified. **That is the field saying, in a ratified proposal, that a silent total function at an error site is wrong because the intent cannot be told from the mistake.** **Nothing equivalent exists on the clamp side.** Python's language reference never mentions the behaviour: PYEXPRREF carries 2,658 lines, zero occurrences of "out of range" and zero of "clamp". The language author's own published account of the slice design argues half-open intervals and 0-based indexing and stops there, GVRINDEXING:521 "So that's why Python uses 0-based indexing."; the words "out of range", "clamp" and "IndexError" occur zero times in it. Lua's manual gives the rule and no reason. **The word "clamp" occurs on 73 lines of ECMA-262 and on none of the Go specification, the Python library reference, the Python language reference, Rust's `str` indexing source or Swift's error rationale.**

  **4. THE STATIC CAMP EXISTS, SHIPS, AND DOES NOT REPLACE THE TRAP.** `FD-26` priced this route at ten systems and nineteen pins and is not repeated here. The two spans that matter for this question: ATS makes the bad substring call unrepresentable over a C `char*`, ATSSTRING:339 "  (str: string(n), st: size_t st, ln: size_t ln):<!wrt> strnptr(ln)" under `{n:int}{st,ln:nat | st+ln <= n}`, and F* states the bound at the seat, FSTARSEQ:64 "val slice:  #a:Type -> s:seq a -> i:nat -> j:nat{i <= j && j <= length s} -> Tot (seq a)". **SPARK is the case that settles the relationship between the static and trapping camps**, because SPARK is Ada. Its verification categories include SPARKPROVE:210 "<td><p>Verification of absence of run-time errors (AoRTE" except those raising `Storage_Error`. **The dynamic semantics do not change**: ADARMSLICE:83 still says `Constraint_Error` is raised. **The proof discharges the check; it does not redefine the out-of-range call as a truncated one.** **In the surveyed record no system reaches totality by clamping; the systems that reach totality reach it by proving the partial case unreachable.**

  **5. C, C++ AND WHAT THE UNDEFINED CASE HAS COST.** The C standard makes the call undefined, CN1570:28427 "<li>  An array subscript is out of range, even if an object is apparently accessible with the" given subscript, where undefined behavior is CN1570:884 " for which this International Standard imposes no requirements". **The cost is two entries in the current CWE Top 25.** Out-of-bounds write is rank 5, CWETOP25:268 carries the row for `CWE-787`, and out-of-bounds read is rank 8, CWETOP25:295 carries the row for `CWE-125`, with 12 and 3 CVEs respectively in the KEV catalog. **CWE's own note on `CWE-125` states the caller-bug position that the trap camp argues from**, CWE125:1717 "<div class=\"indent\">When an out-of-bounds read occurs, typically the product has already made a separate mistake, such as modifying an index or performing pointer arithmetic that produces an out-of-bounds address.</div>". **NIST's safer-languages page defines memory safety by halting**, NISTSAFER:603 quotes CCured as producing a program that "will stop rather than overrun a buffer or scribble over memory that it shouldn't touch". **`CWE-125` contains zero occurrences of "clamp" or "truncat".** The security literature surveyed here names the over-read as the defect and names stopping as the fix; it says nothing about truncating.

  **6. WHERE THE FIELD CHANGED ITS MIND, AND IT MOVED TOWARD TERMINATION.** **C++26 turned a class of library out-of-bounds undefined behaviour into a terminating check, and it has landed in the working draft.** The paper is CPPHARDEN:473 "undefined behavior in the standard library into a contract violation." and its scope is CPPHARDEN:607 "that prevent out-of-bounds memory access, i.e., compromise the memory" safety of the program. The wording is now in the draft's own description clauses: CPPLIBINTRO:395 "are evaluated with a terminating semantic\iref{basic.contract.eval}." in a hardened implementation, with CPPLIBINTRO:397 "When invoking the function in a non-hardened implementation," the violation remains undefined. **The string clause carries nine of these already**, `grep -c hardexpects` over CPPSTRINGS returns 9, for example CPPSTRINGS:1053 "\tcode{pos < size()} is \tcode{true}." on `basic_string_view::operator[]`. **The move was from undefined to terminating, and no surveyed proposal moved anything from undefined or terminating to clamping.** **The one motion in the other direction is about the API shape rather than the failure semantics**: C's Annex K bounds-checking interfaces were added and then reported as a failure, N1967ANNEXK:1032 "seen to lead to worse quality, less secure software than relying on" established approaches, and N1967ANNEXK:1038 "      Therefore, we propose that Annex K be either removed from the next" revision or deprecated and removed. That is a verdict on a trapping API's ergonomics, and it recommends no clamp in its place.

  **7. THE SHARP POINT: DOES THE FIELD SAY A SILENT CLAMP MASKS A CALLER BUG. YES, AND THE CLEAREST STATEMENT IS A COMPILER'S DEFAULT DIAGNOSTIC.** **GCC's `-Wformat-truncation` fires on exactly the condition this tree is asking about.** GCCWARN:7483 "employs a conservative approach that warns only about calls to bounded" GCCWARN:7484 "functions whose return value is unused and that will most likely result" in output truncation. **The warning's own trigger is a clamp whose signal the caller discarded.** **GCC also records a documented case of a silent clamp producing a common defect**, GCCWARN:8983 "necessarily a NUL-terminated string is a common mistake, and so the call" is diagnosed, referring to `strncpy` truncating without the terminator. `-Wstringop-truncation` covers `strncat`, `strncpy` and `stpncpy` for the same reason. **Taken with `STRLCPY:229` and `GOSPEC:7483`, the pattern across the endorsed clamps is one rule: the truncation is returned and the caller is required to test it.** **The one argument for totality at the cost of detection that the survey found is Swift's, it is stated as the objection rather than the position, and Swift declines to adopt it**, SWIFTERRRAT:269 and SWIFTERRRAT:275. **No surveyed source argues that a clamp is preferable because it makes the function total.** That is an absence across twenty-five pins, and it is reported as an absence.

  **8. WHAT THE SOURCES DO NOT SETTLE, AND WHAT CAME BACK EMPTY.** **No surveyed source gives a reason for Python's slice clamp.** The behaviour is specified in the library reference, implemented in `sliceobject.c`, absent from the language reference, and absent from the language author's published account of the slice design. **No surveyed source gives a reason for Lua's.** **No surveyed source measures how often a clamp has hidden a defect**; GCC's warning establishes that the field treats the pattern as a defect class and does not count it. **CISA was unreachable from this sandbox.** `The-Case-for-Memory-Safe-Roadmaps-508c.pdf` returned HTTP 403 twice, and `cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/case-memory-safe-roadmaps` and `.../product-security-bad-practices` returned 403; the memory-safety push therefore enters this row only through `NISTSAFER`, `CWETOP25`, and the C++ committee's own citation of it at CPPHARDEN:494 "security in C++ over the last few years, as exemplified by the" well-known White House report. **ISO/IEC TR 24772:2013 was fetched and not pinned.** The 3.4 MB PDF at `open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg23/docs/ISO_IEC_TR_24772_2013.pdf` uses subset fonts with custom encodings; a content-stream extraction returned substitution-ciphered text, no `pdftotext` or Python PDF library is present in this sandbox, and a garbled transcription would have been the transcriber's reading rather than the source. **The vulnerability-avoidance TR is therefore absent from this row and is the one obvious standards-body source left unread.** **C# and .NET were not pinned**, so the trap camp here is six languages rather than seven. **Two AdaCore SPARK user-guide pages returned 403** (`formal_verification_with_gnatprove`, `overview_of_spark_language`); the AoRTE claim rests on the one page that served.
