## What hit testing has to be given before it can invert layout

### FD-44 no surveyed system makes hit testing the inverse of layout, the specification that would define the inverse declines to and says so inside the property that modifies it, five of six implementations read at least one region layout never wrote, every one returns a path or a list rather than a node, and ten objects the sources declare hold no roster row anywhere in this tree

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question: what must a layout result carry for hit testing to be its EXACT inverse — given a layout that maps a node to a region, does hit testing return exactly the node whose region contains the point, for every point and every node — and does any shipped system achieve that inverse or do they all approximate. Posed so it can come back `no`, and it came back `no` on every system surveyed. **Seventeen pins added, every one origin `raw`; one pin reused, `WLRSCENE`.** **The answer: no system inverts.** CSS does not define hit testing at all and says so in the spec section defining `pointer-events`, the property whose whole purpose is to modify it: CSSUI4:3137 ">hit-testing</dfn> is currently not specified." and CSSOMVIEW:2852 "Hit testing will hopefully be defined in a future" revision. **SVG 2 is the one specification in the survey that does define it, and it defines it as a per-element choice among four different regions** — bounding box, fill, stroke, painted — across a ten-value property whose default is the painted area, not any box layout produced. **Five of the six implementations read at least one region layout never wrote**: egui's `interact_rect` beside `rect` plus a 5.0-unit search radius, Blink's `HitTestLocation` with its own ten-overload intersection kernel, wlroots' `floor()`ed 1×1 integer box plus a per-buffer `point_accepts_input` callback, Dear ImGui's `TouchExtraPadding` and one rectangular hole per window, and GTK4's `can-target` bit and a rounded-rect border box. **Flutter is the sixth and reads `_size`, the layout output, and nothing else.** **Every one returns a path or a list, not a node**: Flutter `List<HitTestEntry> _path`, Blink `list_based_test_result_`, egui four separate answers of which `click` and `drag` may be different widgets, CSSOM `elementsFromPoint`. **Two of the six answer from a position or a frame the point is no longer in**: Flutter caches the down-event result for the pointer's whole life, and egui hit-tests the previous pass's widget list. **Ten objects the sources declare hold no row on any roster in this tree**, checked by grep over `docs/arcs/`; and **no roster row anywhere covers this subject at all** — `grep -rniE 'hit[- ]?test|picking|gtk_widget_pick|point-in|inverse of layout' docs/arcs/` returns one line and it is the word "picking" in a sentence about resuming a session (`docs/arcs/emitted-speed-arc.md:408`).
- measured: **1. THE SPECIFICATION THAT WOULD DEFINE THE INVERSE DECLINES, AND IT DECLINES INSIDE THE PROPERTY THAT MODIFIES IT.** CSSOM View defines `elementFromPoint` by deferring: the step is CSSOMVIEW:2721 ">viewport</a> that would be a target for hit testing at" coordinates x,y, and the note twelve lines later is CSSOMVIEW:2849 "specifics of hit testing are out of scope of this" specification, ending CSSOMVIEW:2852 "Hit testing will hopefully be defined in a future" revision of CSS or HTML. **The same spec states outright that its point query is not the inverse of paint**: CSSOMVIEW:2728 "does not necessarily return the top-most painted element". `elementsFromPoint` is the only place a tie-break is written down and it is paint order: CSSOMVIEW:2762 "in paint order, starting with the topmost box, that would be a target for hit testing at" coordinates, CSSOMVIEW:2763 "even if nothing would be overlapping it, when applying the" transforms. **`pointer-events` is defined in css-ui-4 §6.2, titled "Exclusion from Hit-testing", and its first paragraph is an open issue admitting the base operation is undefined**: CSSUI4:3137 ">hit-testing</dfn> is currently not specified." The property has two values in CSS; `none` means CSSUI4:3186 "acts as if the boxes generated by the element" were not there, CSSUI4:3190 "to become the target of hit-testing-based events instead." **The scope of that opt-out is itself an open issue in the spec**: CSSUI4:3197 "What is the precise set of things for which hit-testing is affected by" `pointer-events`, because text selection keeps taking the element into account. **This is the single most important measurement in the run.** The reference class this tree would inherit from does not have the law condition 3 states; it has an unspecified operation with a documented opt-out bolted onto it.

  **2. SVG 2 IS THE ONE SPECIFICATION IN THE SURVEY THAT DEFINES HIT TESTING, AND WHAT IT DEFINES IS WHICH GEOMETRY TO READ.** §15.5.1 states the inputs: SVG2INTERACT:421 "depends upon the position of the pointer, the size and shape of the" graphics element and the computed value of `pointer-events`. The property is ten values, SVG2INTERACT:559 "bounding-box | visiblePainted | visibleFill | visibleStroke | visible | painted |" fill, stroke, all, none, initial `visiblePainted`. **Four distinct regions are selectable and only one of them is a box**: SVG2INTERACT:594 "The given element must be a target element for pointer events when the pointer is over the" of the element, against fill (the path interior), stroke (the path perimeter), and painted (either, gated on the paint being other than `none`). Five of the ten additionally gate on the computed `visibility`. **So in the one specification that defines the operation, the region the hit test reads is not the region layout produced; it is a per-element selection among four, defaulting to the rendered paint.**

  **3. BLINK: THE HIT TEST CARRIES ITS OWN GEOMETRY KERNEL, ITS OWN REQUEST VOCABULARY AND ITS OWN CACHE.** The query is not a point. `HitTestLocation` carries a point and a rect together, BLINKHITLOC:77 "  bool IsRectBasedTest() const { return is_rect_based_; }", and a point query is widened to a rect on the way in: BLINKHITLOC:84 "  // Returns the 1px x 1px hit test rect for a point." The rect survives even when the test is not rect-based, BLINKHITLOC:56 "  // The bounding box isn't always a 1x1 rect even when the hit test is not" rect-based, because transforming into a box's local space transforms the bounding box too. **Ten intersection overloads are declared on the location**, counted by `grep -cE '^  bool (Intersects|ContainsPoint)' BLINKHITLOC` = 10, running from `PhysicalRect` through `ContouredRect` and `QuadF` to BLINKHITLOC:101 "  bool IntersectsStroke(const gfx::RectF& rect, float stroke_width) const;" and `IntersectsEllipse` and `IntersectsCircleStroke`. **The rect widening exists to be inexact on purpose**: BLINKHITREQ:50 "// This is used to support fuzzy matching with rect-based hit tests as well as" penetrating tests. **The request is fifteen flags**, `grep -cE '^    k[A-Za-z]+ = 1 << [0-9]+,?$' BLINKHITREQ` = 15, among them BLINKHITREQ:69 "    kIgnorePointerEventsNone = 1 << 10," (the opt-out can itself be opted out of), `kListBased`, `kPenetratingList`, BLINKHITREQ:78 "    kHitTestVisualOverflow = 1 << 15," (read the ink overflow, not the layout box) and BLINKHITREQ:76 "    kAvoidCache = 1 << 13,". **The cache is real and the result knows about it**: BLINKHITRES:231 "  bool cacheable_;". **The result is thirteen fields**, among them three separate node references, two separate points, a scrollbar, BLINKHITRES:255 "  bool is_over_resizer_ = false;" and BLINKHITRES:260 "  mutable Member<NodeSet> list_based_test_result_;". A function whose codomain is thirteen fields including a node set is not the inverse of a function whose codomain is a rectangle.

  **4. FLUTTER IS THE CLOSEST TO THE INVERSE IN THE SURVEY, AND IT MISSES IN THREE NAMED PLACES.** The geometry read is layout's own output and nothing else: FLUTBOX:2957 "if (_size!.contains(position)) {", and the framework refuses to answer at all when layout has not run, FLUTBOX:2926 "ErrorSummary('Cannot hit test a render box that has never been laid out.')," with the rule stated in the doc comment, FLUTBOX:2915 "Hit testing requires layout to be up-to-date but does not require painting" to be up-to-date. **So Flutter answers the "can it answer without re-running layout" question with: it requires layout to have run and forbids depending on paint** — FLUTBOX:1543 "Hit testing cannot rely on painting having happened." **Miss one: the result is a path, not a node.** FLUTHITTEST:147 "  Iterable<HitTestEntry> get path => _path;" over FLUTHITTEST:148 "  final List<HitTestEntry> _path;", and `hitTest` adds the node itself after recursing, FLUTBOX:2958 "if (hitTestChildren(result, position: position) || hitTestSelf(position)) {". **Miss two: containment is not sufficient.** FLUTBOX:2980 "bool hitTestSelf(Offset position) => false;" is the default, so a bare `RenderBox` whose region contains the point is not hit; the opt-in is a three-value enum, FLUTPROXYBOX:146 "enum HitTestBehavior {" with `deferToChild`, `opaque`, `translucent`, wired at FLUTPROXYBOX:209 "bool hitTestSelf(Offset position) => behavior == HitTestBehavior.opaque;" and FLUTPROXYBOX:201 "if (hitTarget || behavior == HitTestBehavior.translucent) {" — the translucent case adds itself to the path while returning that it was not hit. **Miss three, and it is the one that breaks the predicate outright: capture overrides position.** FLUTGESTBIND:380 "final Map<int, HitTestResult> _hitTests = <int, HitTestResult>{};" caches the down-event's result and every later event of that pointer reuses it, FLUTGESTBIND:438 "hitTestResult = _hitTests[event.pointer];", stated in the framework's own words at FLUTGESTBIND:371 "pointer is seen as pointing to the same place even if it has moved away". The tie-break is a convention, not a rule: FLUTBOX:2988 "Typically children should be hit-tested in reverse paint order so that" overlapping children hit the one on top — `Typically`, in a doc comment, over a method subclasses override.

  **5. EGUI REWROTE HIT TESTING TO BE DELIBERATELY NOT THE INVERSE, AND IT RETURNS FOUR ANSWERS.** The entry point takes a radius, EGUIHIT:42 "pub fn hit_test(" ... EGUIHIT:47 "    search_radius: f32,", documented as EGUIHIT:40 "/// Find the top or closest widgets to the given position,". The radius is a style field with a non-zero default: EGUISTYLE:912 "    /// How close a widget must be to the mouse to have a chance to register as a click or drag.", EGUISTYLE:916 "    pub interact_radius: f32," , EGUISTYLE:1483 "            interact_radius: 5.0,". **The geometry is a second rectangle declared beside the first**: EGUIWR:32 "    /// The full widget rectangle, in local layer coordinates." against EGUIWR:37 "    /// This is after clipping with the parent ui clip rect." and EGUIWR:38 "    pub interact_rect: Rect,", and every distance test reads the second, EGUIHIT:74 "            let dist_sq = w.interact_rect.distance_sq_to_pos(pos_in_layer);". **The result is four fields, not one**: EGUIHIT:18 "    pub close: Vec<WidgetRect>," , EGUIHIT:27 "    pub contains_pointer: Vec<WidgetRect>," , EGUIHIT:32 "    pub click: Option<WidgetRect>," and EGUIHIT:37 "    pub drag: Option<WidgetRect>,", documented as EGUIHIT:29 "    /// If the user would start a clicking now, this is what would be clicked." and EGUIHIT:34 "    /// If the user would start a dragging now, this is what would be dragged." **`click` and `drag` can be two different widgets for the same point**, by an explicit rule: EGUIHIT:221 "                // No direct hit on anything. Find the closest interactive widget." and, when a small clickable sits on a large draggable, EGUIHIT:267 "                            // This is a smaller thing on a big background - help the user hit it," and ignore the background. **The tie-break is three stacked rules, none of them "topmost region containing the point"**: EGUIHIT:76 "                // In tie, pick last = topmost." on distance; then a layer-set filter that stops at the first hit covering the whole search circle; then a hidden-behind filter discarding any widget fully contained by a later one on a different layer. **And it answers from last frame**: EGUICTX:521 "                crate::hit_test::hit_test(" is called with EGUICTX:522 "                        &viewport.prev_pass.widgets," , so the geometry is the previous pass's, which is the only way an immediate-mode library can answer a point query before this frame's layout exists. Duplicate ids resolve by EGUIWR:196 "                existing.interact_rect = widget_rect.interact_rect; // last wins". **This is the clearest refutation in the survey: egui rewrote hit testing for accuracy and the rewrite consists entirely of departures from the inverse.**

  **6. GTK4 PICKS CHILDREN BEFORE IT CHECKS THE PARENT, AND THE DOCUMENTATION SAYS THE ALGORITHM IS NOT A CONTRACT.** The default region is the CSS border box as a rounded rect, GTKWIDGETC:797 "  return gsk_rounded_rect_contains_point (gtk_css_boxes_get_border_box (&boxes)," , which is a vfunc any widget may replace. `gtk_widget_pick` documents itself as GTKWIDGETC:10610 " * Finds the descendant of the widget closest to a point." and then declines the guarantee: GTKWIDGETC:10618 "Widgets are however free to customize their" GTKWIDGETC:10619 " * picking algorithm." **The recursion checks the parent's own region only after every child has missed**: GTKWIDGETC:10539 "  for (child = _gtk_widget_get_last_child (widget);" walks last-to-first and returns the first child that picks, and only then GTKWIDGETC:10597 "  if (!GTK_WIDGET_GET_CLASS (widget)->contains (widget, x, y))" runs. The only positional gate on descent is an opt-in clip, GTKWIDGETC:10534 "      if (!gsk_rounded_rect_contains_point (gtk_css_boxes_get_padding_box (&boxes)," guarded by `GTK_OVERFLOW_HIDDEN`. **So without `overflow: hidden` a child outside its parent's region is picked, and the returned widget's region need not be inside any ancestor's.** Two non-positional filters run before geometry: GTKWIDGETC:10500 "/* do the checks for gtk_widget_pick that do not depend on position */" gates on mapped-ness, sensitivity and GTKWIDGETC:10509 "      !gtk_widget_get_can_target (widget))". **The inverse also fails where the transform is not invertible**, and the code takes the failure as a miss rather than an error: GTKWIDGETC:10571 "              transform = gsk_transform_invert (gsk_transform_ref (child_priv->transform));" `continue`s on NULL, and the perspective divide has a hard epsilon, GTKWIDGETC:10581 "              if (fabs (p0.z - p1.z) < 1.f / 4096)" then `continue`.

  **7. WLROOTS IS THE ONLY SURVEYED SYSTEM WHOSE SCENE GEOMETRY IS EXACT, AND IT QUANTIZES THE QUERY ANYWAY.** The scene graph is integer throughout: WLRSCENEC:207 "static bool _scene_nodes_in_box(struct wlr_scene_node *node, struct wlr_box *box," takes `int lx, int ly` and accumulates `child->x`, so there is no sub-pixel position to lose. The contract is the strongest in the survey, WLRSCENE:344 " * Find the topmost node in this scene-graph that contains the point at the" given layout-local coordinates. **And the implementation does not answer it for a point.** `wlr_scene_node_at` builds a box, WLRSCENEC:1387 "\t\t.x = floor(lx)," with WLRSCENEC:1389 "\t\t.width = 1," and height 1, and runs the region query, WLRSCENEC:1398 "\tif (scene_nodes_in_box(node, &box, scene_node_at_iterator, &data)) {". **Two distinct double coordinates inside one integer pixel are indistinguishable to this query.** The tie-break is honest paint order, WLRSCENEC:217 "\t\twl_list_for_each_reverse(child, &scene_tree->children, link) {". **And the last word belongs to geometry the scene graph never produced**: WLRSCENE:49 "typedef bool (*wlr_scene_buffer_point_accepts_input_func_t)(" declares a per-buffer callback, consulted at WLRSCENEC:1372 "\t\tif (scene_buffer->point_accepts_input &&" , which in a real compositor resolves to the client's Wayland input region — a region the client set, not one the compositor laid out.

  **8. DEAR IMGUI'S TIE-BREAK IS SUBMISSION ORDER, WHICH IS BACK-TO-FRONT, AND ITS OWN COMMENT CALLS THAT A DEFECT.** The test is a padded rect intersected with the window clip: IMGUICPP:10230 "    if (!rect_clipped.ContainsWithPad(g.IO.MousePos, g.Style.TouchExtraPadding))". The padding defaults to zero, IMGUICPP:1534 "    TouchExtraPadding           = ImVec2(0,0);", and the same line states the consequence of turning it up: IMGUICPP:1534 "Unfortunately we don't sort widgets so priority on overlap will always be given to the first widget." **The arbitration is first-submitted-wins within a frame**: IMGUICPP:5051 "bool ImGui::ItemHoverable(const ImRect& bb, ImGuiID id, ImGuiItemFlags item_flags)" returns false at IMGUICPP:5072 "    if (g.HoveredId != 0 && g.HoveredId != id && !g.HoveredIdAllowOverlap)". Since items are submitted back-to-front, **this is the opposite of paint order**, and the front-to-back behaviour is an opt-in that costs a frame of latency: IMGUICPP:5096 "Generally perceived as a front-to-back hit-test." is implemented as IMGUICPP:5100 "            if (g.HoveredIdPreviousFrame != id)" return false. **Capture overrides position here too**: IMGUICPP:5074 "    if (g.ActiveId != 0 && g.ActiveId != id && !g.ActiveIdAllowOverlap)". **Window picking carries hit-test-only geometry, exactly one rectangle of it, with the generalization recorded as unsolved**: IMGUICPP:6353 "        // Support for one rectangular hole in any given window", IMGUICPP:6354 "        // FIXME: Consider generalizing hit-testing override (with more generic data, callback, etc.) (#1512)", IMGUICPP:6355 "        if (window->HitTestHoleSize.x != 0)". **And the window rect it reads lags**: IMGUICPP:6324 "// - FIXME: Note that we have an inconsequential lag here: OuterRectClipped is updated in Begin(), so windows moved programmatically" with `SetWindowPos` lag by a frame. The claim in `.planning/DISPLAY-LAYER-GAP.md` `B9` that Dear ImGui does not support non-rectangular hit testing is **confirmed by construction and not by a user report**: every hit path in `imgui.cpp` terminates in `ImRect::ContainsWithPad` or `ImRect::Contains`, and the one escape hatch is a single axis-aligned hole.

  **9. THE TABLE. Six implementations and two specifications, on the four questions asked.**

  | system | geometry the hit test reads | same as layout wrote | tie-break on overlap | answers without re-running layout |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | CSS (CSSOM View + css-ui-4) | undefined; `pointer-events` removes a box from a set the spec does not define | n/a | paint order, topmost first, stated only for `elementsFromPoint` | n/a. CSSOMVIEW:2849 puts it out of scope |
  | SVG 2 | one of bounding box, fill, stroke, painted, chosen per element by a ten-value property, five values also gated on `visibility` | **no**, default `visiblePainted` is the rendered paint | not stated in §15.5.1 | not stated |
  | Blink | `HitTestLocation`: a point plus a rect plus a transformed quad, against 10 intersection overloads including stroke, ellipse and contoured rect | **no**, and `kHitTestVisualOverflow` reads ink overflow explicitly | paint order, first hit stops unless `kPenetratingList` | yes, from a cache; `cacheable_` and `kAvoidCache` |
  | Flutter | `_size`, the layout output, and nothing else | **yes**, uniquely in the survey | `Typically` reverse paint order, by convention in a doc comment | **no**, it throws if layout has not run; but a pointer down freezes its answer for the interaction |
  | egui | `interact_rect`, a second rect clipped by the parent, at a distance ≤ `interact_radius` = 5.0 | **no**, and not required to contain the point at all | closest, then last = topmost, then a layer-set filter, then a hidden-behind filter, then a help-the-user override | **yes**, from `prev_pass.widgets`, one frame stale by design |
  | GTK4 | `contains` vfunc, default the CSS border box as a rounded rect; plus `can-target` and sensitivity | mostly, but the vfunc is overridable and the doc declines the guarantee | last child first; parent checked only after all children miss | yes, from the allocated widget tree |
  | wlroots scene | integer node boxes, plus a per-buffer `point_accepts_input` callback | **no**, the callback's region is the client's, and the query is `floor()`ed to 1×1 | reverse child order, topmost wins | yes, the scene graph is the retained state |
  | Dear ImGui | `ImRect` padded by `TouchExtraPadding`, clipped by the window clip rect, minus one rectangular hole | **no** on all three counts | **first submitted wins**, which is back-to-front; front-to-back is opt-in via last frame's `HoveredId` | yes, from last frame's `OuterRectClipped`, which lags a frame |

  **10. WHAT THIS TREE ALREADY HOLDS, AND WHAT NO ROSTER ROW COVERS.** **No roster row anywhere covers hit testing.** `grep -rniE 'hit[- ]?test|hit-testing|picking|pick\(|gtk_widget_pick|point-in|inverse of layout' docs/arcs/` returns exactly one line, `docs/arcs/emitted-speed-arc.md:408`, and it is the word "picking" in "session picking either up". `grep -rniF 'hit test' docs/arcs/` and `grep -rniF 'hit-test' docs/arcs/` each return 0. **The nearest row is `native-window/W2`** (`docs/arcs/native-window-arc.md:54`), "seat input: pointer and keyboard events decoded", which is the wire decode and names no point query. **Unlike `FD-43`, there is no relocation available here**: no arc in the tree rosters this subject under another name. **The coordinate half is designed and awaiting an author call.** `display-calculus/R10` (`docs/arcs/display-calculus-arc.md:215`, designed at `docs/arcs/parts/display-calculus-R10.md`) mints `(data Fix ((d I64)) (fix (v I64)))` with ten operations, `fix-of-int`, `fix-floor`, `fix-round`, `fix-add`, `fix-sub`, `fix-neg`, `fix-lt`, `fix-eq`, `fix-scale`, `fix-rescale` (`docs/arcs/parts/display-calculus-R10.md:321`). **Those ten are scalar. There is no region type over `Fix` and no containment predicate**, and `grep -rniF 'fix-le' docs/arcs/`, `grep -rniF 'point-in' docs/arcs/` and `grep -rn 'rect-contains' prog/ lib/` each return 0. **The tree does hold a `Rect` and a partition invariant, in one live file nobody has rostered against this subject.** `prog/scriba/window.chiral:29-30` declares `(data Rect () (rect (row I64) (col I64) (height I64) (width I64)))`, `:34` states the invariant in a comment, "Tree invariant: children of a w-split partition the parent rect", and the file's 24 `def`s (`grep -c '^(def ' prog/scriba/window.chiral` = 24, 400 lines) cover area, four splits, resize, union, walk and six tree edits — **and no containment predicate and no point query**. `grep -rn 'at-point\|window-at\|find-at\|in-rect\|rect-contains' prog/ lib/` returns only `puffer-insert-at-point`, a text cursor. So the tree has the exact precondition the survey says makes the inverse achievable, a declared non-overlapping partition, and has never written the inverse.

  **11. THE IMPLIED PRIMITIVES. TEN OBJECTS THE SOURCES DECLARE THAT NO ROSTER ROW IN THIS TREE NAMES.** Each was checked against `docs/arcs/` by grep and each returned nothing. **(a) The interaction region as a value distinct from the layout region.** EGUIWR:33 and EGUIWR:38 declare both on one struct; SVG2INTERACT:559 makes the choice a property; BLINKHITREQ:78 makes it a request flag. `grep -rniF` over `docs/arcs/` for `interact_rect`, `interaction region`, `input region`, `hit region`: 0, 0, 0, 0. **(b) The hit-test tolerance as a declared field.** EGUISTYLE:1483 `interact_radius: 5.0`, IMGUICPP:1534 `TouchExtraPadding`, BLINKHITLOC:84 the 1×1 widening, WLRSCENEC:1389 the 1-pixel box. Greps for `interact radius`, `touch slop`: 0, 0. `tolerance` returns 2 and both are `display-calculus/R13`'s curve-flattening tolerance (`docs/arcs/display-calculus-arc.md:122`, `:218`), a different object at a different stage. **(c) The targetability bit, per node, separate from visibility.** GTKWIDGETC:10509 `can-target`, CSSUI4:3186 `pointer-events: none`, FLUTPROXYBOX:146 `HitTestBehavior`, egui `Sense`. Greps for `can-target`, `targetable`, `pointer-events`, `HitTestBehavior`: 0, 0, 0, 0. **(d) The hit result as a path, not a node.** FLUTHITTEST:148, BLINKHITRES:260, CSSOMVIEW:2762. Greps for `hit path`, `hit test`, `hit-test`: 0, 0, 0. **This is the object condition 3's word "inverts" silently assumes away**: an inverse returns one node; every surveyed system returns an ordered sequence, because the event has to be offered to ancestors. **(e) The paint order as a value the picker reads.** EGUIWR:98 "All widgets, in painting order.", WLRSCENEC:217, GTKWIDGETC:10539, CSSOMVIEW:2762. Greps for `paint order`, `z-order`, `stacking`: 0, 0, 0. **A layout that maps node to region does not determine the answer when two regions overlap; a second, independent total order is required, and no row names it.** **(f) The captured pointer binding: a pointer identity bound to a target for the interaction's life.** FLUTGESTBIND:380 and FLUTGESTBIND:371, IMGUICPP:5074 `g.ActiveId`. Greps for `pointer capture`, `grab`: 0, 0. **This one falsifies the predicate outright and no roster row acknowledges it exists.** **(g) The absorption rule: whether a hit stops the descent, and whether a node may be added without absorbing.** FLUTPROXYBOX:201 `translucent`, BLINKHITREQ:75 `kPenetratingList`, EGUIHIT:27 `contains_pointer` against `click`. Greps for `translucent`, `opaque`: 0, and 5 for `opaque` of which none is this object (all are opaque payloads and opaque text cases). **(h) The previous frame's geometry as this frame's hit-test input.** EGUICTX:522 `prev_pass.widgets`, IMGUICPP:5100 `HoveredIdPreviousFrame`, IMGUICPP:6324 the `OuterRectClipped` lag. Greps for `previous frame`, `prev frame`, `last frame`: 0, 0, 0. **A tree that states condition 5 as "a frame is a function of state and time" has to say which frame the point query reads, and nothing does.** **(i) The clip as a second region the test intersects.** IMGUICPP:10230 clips before testing, EGUIWR:37 bakes the clip into `interact_rect`, GTKWIDGETC:10534 gates descent on the padding box under `GTK_OVERFLOW_HIDDEN`. `grep -rniF 'clip' docs/arcs/` returns **0**. **(j) A region type over the coordinate, and a containment predicate on it.** Every system in the survey has one; this tree has `Rect` over `I64` in one program file (`prog/scriba/window.chiral:29`) with no containment, and `R10`'s ten `Fix` operations are all scalar. Greps for `fix-le`, `point-in`, `rect-contains`: 0, 0, 0. **`R10` as designed cannot express condition 3's second clause, and `R10`'s own design says it absorbs neither `R11` nor `R13` (`docs/arcs/parts/display-calculus-R10.md:278`); it does not consider a region at all.**

  **12. WHAT CONDITION 3 WOULD HAVE TO CONTAIN IF AN ARC OPENED OVER IT. Stated as input to the author's call, not as a call taken here.** The condition reads "A box and a glyph have positions, and hit testing inverts them" (`docs/goals/display.md:61`). **The survey says the second clause is false of every shipped system, so as written the condition states a property no reference class has, and a row minted on it would be minted on a category statement — the exact defect the 2026-09-22 directive names.** Four things the survey says the condition would have to add before it is checkable. **(i) A region type and a containment predicate over `Fix`, half-open on two edges so that adjacent regions partition rather than overlap.** This is the cost: one type and one predicate beside `R10`'s ten scalar operations, on the same `Fix d` index, no new compiler surface. `prog/scriba/window.chiral` supplies a worked non-overlapping partition over `I64` as the precedent. **(ii) A declared total order on siblings, separate from the layout function.** Without it "hit testing inverts layout" is not even well-formed when two regions overlap, and four of the six implementations spend most of their hit-test code on exactly this. If the tree instead requires a partition — no two sibling regions overlap, which `window.chiral:34` already asserts in a comment — then the order becomes unnecessary and **the inverse becomes achievable, which no surveyed system attempts.** That is the fork, and it is the author's: **a partition invariant enforced by the type, which buys the exact inverse and forbids overlap, or an order, which permits overlap and gives up the inverse.** **(iii) A statement of what the query returns: one node, or the ancestor path.** Six of six surveyed return a path or a list. If the condition means one node, it is stating a stronger property than any reference class and owes the reason. **(iv) A statement about capture, tolerance and the clip, even if the statement is that the floor has none of them.** All three are present in every surveyed system, all three break the inverse, and a condition that says nothing about them will acquire them later at a seam. **What this run does not do**: it proposes no denominator, per `docs/decisions/decision-display-numerics.md:72-73` and the open `R10` call, and it edits no goal, arc or `records/author-calls.md`.

  **13. WHAT THE SOURCES DID NOT SETTLE, AND WHAT CAME BACK EMPTY.** **No source in the survey states the inverse as a design goal, and none states why not.** Not one of the eight carries a note saying hit testing should or should not be the inverse of layout; the property was tested against the code and the specs, and the specs that speak at all speak to say the operation is undefined (CSSUI4:3137) or out of scope (CSSOMVIEW:2849). **No surveyed system publishes a test that a layout and its hit test agree.** Web Platform Tests are linked from CSSOM View for `elementFromPoint` but the test files were not fetched, so what they assert is unmeasured by this run. **Flutter's `hitTestChildren` default was not pinned.** `RenderBoxContainerDefaultsMixin.defaultHitTestChildren` lives in `box.dart` and this row's reverse-paint-order claim rests on FLUTBOX:2988's doc comment, which says `Typically`, not on that method's body. **egui's `Sense` type was not pinned**, so the `senses_click` / `senses_drag` split enters this row through its call sites in `hit_test.rs` alone. **GTK's per-widget `contains` overrides were not surveyed.** GTKWIDGETC:10618 says widgets may customize picking; how many of GTK4's widgets do, and what regions they use, is unmeasured, so the claim "mostly the border box" is about the default and not about the toolkit. **wlroots' `point_accepts_input` has no in-tree implementation in the pinned files**; the claim that it resolves to the client's Wayland input region rests on the callback's signature and `wlr_scene.h`'s own gloss at WLRSCENE:344-347 and not on a pinned compositor. **AccessKit, Servo, Taffy, Skia and Qt were not consulted.** **Dear ImGui's `imgui_internal.h` was not pinned**, so `ImGuiLastItemData` and `ItemAdd` enter through `imgui.cpp`'s uses of them. **Nothing in the survey measures the cost of the partition option**, because no surveyed system takes it; item 12(ii) is a fork the sources can price only on one side.

### FD-45 no surveyed layout algorithm is a pure function over a child list and none partitions the parent in normal flow, three systems overlap with no positioning feature, the one exact tiling in the survey is a level below the children where the spec makes the gutter an empty track, and twelve objects the sources declare hold no roster row anywhere in this tree

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question: when a layout algorithm runs as a pure function over a child list, what does it take in, what does it return, and does the result **partition** the parent's region (children tile it with no gap and no overlap) or merely **populate** it. Posed so it can come back `no` on both halves, and it came back `no` on both. **Twenty pins added, every one origin `raw`.** **Not a pure function.** No surveyed engine returns the children's regions; every one returns the **parent's own size** and writes each child's rectangle into the tree by effect: Taffy through `set_unrounded_layout` on a `&mut self` tree, Yoga through a `void` entry point reading a process-global atomic counter, Morphorm through `cache.set_rect`, SwiftUI through a subview proxy from a method that returns nothing. **And not a partition.** Free space is a named variable the algorithm spends as offsets, so a gap is the normal outcome rather than an oversight, and **three of the surveyed systems overlap with no positioning feature at all**: CSS Grid items overlap when placed into intersecting grid areas with `z-index` as the tie-break, Morphorm ships `LayoutType::Overlay` as one of four core layout types, and CSS Flexbox says in normative text that on negative free space the items overflow equally in both directions. **The one exact tiling in the survey is a level below the children.** CSS Grid makes a gutter an extra, empty, fixed-size track and folds distributed alignment's leftover into it too, so the **track list** tiles the content box exactly while the **items** do not — which is a construction the partition arm of the author fork can be built from: make the gap a member of the child list. **Intrinsic sizing is not a second traversal**: Taffy folds it into the same call behind a `RunMode`, a `SizingMode` and a `RequestedAxis`, memoized on the whole input, and Yoga sizes its per-node measurement cache at 8 on the published finding that 98% of analysed layouts need fewer. **No surveyed function is total**: Yoga aborts through `assertFatalWithNode`, Taffy's public API returns `Result`, Cassowary returns `UnsatisfiableConstraint` and resolves an over-constrained system nondeterministically by its own documentation, and SwiftUI is total only because an unplaced subview has a defined default. **Twelve objects the sources declare hold no row on any roster in this tree**, checked by grep over `docs/arcs/`; **no roster row anywhere covers layout**; and the tree's own only layout function, `prog/scriba/window.chiral`, **fails the partition invariant its own comment asserts, in three named ways**.
- measured: **1. THE SHAPE, ON THE REFERENCE THE BRIEF CALLS THE CLOSEST TO A PURE FUNCTION.** Taffy's algorithms run against one trait and the crate states the scope: TAFFYTREE:172 "/// node that only has access to it's immediate children." **The trait is not pure and cannot be**, because both of its methods take `&mut self`: TAFFYTREE:83 "//!     fn set_unrounded_layout(&mut self, node_id: NodeId, layout: &Layout);" and TAFFYTREE:89 "//!     fn compute_child_layout(&mut self, node_id: NodeId, inputs: LayoutInput) -> LayoutOutput;" (the module doc comment at `:78-102` restates the trait verbatim and the live declarations at `:173-200` are byte-identical to it, so only the `//!` copies are quotable uniquely). **The input is nine fields.** TAFFYLAYOUT:113 "pub struct LayoutInput {" carries a run mode, a sizing mode, a requested axis, two known dimensions, a definiteness bit **per axis** — TAFFYLAYOUT:141 "    pub known_dimensions_are_definite: Size<bool>," — a parent size, TAFFYLAYOUT:146 "    pub available_space: Size<AvailableSpace>," and a collapsible-margin line. The available space is a three-way sum rather than a number: TAFFYAVAIL:15 "pub enum AvailableSpace {" over TAFFYAVAIL:17 "    Definite(f32)," plus `MinContent` and `MaxContent`. **The output contains not one child region.** TAFFYLAYOUT:397 "pub struct LayoutOutput {" returns TAFFYLAYOUT:398 "    /// The size of the node", a scrollable overflow rect, baselines, two collapsible margins, a collapse-through bit, TAFFYLAYOUT:427 "    pub oof_candidates: OofCandidates," and an out-of-flow positioning area. **The child rectangles leave by the side channel**: TAFFYFLEX:511 "            tree.set_unrounded_layout(child, &Layout::with_order(order as u32));". The per-node result is TAFFYLAYOUT:481 "/// The final result of a layout algorithm for a single node." carrying TAFFYLAYOUT:490 "    /// The top-left corner of the node", a size, and **a render order** — TAFFYLAYOUT:488 "    /// This is effectively a topological sort of each tree." on a `pub order: u32` whose doc says a higher order draws on top. **A layout result that carries a stacking order has already conceded that its regions may overlap.** The whole computation is memoized on its input: TAFFYTREE:256 "    fn cache_get(&mut self, node_id: NodeId, input: &LayoutInput) -> Option<LayoutOutput>;".

  **2. THE PARTITION ANSWER IS `NO`, AND THE UNCOVERED SPACE IS A NAMED VARIABLE IN THE ALGORITHM.** In flexbox the leftover is computed explicitly and then spent as per-child offsets: TAFFYFLEX:2194 "        let mut free_space = constants.inner_container_size.main(constants.dir) - used_space;", and it can be consumed by auto margins before `justify-content` ever sees it — TAFFYFLEX:2226 "            // The auto margins have absorbed all of the free space, leaving none for ". The space the algorithm is handed is not the children's total and need not even be finite: CSSFLEX:5223 "This might result in an infinite value." **With `justify-content: flex-start` and items shorter than the line the tail of the parent is covered by nothing; with `space-between` the interior is; with a `gap`, the gaps are; with a margin on any child, the margin band is.** None of those four is a positioning feature and none is optional to model. The spec's status is normative and its freedom is only in method: CSSFLEX:5142 "but must produce the same results as the algorithms described here."

  **3. OVERLAP ARRIVES WITH NO POSITIONING FEATURE, IN THREE OF THE FIVE ENGINES.** **(i) CSS Flexbox, normatively, on negative free space.** `justify-content: center` states CSSFLEX:4453 "flex items</span> will overflow equally in both directions.)", and the spec's own definition of a flex container's min-content main size sets the case aside as expected behaviour: CSSFLEX:5989 "such that no items overflow it," followed by CSSFLEX:5990 "setting aside the cases in which the boxes layouts are <em>defined</em> to overflow". **(ii) CSS Grid, by construction, in its core placement.** CSSGRID:2214 "can overlap when they are positioned into intersecting" grid areas, and CSSGRID:2215 "or even when positioned in non-intersecting areas because of negative margins or positioning." The grid module's own comparison with flexbox names it as a capability rather than a hazard: CSSGRID:1260 "allows explicit overlapping of items,". The overlap is arbitrated by a **second, independent total order**, `z-index`, which the spec extends to statically positioned grid items precisely so it can be used here. Auto-placement is the only part of grid that avoids overlap and it avoids it only against cells already occupied, never against an explicitly placed item. **(iii) Morphorm, as a first-class layout mode.** MORPHTYPES:3 "pub enum LayoutType {" has four arms; beside MORPHTYPES:4 "    /// Stack child elements horizontally." sits `Overlay`, documented as MORPHTYPES:9 "    /// Place child elements independently within the parent's padded box." and wired through the same write path as the others: MORPHORM:423 "        cache.set_rect(child, LayoutType::Overlay, child_posx, child_posy, child_size.main, child_size.cross);". **Overlap is not bolted onto these algorithms. It is one of the four modes, or it is the normative behaviour of the main axis whenever the children do not fit.**

  **4. THE ONE EXACT TILING IN THE SURVEY IS A LEVEL BELOW THE CHILDREN, AND THE SPEC BUILDS IT BY MAKING THE GAP A CHILD.** CSS Grid's tracks are declared to pack: CSSGRID:1730 "but are otherwise packed tightly." And the gap is not an absence, it is a track — CSSGRID:4438 "an extra, empty, fixed-size track of the specified size,". Even the leftover that distributed alignment introduces is folded back into the gutters rather than left over: CSSGRID:4444 "This space effectively increases the size of the" gutters. **So the track list, gutters included, tiles the grid container's content box exactly, and this is the only exact tiling anywhere in the survey.** Taffy implements it the same way: TAFFYGRID:268 "    // This resolves the min and max track sizing functions for all tracks and gutters". Morphorm reaches the same idea from the other direction by putting the space into the same distribution list as the size: MORPHORM:16 "/// Represents a space or size which has stretch units." over MORPHORM:11 "enum ItemType {" and MORPHORM:23 "    // The type of stretch item, either space-before, size, or space-after." **This is the run's contribution to the author fork, and it is a construction rather than an opinion: a partition is reachable by making the gap a member of the child list, and one specification and one implementation already do it — one level away from the level the fork is about.** The items inside those tracks still do not partition: a grid item is aligned inside its grid area by `justify-self`/`align-self`, may span several areas, and may share an area with another item.

  **5. INTRINSIC SIZING IS NOT A SECOND TRAVERSAL. IT IS AN UNBOUNDED NUMBER OF PROBES, MEMOIZED.** Taffy folds it into the same call: the input carries a `RunMode` over TAFFYLAYOUT:14 "    PerformLayout," and TAFFYLAYOUT:17 "    ComputeSize," plus a hidden mode, a `SizingMode` over content-size and inherent-size, a `RequestedAxis` over horizontal, vertical and both, and the cache above keys on the entire `LayoutInput`. **Yoga publishes the measured count**: YOGARESULTS:24 "  // 98% of analyzed layouts require less than 8 entries." sizing YOGARESULTS:25 "  static constexpr int32_t MaxCachedMeasurements = 8;" — a per-node ring of eight measurement results that wraps to index 0 when it fills. **SwiftUI states the protocol outright**: SWIFTUISIZE:1 "view that calls this method might call the method more than once" with different proposals before choosing one. **The CSS specs make it worse than a traversal count.** Flexbox's intrinsic main size has **two conformant answers**: CSSFLEX:6003 "if it conforms to either the Ideal Algorithm or the Web-compatible Algorithm," — the spec declines to determine the function. Grid's sizing algorithm is a five-phase alternation between the two axes with two bounded re-resolutions, CSSGRID:4762 "based on the row sizes and alignment calculated in step 2," ... `(once only)`, and the spec explains why the repetition cannot be dropped: CSSGRID:4775 "This repetition is necessary for cases where the " inline size of an item depends on the block size of its area, CSSGRID:4777 "Examples include wrapped column " flex containers, orthogonal flows, multi-column containers and aspect-ratio items. And css-sizing states the base case is not well-founded at all: a percentage-sized box whose containing block depends on it is CSSSIZING:3023 "creating a cyclic dependency.", broken by a rule that substitutes the property's initial value. **`B5`'s "a second traversal" is the cheapest possible reading of what four sources measure.**

  **6. TOTALITY: `NO`, IN FOUR DIFFERENT WAYS.** **Yoga aborts.** Its per-node entry asserts a relation between two of its own arguments and dies if it fails: YOGACALC:1743 "availableWidth is indefinite so widthSizingMode must be" `SizingMode::MaxContent`, under `assertFatalWithNode`. **Yoga is also not a function of its arguments**: the entry point YOGACALC:2873 "void calculateLayout(" returns nothing and reads a process-global atomic, YOGACALC:2885 "      gCurrentGenerationCount.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed) + 1;". **Taffy's public surface returns `Result`**: TAFFYREADME:69 "tree.compute_layout(root_node, Size::MAX_CONTENT).unwrap();". **SwiftUI is total only by default.** Placement is an effect on a proxy, so the protocol has to say what an unplaced subview does: SWIFTUIPLACEAT:1 "If you call this method more than once for a subview, the last call" takes precedence, and SWIFTUIPLACEAT:1 "subview appears at the center of its layout container and uses the" container's own proposal when it is never placed at all. **This is `FD-42`'s pattern one lane over: the function is total because absence has a default.**

  **7. THE CONSTRAINT SOLVER IS DIFFERENT IN KIND ON ALL FIVE AXES.** Cassowary takes no child list and returns no region. Its input is **linear constraints over free variables**, each carrying a strength, and its output is a **delta**: CASSOWARYRS:122 "only lists" *changes* to variables, because the solver is a retained object rather than a call. It is built to be incremental and to fail softly — CASSOWARYRS:5 "and it will perform the minimum work to update the result) and that the constraints can be violated if" necessary, in strength order. **Its refusal is a value**, CASSOWARYRS:575 "    UnsatisfiableConstraint,", and it arises only for `REQUIRED` constraints. **And it is not a function**: under an over-constrained system the documentation states the outcome is picked CASSOWARYRS:135 "nondeterministically, so there are two possible results. This could be" either. **A partition is expressible in Cassowary as a chain of `a.right == b.left` equalities and nothing whatsoever enforces that the author wrote them**; the solver has no notion of a parent region to tile. SwiftUI replaced this technique in Apple's own stack, and what it replaced it with is §8.

  **8. SWIFTUI IS THE PUBLISHED PURE-FUNCTION SHAPE AND IT IS TWO FUNCTIONS, ONE OF WHICH RETURNS NOTHING.** The two required methods, read off the two documents' `declarations` token lists, are `func sizeThatFits(proposal: ProposedViewSize, subviews: Self.Subviews, cache: inout Self.Cache) -> CGSize` and `func placeSubviews(in bounds: CGRect, proposal: ProposedViewSize, subviews: Self.Subviews, cache: inout Self.Cache)`. **Both carry `cache: inout`** — SWIFTUILAYOUT:1 "Create and manage a cache to store computed values across different" layout protocol calls — so neither is pure in the protocol's own statement, and the sizing half's example signature is quotable at SWIFTUISIZE:1 "        cache: inout ()". **The measuring half returns one size**; the placing half returns nothing and SWIFTUILAYOUT:1 "assigns positions to the container’s subviews." by effect. **Its contract about the region is populate, not partition, in the document's own words**: SWIFTUIPLACE:1 "Place all the container’s subviews within the region." — a one-directional obligation with no converse. The placement primitive is a point and an anchor, SWIFTUIPLACE:1 "            subview.place(at: point, anchor: .topLeading, proposal: .unspecified)", explained at SWIFTUIPLACEAT:1 "The place where the anchor of the subview should" appear relative to the container's bounds. **And the subview is not obliged to accept the size it is proposed**: SWIFTUISIZE:1 "SwiftUI views choose their own size, so the layout engine always" uses what the layout returned as the container's actual size. **So a SwiftUI subview may be any size, placed anywhere against any anchor, more than once, or never.** It is the furthest from a partition in the survey and it is the most recently designed.

  **9. THE ONE PLACE ANY SURVEYED SYSTEM MENTIONS GAPS IS THE ROUNDING PASS, AND IT IS A SEPARATE TREE TRAVERSAL OVER ABSOLUTE COORDINATES.** Taffy's `round_layout` is a distinct trait and a distinct pass, and its rationale is TAFFYCOMPUTE:264 "/// In order to ensure that no gaps in the layout are introduced we:" — TAFFYCOMPUTE:265 "///   - Always round based on the cumulative x/y coordinates (relative to the viewport) rather than" parent-relative ones, and TAFFYCOMPUTE:267 "///   - Compute width/height by first rounding the top/bottom/left/right and then computing the difference" rather than rounding the size directly. The body is the rule: TAFFYCOMPUTE:289 "        layout.size.width = round(cumulative_x + unrounded_layout.size.width) - round(cumulative_x);". **Rounding a size in isolation opens a one-pixel gap between two adjacent boxes; rounding two absolute edges and subtracting cannot.** The doc comment links the Yoga commit that established it. **This is the most load-bearing measurement in the run for `R10`**, and §12(d) prices it.

  **11. WHAT THIS TREE ALREADY HOLDS, AND THE DEFECT IN IT.** **No roster row anywhere covers layout.** `grep -rniF` over `docs/arcs/`: `flexbox` 0, `grid layout` 0, `layout algorithm` 0, `min-content` 0, `max-content` 0, `box model` 0, `normal flow` 0, `margin collaps` 0, `line box` 0, `scroll container` 0, `taffy` 0, `yoga` 0, `morphorm` 0, `cassowary` 0, `constraint solver` 0. `flex` returns **2** and both are the word *reflexivity* or *reflex* (`docs/arcs/parts/enforcement-N14.md:263`, `docs/arcs/parts/native-window-W6.md:220`). `layout` returns 37 and every one is either `decision-part-layout`, a directory layout, or `diagnostics-arc`'s `Doc`/`Rendering` group, which is terminal text composition: `docs/arcs/diagnostics-arc.md:253-257` rosters five rows under the group name `layout` and not one of the five is box layout. `intrinsic sizing` returns **1**, `docs/arcs/display-calculus-arc.md:503`, and it is the nearest arc naming `B5` as the row that will surface a staging risk **it declines to take**: *"The row that surfaces it is `B5`, intrinsic sizing, in the unopened geometry condition of [[goals/display]]."* **So lane B is confirmed unrostered, by the arc closest to it, in writing.** ⚑ **The tree's only layout function already exists and already fails its own partition invariant.** `prog/scriba/window.chiral:34` states *"Tree invariant: children of a w-split partition the parent rect"*, and the same file refutes it three times. **(i)** `rect-split-n` (`:101-113`) computes `each = (max 1 (/ height n))` and lays `n` children of height `each`; chirality division is Euclidean so it truncates, `n · each ≤ height`, and the remainder rows are covered by nothing. The file says so itself at `:100`: *"Integer division — remainder cells are unused."* **(ii)** that same `(max 1 …)` means for `n > height` the children total `n` rows and **leave the parent rect entirely**. **(iii)** `rect-split-horizontal` (`:75-83`) partitions exactly on its general path, `half` plus `height - half`, but its guard returns `(pair r r)` — **two identical, fully overlapping rects** — with the obligation pushed to the caller in a comment, `:74`, *"Caller must detect this and refuse the split."* **This is the partition arm's real price, measured in the tree rather than argued: the tree has already written a partitioning layout, has already asserted the invariant in a comment, and the comment is false.** The two-way split is the case that works; the n-way split and the degenerate case are the two that do not, and both fail on exactly the arithmetic §9 shows Taffy solving by rounding absolute edges and subtracting.

  **12. WHAT LAYOUT NEEDS BEYOND `R10`'s TEN SCALAR OPERATIONS.** `docs/arcs/parts/display-calculus-R10.md` §5 ships `fix-of-int`, `fix-floor`, `fix-round`, `fix-add`, `fix-sub`, `fix-neg`, `fix-lt`, `fix-eq`, `fix-scale`, `fix-rescale` on `(data Fix ((d I64)) (fix (v I64)))`. Every one is scalar and every one is closed over a single coordinate. **Five things the survey says a layout result needs that those ten do not provide.** **(a) A region type over `Fix d`, and a containment predicate on it.** Every system in §10 returns or writes a rectangle; `R10` names no point, no size and no rect, and its own §5 question 11 says it absorbs neither `R11` nor `R13`. `grep -rniF 'point-in' docs/arcs/` 0 and `grep -rn 'rect-contains' prog/ lib/` 0. `prog/scriba/window.chiral:29` is the tree's only `Rect` and it is over bare `I64`. **(b) `fix-le`, `fix-min` and `fix-max`.** Clamping a size between a minimum and a maximum is in the inner loop of every engine surveyed: flexbox's hypothetical-size clamp, grid's growth limits, Morphorm's `min` and `max` on every `StretchItem`. `R10` ships `fix-lt` and `fix-eq` and no `≤`, no min and no max — and a **half-open** containment predicate, which is what makes two adjacent regions partition rather than overlap on their shared edge, needs `≤` on one side and `<` on the other. `grep -rniF 'fix-le' docs/arcs/` 0. **(c) A divide.** `fr` units, `space-between`'s free space over `n-1`, grid's equal distribution and Morphorm's stretch factors are all a `Fix d` divided by an integer count, and a flex factor is a `Fix d` divided by a `Fix d`. `fix-scale` is a multiply by a plain `I64` and reaches for no divide at all; `R10`'s §5 question 6 records the *multiply* of two `Fix d` as an open NEEDS-AUTHOR and **the divide is not raised anywhere**. **(d) A tree-level rounding pass over absolute coordinates.** §9: rounding a size opens a gap, and the fix is to round two cumulative absolute edges and subtract. `fix-round` is the scalar half of that; the pass that threads a cumulative origin down the tree and takes differences is an operation over a region, not over a scalar, and `R10` has nowhere to put it. **This is the one item on the list that is load-bearing for the partition arm specifically**, because a partition stated in `Fix` does not survive the trip to device pixels unless the rounding is done this way. **(e) A signed free-space value, and the branch on its sign.** `fix-neg` and `fix-lt` give the sign test; nothing in the ten names the quantity, and it is the variable the whole flex algorithm is organised around. **None of (a) through (e) asks for new compiler surface** — they are more operations on the same `Fix d` index plus one indexed record, which is the cost shape `R10`'s own mint packet already argues.

This row measures the outside world, opens no roster row and designs nothing. **On the author fork `FD-44` opened, this run's input is: the partition arm is constructible, and the survey now prices it on the side the sources could not.** No surveyed system partitions at the level of the children, and the reason is structural rather than accidental — free space is a quantity the algorithm computes and spends, so a gap is the normal outcome. **But two constructions in the record reach a partition by one move: make the gap a member of the child list.** CSS Grid does it in normative text, a gutter being an extra empty fixed-size track with distributed alignment's leftover folded into it; Morphorm does it in code, space and size being the same `StretchItem`; Taffy implements grid that way. **The cost of the partition arm is therefore not "forbid a feature every engine ships"; it is one constructor in the child sum and a half-open containment predicate, plus §12(d)'s rounding rule so the partition survives the trip to device pixels.** **Five roster edits this row implies and does not make.** **`.planning/DISPLAY-LAYER-GAP.md` row `B3` is refuted in its chirality column and in one of its three reference claims.** *"a pure function over the child list"* is false of all five engines: none is pure (a `&mut self` tree, an `inout` cache, or a process-global counter) and none returns the child list's regions. The microcontroller claim is unsupported by any pinned byte, per evidence item 3. Its remaining claim, *"Main and cross axis parameterised so one implementation serves both directions"*, **holds and is confirmed**: Taffy threads `constants.dir` through every axis read, and Morphorm carries `parent_main`/`parent_cross` with a swap at each layout-type boundary. **Row `B4`'s chirality cell, "same shape as B3 with a two-dimensional placement pass", is right about the placement pass and wrong about the shape**: grid's sizing algorithm is a five-phase alternation between the axes with two bounded re-resolutions, not one pass carrying a second dimension. **Row `B5`'s "a second traversal" is refuted** by §5, on four sources. **Row `B11`, the constraint-layout fork, is the one lane-B cell this run finds accurate**: Cassowary is incremental, is strength-ordered, and SwiftUI did replace it with the proposal-and-response protocol §8 measures. **Row `B7` is untouched** except that §13(j) names the scrollable overflow rectangle as an object its "three separate constructors" would each have to carry. **`display-calculus/R10` is unaffected as designed and is measured here as insufficient for a layout result**, on the five counts in §12, of which (d) is new to this run. **One in-tree defect found and not fixed, outside this run's write surface**: `prog/scriba/window.chiral:34` asserts a partition invariant that `:74`, `:100` and `:101-113` each refute (§11). The file is under `prog/` and this run writes nothing there; the measurement is recorded here and the fix belongs to whichever row eventually rosters the subject, which today is none.

### FD-46 the field does not agree on whether a service must tell its callers apart, and the disagreement is about where the distinguishing gets paid: four families revoke one caller with the service unable to tell two callers apart, every one of them relocates the distinguishing to a second party, a per-context tag, or a client-side proof linear in the blocklist, this tree's own cited precedent hands the service a stable 32-byte per-client key on every visit, and every construction in the survey that keeps callers indistinguishable dies under Shor with the post-quantum replacements at 80 KB to 46 MB

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question, posed so it can come back `no`: when a system gates access to a service, do the people who design these systems treat the service's ability to **distinguish its individual callers** as necessary, and is there a construction that gives revocation of one caller, rate limiting, abuse response and per-caller authorisation **without** the service telling its callers apart or linking one caller's visits to each other. It came back `no` on the first half and `yes` on the second, and the two answers are the finding. **Nineteen pins added, ten origin `raw` and nine origin `transcribed` from `pdftotext`.** **The field splits, and the split is legible.** The IETF's deployed answer states the opposite of the author's premise as its architectural goal: PPARCH:102 "without learning any unique, per-Client information through the" authentication protocol, with the authorization decision resting on that authentication succeeding or failing, and PPARCH:123 "Origins verify the token to authenticate the Client" with no per-client information reaching the Origin. The blocklisting-credential literature agrees and goes further, BLAC:36 building "the first anonymous credential system in which" services can blacklist, BLAC:37 "misbehaving users without contacting a TTP. Since blacklisted users remain anonymous". **Four properties have to be kept apart to read any of this**: authentication (the caller is entitled to enter), identification (which caller), linkability (two visits, one caller, name unknown), accountability (revoke, throttle or block one caller afterwards). **1 and 4 without 2 and 3 is constructed, proved, and in two cases shipped.** What no surveyed system does is make the distinguishing disappear. It moves: to a second party that counts per client (Privacy Pass rate limiting, Nymble), to a tag that is deterministic inside one named context and random across contexts (ARC, EPID), to a proof the client carries whose size grows with the blocklist (BLAC, BBS set non-membership), or to the moment of issuance, where the grantor mints one forwarder per grantee (object capability). **The author's premise therefore holds as a statement about cost and fails as a statement about necessity**, and the post-quantum constraint is where the cost stops being theoretical.
- measured: **§1 THE TABLE. Eighteen systems, the four properties, the price.** `auth` is 1, `ident` is 2, `link` is 3, `revoke` is 4. `PQ` is whether the construction as specified survives a quantum adversary.

  | system | auth | ident | link | revoke | cost | PQ | ships |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | Tor v3 onion, client authorisation | yes | **yes** | **yes** | yes, drop the key | one x25519 and one ed25519 keypair per client, pre-shared out of band; a 112 B extension on every introduction | **no** | yes |
  | Privacy Pass VOPRF(P-384), `RFC 9578` type 0x0001 | yes | no | no | one token is one visit; revoking a caller is the Attester refusing to issue | `Nk` 48, a 146 B token (derived) | **no** | yes |
  | Privacy Pass blind RSA 2048, type 0x0002, publicly verifiable | yes | no | no | same | `Nk` 256, a 354 B token (derived) | **no** | yes |
  | `draft-ietf-privacypass-rate-limit-tokens-06` | yes | no | no at the Origin | **yes, per origin**, by an Attester holding per-client counters | a third party, a policy window, and one bit to the Origin | **no** | no, the draft expired 3 October 2024 |
  | ARC, `draft-ietf-privacypass-arc-crypto-01` | yes | no | no across contexts, **yes inside one** | yes, a fixed presentation limit | 357 + 129·k bytes, k = ceil(log2 limit), so 744 B at limit 8 (derived); keyed-verification, so only the issuing server verifies | **no** | no |
  | BBS, `draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-signatures-09` | yes | no | no | only by a set non-membership proof the draft names and does not specify | 80 B signature, 272 B proof floor (derived) | **no** | yes, as a credential format |
  | BLAC | yes | no | no | **yes, with no third party at all** | linear in the blocklist n: (n+2) ℓ-bit strings, 3 G1, (2n+1) G, 12 Zp | **no** | no |
  | PEREA | yes | no | no | yes | linear in K, a revocation window, independent of the blocklist L | **no** | no |
  | Nymble | yes | no | yes inside a linkability window, after a complaint | yes | **two non-colluding third parties** | core survives, §4 | an open-source implementation |
  | EPID from bilinear pairing | yes | no | optional | yes, signature-based, **and it refuses an opening authority** | pairings | **no** | yes, SGX and TPM and ISO/IEC |
  | hash-based EPID, eprint 2024/651 | yes | no | optional | yes | **11.8 MB to 46.1 MB per signature, 89 s to 453 s to sign** | **yes** | no |
  | lattice anonymous credential, eprint 2024/131 | yes | no | no | not on its own | **under 80 KB**, 400 ms to issue, 500 ms to show and verify | **yes** | no |
  | lattice accumulator revocation, eprint 2025/1099 | n/a | n/a | n/a | **yes, bolted onto the above** | 50 KB accumulator, **14.7 MB membership witness**, ≤125 KB proof | **yes** | no |
  | Signal sealed sender | yes, by a sender certificate | no to the service | no | relocated to the recipient's contact graph via a 96-bit delivery token | one certificate fetch, one profile key | **no** | yes |

  | object capability, the caretaker | yes | no | no | yes, per grantee | **one forwarder pair per grantee, created at grant time** | n/a, no crypto | KeyKOS, EROS, CAP-III |

  **The `ships` column carries a VERIFY caveat except in four cells, and the exceptions are named.** Pinned: EPIDHASH:9 EPID "is broadly used for hardware enclave attestation by many platforms that" implement SGX, and EPIDHASH:12 "(TPM) specifications and ISO/IEC standards. However, it is insecure" against quantum attackers; NYMBLE:94 "we have built an opensource implementation of Nymble"; OCAPMYTHS:580 "KeyKOS [9] and EROS [21] both employ this" revocation pattern. **Tor is a near-miss**: `TORRENDV3` carries the note that client authorisation is implemented as of Tor 0.3.5.1-alpha at `:679`, `:2545` and `:2554`, three identical lines, so the span is not quotable as a unique citation and the fact is stated here rather than cited. **Every other cell in that column is VERIFY, from memory**: Privacy Pass in Apple Private Access Tokens and at Cloudflare, Oblivious HTTP, macaroons beyond the paper's own Belay prototype, biscuit, BBS as a credential format, and Signal sealed sender past the beta the pin describes. Nothing in this run measured a deployment.

  **§2 THE PRECEDENT THIS TREE CITES IS THE ONE THAT IDENTIFIES.** `.planning/REACH-MODEL.md:130-134` names Tor v3 with and without client authorisation as the precedent for its two positions, and `:117-119` asserts that "Anonymity survives the gate, because a `Grant` proves permission and never proves identity". The pinned spec says otherwise about Tor. TORRENDV3:650 "each authorized client of a hidden" service holds two keypairs, TORRENDV3:654 has them "exchanged between the hidden service and its clients in a secure out-of-band" fashion, and the introduction cell carries the client's raw key: TORRENDV3:2102 "Pubkey    [32 bytes]", checked by TORRENDV3:2115 "and would accept a signature from the provided public key". The current rendered spec is identical at TORINTROAUTH:770 and TORINTROAUTH:782. The spec then names the linkability it created and pushes the fix onto the user, TORRENDV3:2122 "Users SHOULD NOT use the same public key with multiple hidden" services. **Tor v3 client authorisation is per-service pseudonymity.** The service distinguishes its authorised clients, every visit, by a stable 32-byte value it enrolled. It is a precedent for the author's premise. The sentence at `:117-119` has no precedent in it.

  **§3 WHAT ACCOUNTABILITY COSTS WHEN IDENTIFICATION IS REFUSED.** Three prices, each measured. **A second party.** `draft-ietf-privacypass-rate-limit-tokens-06` splits the knowledge, PPRATELIMIT:244 "the Issuer learns redemption information like origin" identity and PPRATELIMIT:246 "Attester learns attestation information like client identity (used to" track prior issuance, with the Attester holding PPRATELIMIT:968 "A counter of successful tokens issued" per client per window. The Origin still learns something, PPRATELIMIT:2148 "the origin only learns a single bit of information: whether" the client had quota left. Nymble pays the same price twice over, NYMBLE:226 anonymity holding only if "PM and the NM do not collude, the Nymble system" is secure. **A client-side proof that grows.** BLAC removes the third party and hands the client the blocklist: BLAC:679 "proof Π2 of SP K2 consists of 3 G1 elements", n G elements and 12 Zp, and BLAC:681 "for an authentication is thus (n + 2)" ℓ-bit strings plus (2n+1) G, so BLAC:676 both costs grow with "the current size of the SP's blacklist". PEREA's contribution is exactly this bound, PEREA:28 "the computation required" at the server being linear in L in BLAC and EPID, replaced by PEREA:32 "the time complexity of authentication is linear in the size" of a revocation window K ≪ L, PEREA:33 "the number of subsequent" authentications inside which a misbehaviour must be caught. BBS names the same shape and stops, BBSSIG:3048 offering a proof that "a signed unique revocation identifier is not" part of the revoked set, with no construction for it in the draft. **A per-context tag.** ARC keeps ARCCRED:175 credentials "presented multiple times without violating unlinkability of different" presentations, and buys the limit with a deterministic tag: ARCCRED:1029 the server checks "the tag (presentation.tag) has not previously been seen, to prevent" double spending. Inside one `presentationContext` a repeat is detectable, which is exactly one bit of distinguishing, deliberately purchased.

  **§4 POST-QUANTUM, WHICH IS WHERE THIS GETS EXPENSIVE.** `docs/goals/own-web.md` condition 4 requires every layer post-quantum, and most of this literature is pairing-based. **Dead under Shor as specified**: Tor v3 client auth (x25519, ed25519), Privacy Pass (P-384 VOPRF and RSA-2048), ARC, whose P-256 ciphersuite deserialises by ARCCRED:2027 the "compressed Octet-String-to-Elliptic-Curve-Point method" at ARCCRED:2021 "compressed Elliptic-"Curve-Point-to-Octet-String with Ne 33 and ARCCRED:2038 "Ns = 32", BBS (BLS12-381 pairings), BLAC (BLAC:698 "pairings over Type-A curves"), PEREA, EPID, biscuit (BISCUITSPEC:819 "The default signature algorithm is Ed25519"), OHTTP as specified, sealed sender. The survey's own verdict on the family is PQANONCRED:28, blind signatures, group signatures and anonymous credentials "does not have, at this stage, an efficient post-"quantum counterpart, PQANONCRED:27 "which standards already exist, and which are deployed in billions of" devices. EPID says it plainly, EPIDHASH:12 "(TPM) specifications and ISO/IEC standards. However, it is insecure" against quantum attackers. **Alive under Shor**: macaroons, MACAROONS:22 a construction that "uses nested, chained MACs (e.g., HMACs", symmetric throughout; the object-capability caretaker, which uses no cryptography at all; and Nymble's core, NYMBLE:92 built from "inexpensive symmetric cryptographic operations to" outperform the alternatives, NYMBLE:1335 "HMAC-SHA-256 for the message authentication MA" with SHA-256 and AES-256, its one public-key part being 2048-bit RSASSA-PSS signatures that a lattice signature replaces. **The post-quantum replacements, priced.** A credential alone: PQANONCRED:214 "Ours       M-SIS/M-LWE              No          Adaptive     80 KB", against PQANONCRED:215 a survey "Comparison of exisiting post-quantum anonymous credentials reaching 128" bits that runs from PQANONCRED:207 "No       Adaptive       724 KB" to PQANONCRED:213 "No      Adaptive       25365 KB", with PQANONCRED:388 issuance and showing of "a credential take respectively 400 ms and 500 ms on average". Revocation on top of it: PQACCUM:276 for a 32-length revocation attribute they "obtain the accumulator value c of size 50KB, while a membership witness" is 14.7 MB, with PQACCUM:278 "proofs of size at most 125KB" and the authors' own "Although not yet fully ready for practical deployment". Group-signature-shaped revocation, post-quantum, is worse by three orders: EPIDHASH:1606 "n = 129, GS = 240           17 bytes               89                 43                11.8" MB per signature and EPIDHASH:1609 "n = 255, GS = 260           32 bytes               453               216                46.1" MB, against a 1000-entry signature revocation list, with the lattice alternative at EPIDHASH:1605 "LEPID [30]               100 KB                 374               121                854" MB. **So the post-quantum answer today is 80 KB per showing with no revocation, or 80 KB plus a 14.7 MB client-held witness and a 125 KB proof with it.**

  **§5 THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT AGAINST THE AUTHOR'S PREMISE**, in the sources' own words, is that distinguishing is the attack surface, and it is made by people who ship. EPID's designers had the option of an opening authority and refused it: EPIDBP:95 "EPID scheme chooses not to have traceability from the" revocation manager, because traceability lets a manager determine which platform signed what, EPIDBP:98 "without any acknowledgement from the user that is being traced", and they took a harder revocation problem to avoid it, while still delivering EPIDBP:17 revocation where "the revocation manager can revoke a device based on the signatures the device has signed". BLAC:36 removes the trusted party entirely. OHTTP shows what happens when the distinguishing is reintroduced for a good reason: OHTTP:1090 "only the gateway" or the target can see abuse, and acting on that signal at the relay OHTTP:1096 "to Client deanonymization" is the risk the RFC names. **The strongest argument for the author's premise** is that every construction above still pays for per-caller effects somewhere, and the deployed record is that the payment lands on a party who can count. Signal is the cleanest instance: sealed sender removed the sender's identity from the envelope, and SEALEDSENDER:1 states what authentication had been doing, "The service can use the sender"'s identity to apply rate limiting and abuse protection, and replaced it with a 96-bit delivery token derived from the recipient's profile key, which restricts sealed sender to contacts. The rate-limited Privacy Pass variant did the same by adding a whole party. PEREA:126 makes the point as a design constraint on the whole family: "We argue that rate limiting is an implicit scalability requirement in both BLAC and EPID", because the client-side proof grows. And the bearer-token camp, which is closest to this tree's `Grant`, has no revocation story that does not reintroduce a handle: MACAROONS:328 "revocation of authority is a long-standing" challenge, answered at MACAROONS:1256 by short-lived credentials or "revocation may be done via" a database whitelist or blacklist of valid macaroons; biscuit is concrete about what that handle is, BISCUITSPEC:654 "The revocation identifier for a block is its signature", so a verifier that checks a revocation list can link every use of one token. **The object-capability answer is the sharpest version of the distinction the author is drawing.** OCAPMYTHS:541 "Alice would send Bob access to F" and keep the revoking facet R, so OCAPMYTHS:559 "she has" revoked the access without revoking any capability. Carol, the service, learns nothing about who called. Alice, the grantor, had to mint Bob his own forwarder to be able to revoke him alone. **Distinguishability at grant time, anonymity at call time**, which is a third position neither the premise nor its negation states.

  **§6 WHAT THE SOURCES DID NOT SETTLE, AND WHAT CAME BACK EMPTY.** **Camenisch-Lysyanskaya, Idemix and U-Prove were not pinned.** The U-Prove Cryptographic Specification V1.1 returned HTTP 403 from `microsoft.com`, no Idemix specification was fetched, and no CL paper was pinned; they enter this row only as `[CL02b]` inside PQACCUM and PQANONCRED, and **no size for either is quoted here**. **k-times anonymous authentication was not pinned**; ARC is its standards-track descendant and stands in for it, which is a substitution and not a measurement. **BLACR, Nymbler and the post-2012 blocklisting literature were not read.** **No group-signature paper defending an opening authority was pinned**, so §5's argument against one is quoted from its opponents and the other side is absent from this row. **No pin measures deployment.** That Apple ships Private Access Tokens on the basic Privacy Pass issuance protocol is VERIFY, from memory, and the `ships` column is read off what each specification and paper says about itself. **Nothing here measures a real anonymity set.** PPARCH:382 makes redemption context unlinkability conditional on "the Origin cannot determine which issuance and attestation" contexts a redemption came from, and PPARCH's §6 partitioning discussion was read and is not quoted, so the practical anonymity these systems deliver stays outside this row. **The rate-limited token draft's fate is unmeasured**: version 06 expired 3 October 2024 and nothing pinned says whether it was adopted, abandoned or superseded by ARC. **`docs/decisions/decision-inspiration-policy.md:94` says ccbox egress is blocked, and it is not.** Every fetch in this run returned HTTP 200, including `rfc-editor.org`, `ietf.org`, `eprint.iacr.org`, `spec.torproject.org`, `signal.org`, `raw.githubusercontent.com` and three university hosts. `poppler-utils` installed from Debian in the same sandbox, which is how nine PDFs became `transcribed` pins rather than staying unread.
