  **4. STANDARDISATION.**

  **Ascon is a NIST standard.** SP 800-232 is final, dated August 2025, `SP800232:77 "Approved by the NIST Editorial Review Board on 2025-07-09"`, at `SP800232:95 "https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/232/final"`. The permutation is approved inside modes only: `SP800232:1573 "The Ascon permutations, including variants with different numbers of rounds, may be"` approved for further applications if modes for them are approved.

  **NIST's reasons for selecting Ascon, in its own words** (NIST IR 8454, June 2023). The decision: `NISTIR8454:85 "On February 7, 2023, NIST announced the decision"` to standardize the Ascon family. Security maturity: `NISTIR8454:668 "ASCON is the most mature of the fnalists in terms of security."` Its second-round variants were never modified, `NISTIR8454:684 "This is in"` `NISTIR8454:685 "contrast to some other fnalists that included design tweaks to address attacks."` Scrutiny: `NISTIR8454:686 "It was the submission with the"` `NISTIR8454:687 "most third-party analysis and implementations. Despite the head-start on cryptanalytical"` attacks, Ascon remained strong. Performance: `NISTIR8454:694 "Performance in constrained environments, such as dedicated hardware and embedded sys-"` tems was a significant factor. And no second algorithm: a secondary one is `NISTIR8454:712 "not necessary at this time as the performance of ASCON is expected to be acceptable for"` target devices.

  **Xoodyak was a finalist and lost to Ascon.** The selection section gives reasons for Ascon and names no reason against Xoodyak. The report's Xoodyak section describes it, `NISTIR8454:1722 "Xoodyak is built from a"` `NISTIR8454:1723 "fxed 384-bit permutation (called Xoodoo) operated in Cyclist mode."`, and `NISTIR8454:1723 "The design approach"` `NISTIR8454:1724 "of Xoodoo is closely related to that of the KECCAK permutation."`, then records the 50% margin above and the 2023 bounds, citing Daemen et al. who `NISTIR8454:1786 "proved that the minimum weights of any 4-round, 6-round, and"` 12-round trails of Xoodoo are 80, at least 132 and at least 264. No other standardisation of Xoodyak was found.

  **Keccak-p[200] and Keccak-p[400] are defined by FIPS 202 and approved for nothing.** `FIPS202:31 "The KECCAK-p[1600, 24] permutation is approved for use in the context of its approved modes of operation"`, and `FIPS202:31 "other KECCAK-p permutations may also become approved if any modes of operation for them are developed and approved within a FIPS Publication or a NIST Special Publication."` The two small-width Keccak designs that reached a public competition did not win it. Ketje is listed as a `KETJE:188 "Third-round candidate in the CAESAR competition"`, and Elephant, whose Delirium variant is the Keccak-f[200] instance, was a NIST finalist and lost to Ascon.

  **5. THE ONE-PLANE QUESTION.** **No source consulted analyses a Keccak-structured round at one plane, and none declines it in those terms.** Three published statements come nearest.

  **(a) The column parity mixer theory has no content at one row.** Stoffelen and Daemen define θ's generalisation over `CPMIXERS:125 "We consider linear mappingsθthat operate on arrays withm rows andn columns."`, where m is the column height, which is the plane count in Keccak's geometry (Keccak-f[200]'s sheet is their m = 5 example). The θ-kernel, on which Keccak's low-weight trails live (FD-58 section 1), has dimension n(m − 1): `CPMIXERS:429 "The set of statesA with column parity equal to zero form a vector space with dimension"` `CPMIXERS:430 "n(m−1). Following [Ber+11b], we call this the(column parity) kernel."` The branch-number result is stated from two rows up: `CPMIXERS:439 "Lemma 4.An invertible CPMθwith m≥2 and whereZ has no all-zero rows or columns,"` `CPMIXERS:440 "has diﬀerential and linear branch numbers 4, with the only exception of the case where"` m = n = 2 and Z = I. **This row's reading, which the paper does not state:** at m = 1 the kernel is the zero space, the column parity of a state is the state itself, and θ is the plain linear map A(I + Z) with no parity structure. The theory's kernel, orbitals and branch number 4 all have no object there, so a one-plane θ is a different linear layer that no published analysis has characterised. The paper does observe that `CPMIXERS:555 "In this respect, it is advantageous for a given state size to have a small number of rows"`, a statement about the kernel's size relative to the state that says nothing about m = 1.

  **(b) Xoodoo's designers considered a 320-bit design with Keccak's χ and chose 384 bits.** `XOODOODESIGN:924 "Another option would be to aim for a320-bit permutation and to stick"` `XOODOODESIGN:925 "to Keccak-p’sχ on 5 bits, but we thought that384 bits would be better suited."` The sentence gives no geometry for the 320-bit option and no analysis of it, so it does not settle whether that option was one plane.

  **(c) Ascon's designers rejected θ for a small state.** `ASCONV12:1014 "The mixing layer of Keccak is best used with a large number of large words."` FD-58 quotes it. It is a design judgment and carries no analysis of θ at one plane.

  **Searched and empty:** the Keccak team's third-party cryptanalysis page (`KECCAKCRYPT`), NIST IR 8454's summaries of every finalist's third-party analysis, the eight new pins, the pins reused from FD-58, and two web searches for single-plane or one-plane Keccak variants and 320-bit Keccak-χ permutations. None returned an analysis of `planes = 1`.

  **6. WHAT THE EVIDENCE SETTLES IN `C2`.** `C2` at `.planning/CRYPTO-MODEL.md:508` asks for the family's initial instances and whether Ascon-p is one of them or a second design. The evidence settles four things and leaves the call with the author.

  - **The family at `planes = 1` has no published analysis of any kind**, and the only general theory of its θ has no object at one row (section 5). A `planes = 1` member would carry every bound it has from this tree's own analysis, which KR3 asks about.
  - **Ascon-p is the best-evidenced permutation in the niche.** It has proven bounds to 12 rounds from two independent teams, a NIST standard, the most third-party analysis in the lightweight competition in NIST's words, and a 5-round margin. Its evidence belongs to its own composition (FD-58), so it arrives only if Ascon-p is adopted as it stands.
  - **The Keccak family itself reaches small state at five planes with its own published evidence.** Keccak-p[200] is 25 bytes and Keccak-p[400] is 50 bytes, on either side of Ascon's 40. Their proven bounds stop at 6 rounds, except the 18-round bound at b = 200, and neither is standardised. Reaching small `budget` by shrinking `w` at five planes is the family's own dial, and it is the only one of the three routes that keeps Keccak's published per-width analysis.
  - **The generic sponge bound caps the smallest widths.** At c/2 bits of generic security (`KECCAKREF:254 "For each of the supported parameter values, we make a"` flat sponge claim, and the crunchy contest's 160-bit capacity at 80 bits), a 128-bit target needs c ≥ 256. That leaves b = 200 no room at all and b = 400 a 144-bit rate. This is arithmetic from the claims and no source states it for these widths.

  Xoodoo sits at three planes with a 3-bit χ and its own ρ, so it is a second design in the same sense Ascon-p is. It is the nearest Keccak-shaped member with proven bounds to 12 rounds, and no standard carries it.

  **7. WHAT CAME BACK EMPTY OR IS NOT SETTLED.**

  **No linear trail bound for Keccak-p[400], and no bound at its 20 rounds.** `KECCAKTRAILS` is differential only. The Keccak reference's small-width linear table stops at w = 8.

  **No bare-permutation distinguisher at b = 200 or 400 was found.** The third-party page lists keyed and hash-mode results at these widths and none on the bare permutation. The search covered the one page and the IR and stopped there.

  **The 2023 Xoodoo bounds are pinned from the ePrint.** The file carries the ToSC 2023(4) header. Makarim and Rohit's SMT and MILP paper (ToSC 2022(3), the MR22 of `ASCONTRAILS`, which also lowers the heuristic 4- and 5-round upper bounds to 43 and 72 active S-boxes) was read on its abstract page and not pinned. Nothing above rests on it beyond the table credit `ASCONTRAILS` gives it.

  **NIST states no reason why Xoodyak lost.** The selection section argues for Ascon and names no other finalist's weakness except ISAP's leakage-mode cost and a general statement that no second algorithm is needed.

  **No bound was reproduced.** Every weight quoted is its authors' claim under their own method.

## What it takes to compute a new configuration's security evidence, and whether this project can

### FD-60 the evidence can be computed on CPUs and no published tool computes it for this family: every headline trail bound surveyed came from a dedicated tree-search program written for one round function, run single-core for between four days and about four CPU months per bound on commodity x86, the method is published as generic and needs only a linear layer, a non-linear layer and a symmetry to prune by, the Keccak and Xoodoo programs build their two-round generation on θ's column parity and kernel, which at one row have no object, so a `planes = 1` round needs a new generation phase whose nearest published model is the Ascon tool, general-purpose SAT and MILP models apply to any round unchanged and prove only active S-box counts at costs of hundreds to thousands of CPU days by four rounds, the algebraic analyses are cheap degree-propagation computations with no published CPU cost, the Keccak and Xoodoo tools carry no licence their repositories declare, and no designer or NIST text states a minimum analysis a new permutation owes before use

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question, as dispatched for the crypto arc's own permutation family (`docs/arcs/crypto-primitives-arc.md`), third of four pre-wave research runs after FD-58 and FD-59: **what does it take to establish the security evidence FD-58 names as non-transferable, for a new configuration of a Keccak-structured permutation? That means the methods that produce proven trail-weight bounds per round count, the algebraic and structural analyses designers run beside them, the tools that implement each, their licences and published compute costs, and whether any of them reaches a θ over one row, where the column-parity kernel machinery does not apply.** Posed so it could come back `no` in part, as "no published method handles case X" or "the published cost is out of reach for a CPU-only machine". **The compute answer is `yes`.** Every headline bound in the pins was produced on ordinary x86 CPUs, and the costs run from about 100 single-core hours (Keccak-f[200] at 6 rounds) to about 190 CPU days (Xoodoo at 4 rounds, both trail kinds). No GPU appears in any source. **The method answer is `yes` for the method and `no` for any tool.** Trail core tree search is stated as generic by its authors, and each application was a new program with units, orderings and bounding functions written for its own round function. The Keccak and Xoodoo programs generate two-round trail cores from θ's column parity and its kernel. At one row that decomposition has no object (FD-59 section 5), so the published programs do not reach `planes = 1` as written. The nearest published instance is El Hirch et al.'s Ascon tool, which ran tree search on a 320-bit state of 5-bit S-boxes with a linear layer that has no kernel. That the tool is the right model for `planes = 1` is this row's reading. **The designer-obligation answer is `no`.** No Keccak, Xoodoo, Ascon or NIST text consulted states what analysis a new permutation must carry before use. What exists is practice (every design surveyed publishes trail bounds), a NIST competition's submission rules, and NIST's statement that it approves a permutation only inside approved modes.
- measured: **1. TRAIL-BOUND METHODS, WHAT EACH PROVES, AND WHERE IT STOPS.**

  | method | proves | reaches | the source says |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | **trail core tree search**, dedicated program (Mella, Daemen, Van Assche and successors) | a lower bound on trail **weight**, so on the probability or squared correlation of every trail, by exhausting all trail cores below a threshold `T` | Keccak-f[200 to 1600] to 6 rounds at weight 92, Xoodoo to 12 rounds at 264, Ascon-p to 12 rounds at 2^-258 (FD-59 section 2) | `KECCAKTRAILS:56 "the best results can be obtained by computer-assisted proofs, where a program scans the"` space of all trails below `T`. Beyond the searched rounds a bound comes from splitting: Xoodoo's 12-round bound took no search of its own, since `XOODOOTRAILS:1372 "6-round trails with weight below132, we can conclude that there are no 12-round trails"` below 264 |
  | **SAT or SMT on active S-boxes** (Mouha and Preneel; Dobraunig et al.; Erlacher, Mendel, Eichlseder) | a lower bound on the **number of active S-boxes**, from which a probability bound follows by the S-box's maximum DP | Ascon-p: 3 rounds by SMT, 4 rounds at 36 active S-boxes (2^-72) and 6 at 54 (2^-108) by SAT (FD-59) | the weight is out of reach by this route. `ASCONTRAILS:95 "bounds on the number of active S-boxes. Directly bounding the probability would require"` `ASCONTRAILS:97 "a more expensive model for the SAT solver compared to bounding the number of active"` S-boxes |
  | **MILP** (Mouha et al.; Sun et al.; Makarim and Rohit) | active S-box counts, and in Makarim and Rohit a tight 3-round Ascon differential bound | 3 rounds proven on Ascon; heuristic trails beyond | `KECCAKTRAILS:59 "as (mixed) integer linear programming ((M)ILP) or SAT solvers. MILP has been used by"` Sun et al. for Serpent and PRESENT. `ASCONTRAILS:157 "3 2−40 nldtool [DEMS15] 2−40 MILP [MR22]"` |
  | **heuristic search** (nldtool, lineartrails, CP) | nothing. It finds the lightest trail it can, an upper bound on the minimum | Ascon's best known trails at 4 to 6 rounds | FD-59 section 2, `ASCONTRAILS:158` |

  **The published ranking of the two families.** El Hirch et al.: `ASCONTRAILS:17 "tools based on general-purpose solvers and dedicated tools. General-purpose solvers"` `ASCONTRAILS:18 "such as SAT and MILP are widely used to prove these bounds, however they seem to"` `ASCONTRAILS:19 "have lower capabilities and thus yield less powerful bounds compared to dedicated"` tools. The Keccak team measure it in weight per round: `KECCAKTRAILS:73 "Results obtained with standard tools cited above never reached a weight per round"` above 9, where their 2017 program reached 15. By 2022 SAT had closed some of the gap, with Erlacher et al. at 17 per round on Ascon, and the dedicated tools for Xoodoo and Ascon reached 21 (`ASCONTRAILS:82`, `ASCONTRAILS:84`, `ASCONTRAILS:90`).

  **Where the solver route stops.** Single-threaded SAT on 4-round Ascon ran `ASCONBOUNDS:457 "for up to 40 days. This refers to wall-clock runtime in a single-threaded solver"` with no result at 43 active S-boxes. The 36-S-box proof needed partitioning into many small problems, and the next step up was priced and not run: 40 active S-boxes at 4 rounds would take `ASCONBOUNDS:818 "with Totalizer [BB03] encoding and estimate that this bound takes38 ·176 = 6688 CPU"` days. Every SAT or MILP bound past 6 rounds in the pins is assembled from 4- and 6-round results.

  **2. WHAT THE TREE SEARCH NEEDS FROM A ROUND FUNCTION, AND THE ONE-ROW CASE.**

  **The method is stated as generic.** `KECCAKTRAILS:96 "Thanks to its abstraction level, the tree traversal approach can be applied to primitives"` `KECCAKTRAILS:97 "with round functions consisting of a bit-oriented mixing layer, a bit transposition layer"` and a lightweight non-linear layer. El Hirch et al. repeat it: the approach `ASCONTRAILS:130 "same and is generic, so it can in principle be applied to other ciphers. In a few words,"`. **Each application is a new program.** `KECCAKTRAILS:99 "relations and cost bounding functions depends on the targeted primitive and its properties."` Stoffelen and Daemen, applying it to column parity mixer designs, `CPMIXERS:755 "We use techniques that are based on that work to ﬁnd trails for our design. However,"` `CPMIXERS:756 "to make it work for our design, we have to make a number of modiﬁcations. In this"` section.

  **Canonicity pruning needs a symmetry, and a one-plane round keeps the one it uses.** `KECCAKTRAILS:305 "The tree traversal approach can be extended when there are symmetry properties that"` we wish to take into account, and `KECCAKTRAILS:363 "A direct consequence of Lemma 1 is that a pattern that is not canonical cannot have"` a canonical descendant, so whole subtrees are cut. For Keccak the symmetry is translation along z. **This row's reading, which no source states:** a `planes = 1` round built from θ, ρ, π, χ and ι keeps z-translation symmetry in every step except ι, exactly as Keccak-p does, so canonicity pruning applies unchanged.

  **The two-round generation phase is where the Keccak and Xoodoo programs depend on θ's parity.** Keccak's cores are generated in and out of the kernel, and the Keccak program's own source layout names the dependency: `KTOOLSSRC:307 "\"name\": \"Keccak-fParity.h\","`, `KTOOLSSRC:531 "\"name\": \"Keccak-fTrailCoreInKernelAtC.h\","`, `KTOOLSSRC:659 "\"name\": \"Keccak-fTrailExtensionBasedOnParity.h\","`. Stoffelen and Daemen's CPM program decomposes a state into a parity-bare state plus free orbitals, `CPMIXERS:820 "As withKeccak-f, we can uniquely decompose every state pattern into aparity-bare"` state and a list of free orbitals. Xoodoo's 2023 speed-up is also parity-specific: it `XOODOOTRAILS:81 "This technique leverages the propagation properties of column parity mixers to compute a"` tighter bound. **At one row the column parity of a state is the state, the kernel is zero (FD-59 section 5), and there are no free orbitals, so none of these decompositions has an object.** A `planes = 1` search needs its own units and bounding functions for a θ that is a plain linear map. **The nearest published instance is Ascon.** El Hirch et al. generated two-round trail cores by tree search for a 5 × 64 state with 5-bit S-boxes across the words and a per-word linear layer with no kernel, and proved bounds to 12 rounds. A Keccak round at one plane has the same S-box geometry, 5-bit χ across 5 lanes of 64 bits, and a different linear layer. Reading Ascon's tool as the model is this row's inference.

  **The general-purpose solvers need no adaptation.** A SAT or MILP model encodes whatever round is given, so a `planes = 1` round is modelled as directly as Ascon was. Their limits are those in section 1: active S-box counts only, and costs that grow steeply past 3 or 4 rounds. CryptoSMT is such a tool, `ASCONBOUNDS:1055 "[Köl15] Stefan Kölbl. CryptoSMT: An easy to use tool for cryptanalysis of symmetric"` primitives.

  **3. THE ANALYSES DESIGNERS PUBLISH BESIDE TRAIL BOUNDS.**

  | analysis | how it is computed | published tool | cost stated |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | **algebraic degree growth** | an upper bound per round count, from the round's degree and the Boura and Canteaut bound, or by division-property propagation solved by MILP | Ascon's table is analytic: `ASCONV12:1345 "The algebraic degree of the round functionp is 2, so the degree afterR rounds"` is at most 2^R, tightened by Boura and Canteaut. Gimli's is computed: `GIMLI:468 "(bit-based) division property[28,29] to evaluate the algebraic degree, and the"` `GIMLI:469 "propagation search is assisted by mixed integer linear programming (MILP)[32]."` | none stated in either source |
  | **zero-sum and higher-order differential distinguishers** | inside-out: a set of middle states whose forward and backward images both sum to zero, sized by the forward and inverse degree bounds | the Keccak reference credits the idea to Aumasson and Meier, `KECCAKREF:2258 "In [2] Aumasson and Meier introduced very simple and elegant distinguishers against reduced-"` round Keccak-f. Hu, Peyrin, Tan and Yap's tools (HATF in C++, DSF in Python) gave the full-round Ascon result, a `HUPEYRIN:318 "full 12-round Ascon permutation requiring only 255 calls while the previous best"` needed 2^130 | none in CPU time. HATF's complexity is stated in the order of the approximation, and the tools suit `HUPEYRIN:25 "quadratic round functions, such as Ascon and Xoodyak. DSF provides"` good linearisations. Erlacher et al. flag it as the caveat on every trail bound, `ASCONBOUNDS:77 "a grain of salt. Clustering eﬀects may lead to diﬀerentials with a higher overall probability"` | none stated |

  **What these analyses have reached.** The zero-sum distinguishers reach full rounds on Ascon-p (2^55) and Xoodoo (2^33, Liu et al., FD-59 section 3), and neither extends to the modes in its authors' or the designers' words: Hu et al. `HUPEYRIN:1662 "these two distinguishers work for the Ascon permutation rather than the keyed"` mode. **So a degree-2 round will be distinguished at full rounds as a bare permutation, and the evidence that matters is whether that reaches the mode.** That is KR4's question.

  **What a CPU-only machine could reproduce.** Every figure above is single-core CPU time on commodity x86. The dedicated searches parallelise by splitting the space, as Xoodoo's four parts and Ascon's partitioned SAT runs show. Wall-clock time on many cores is bounded by the longest single part unless that part splits further, and no source says whether it does. On this arithmetic, which no source states: the Keccak-f[200] 6-round search is about 102 single-core hours with a longest part of 37 hours, so about two days. The Xoodoo 2018 search is 16 core-days with a longest part of 5 days. The Xoodoo 2023 4-round search, the largest dedicated run, is 189 CPU days for both trail kinds, which is about 12 days on 16 cores if it splits evenly, and its single backward-extension step is reported at 1942 hours, about 81 days, if it does not. The SAT route to Ascon's 2^-72 was partitioned by its authors into many small problems, so 600 CPU days is about 38 days on 16 cores. The 2^-80 estimates, at 3898 to 6688 CPU days, would take 240 to 420 days on 16 cores, which is out of reach for a single machine. **The cost that dominates for a new configuration is writing the tool.** For every design surveyed the program was new work by the design's own authors, and the published CPU times cover only the run. No source states how long a tool took to write.

  **6. WHAT A DESIGNER OWES BEFORE A NEW ROUND IS TRUSTED.** **No source consulted states a minimum.** The nearest statements are these.

  - **Designers call trail bounds standard.** El Hirch et al.: `ASCONTRAILS:13 "squared correlation of linear trails is a standard requirement to evaluate the security"` of cryptographic primitives. Mella, Daemen and Van Assche: such bounds `XOODOOTRAILS:11 "security evaluation of a permutation. ForXoodoo, such bounds were proven using"` tree search. Stoffelen and Daemen, as design advice: resistance `CPMIXERS:747 "linear and diﬀerential cryptanalysis should be quantiﬁed by scanning a large search space"` of trails. Hu et al. state it as current practice and add its limit: `HUPEYRIN:54 "uating the security of a cipher [8,29]. Nowadays, all new schemes are requested"` `HUPEYRIN:55 "to claim resistance against these two attacks. However, resistance against the"` `HUPEYRIN:56 "plain diﬀerential and linear cryptanalysis does not necessarily lead to resistance"` against their variants.
  - **NIST's competition rules ask for a rationale and a list of known attacks, and discourage the unanalysed.** The lightweight call requires `LWCREQ:209 "algorithms. The document shall also include a design rationale, and an explanation for all the"` important design decisions, and a `LWCREQ:262 "statement that summarizes the known cryptanalytic attacks on the variants of the submission, and"` estimates of their complexity. It adds `LWCREQ:267 "The submission of algorithms that are not well-understood is discouraged. Submissions are"` `LWCREQ:268 "expected to have third-party analysis of the design, or leverage existing standards or heavily-"` analyzed components. These are entry rules for a competition, and they name no analysis method or bound.
  - **NIST approves a permutation only through a mode.** `SP800232:1573 "The Ascon permutations, including variants with different numbers of rounds, may be"` approved if modes for them are approved (FD-59 section 4). FIPS 202 says the same of Keccak-p.

  **What the practice shows a new round must carry, read from FD-58, FD-59 and this row together.** Proven trail bounds to the round count used, from a tool written for that round. A degree-growth table and a zero-sum or division-property reach. An invariant-subspace check of the linear layer with its constants. A clustering argument. And third-party analysis, which no amount of the designer's own computation replaces in NIST's criteria. This list is this row's inference.

  **7. WHAT CAME BACK EMPTY OR IS NOT SETTLED.**

  **No published trail search handles a Keccak θ at one row.** No source consulted runs one. Whether Ascon's tool structure transfers is an inference.

  **No released source for the Ascon tree-search tool was found.** Only the paper was read. The authors may have released it elsewhere.

  **No MILP or SAT survey was pinned.** The comparison in section 1 rests on the three trail papers' own related-work sections, which agree with one another. This run left the 2014 Sun et al. MILP paper and Mouha's MILP paper unfetched. No pin states CryptoSMT's scaling on Keccak-like rounds.

  **No CPU cost is published for any algebraic analysis** in the sources read. The degree tables and zero-sum constructions are presented as computations with no reported cost.

  **The licences of KeccakTools, XooTools, cpm and HDL are unsettled.** Section 4 records what the repository metadata declares, and file headers were left unread under the inspiration policy.

  **The pin names no hardware behind El Hirch et al.'s CPU days**, and no source consulted publishes the time to write any tool.

  **No bound was reproduced.** Every cost quoted is its authors' figure.

## What a mode's proof consumes of its permutation, and what a bare-permutation distinguisher does to it

### FD-61 every mode proof surveyed is stated over a random permutation and gives nothing for a concrete one, the bridge from ideal to real is a claim the designer makes on the function built over the permutation and cryptanalysts attack, the designers and the attackers both state that the full-round zero-sum distinguishers on Keccak-f, Ascon-p and Xoodoo reach no mode claim, the Keccak team's quantitative reason for that covers Keccak-f[1600] and does not reach 320- or 384-bit widths, where the designers rest instead on the attacker's lack of access to the inner state, Farfalle has no proof at all and runs 6 rounds on the argument that no adversary sees both sides of one permutation call, two of its round schedules fell to key recovery, and no source states a minimum a new permutation owes before a mode bound is stated over it

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question, as dispatched for the crypto arc's own permutation family (`docs/arcs/crypto-primitives-arc.md`), fourth of four pre-wave research runs after FD-58, FD-59 and FD-60: **what do the sponge, duplex, Farfalle and tree-hashing modes' security proofs assume of the underlying permutation? What happens to those claims when the permutation has a known bare-permutation distinguisher, or has no public cryptanalysis at all? And what must a permutation show before a mode's bound can honestly be stated over it?** Posed so it could come back `no`, as "the proofs assume an ideal permutation, and nothing short of the absence of any distinguisher connects a real permutation to them". **The first half of that `no` is what the sources say.** Every proof pinned here is a theorem about a random permutation: the sponge's indifferentiability bound, the full-state keyed duplex bound and Sakura's soundness. The sponge paper's authors state that no bound can be given for a concrete permutation. Farfalle has no proof, and its designers say so by design. **The second half does not hold as stated.** What connects a real permutation to a mode is a security claim on the function built over it, stated in the form of the ideal bound, with the permutation's own weaknesses left for cryptanalysts to find at the mode. Keccak's designers call the strict version, a permutation free of all structural distinguishers, the hermetic sponge strategy, and they say their own 24-round choice contradicts it strictly speaking. Xoodyak's designers adopt a weaker version by name, one that claims nothing about distinguishers on Xoodoo. **On a known distinguisher, the sources give `no effect on the claim` every time they speak.** The designers of Keccak, Ascon and Xoodyak and the attackers on Ascon all say the full-round zero-sum results do not reach the modes. The Gimli attackers add that the notion of distinguishing a fixed permutation is itself ill-defined. **On a permutation with no public cryptanalysis, no source says anything directly.** Every claim surveyed was accepted only after years of third-party analysis at the mode, and two Kravatte schedules fell within months of publication. **On what a permutation owes, no source states a minimum.** What the sources imply is in section 4.

  **What the proofs deliver for a concrete permutation.** The sponge paper's own conclusion: `SPONGEINDIFF:672 "concrete transformation or permutation is taken, no such bo unds can be given."` What the bound does exclude is generic attacks, `SPONGEINDIFF:678 "tacks we mean here attacks such as those described in [9–11], that do not exploit"` the permutation's specific properties. The same authors note that an indistinguishability result where the adversary cannot query `f` is weak for a hash, since `SPONGEINDIFF:64 "In a concrete hash function, f is pub-"` `SPONGEINDIFF:65 "licly speciﬁed and this is of limited interest."` The Gimli attackers state the assumption from outside: `GIMLIATK:42 "it is assumed in the underlying security proofs that the permutation"` `GIMLIATK:43 "used behaves like a permutation picked uniformly at random—apart of course"` from having a compact implementation.

  **Two limits on what an indifferentiability proof buys, stated by others.** Ristenpart, Shacham and Shrimpton found a scheme secure with a random oracle and broken with indifferentiable hash constructions, which `CAREFULCOMP:12 "contradicts the widely accepted belief that the indifferentiability composition theorem applies to any"` cryptosystem. They show `CAREFULCOMP:14 "ing that the formalizations used thus far implicitly exclude security notions captured by experiments"` with several disjoint adversarial stages. Xoodyak's hash claim writes that exclusion in, removing properties that `XOODYAKSPEC:474 "cannot be modeled as a single-stage game [ 27]."`. Separately, Gilbert, Heim Boissier, Khati and Rotella state that the keyed duplex's proven bound sits at `2^(c/2)`, and `DUPLEXGENATK:11 "However this bound is not known to be tight"`. Their generic forgery at `O(2^(3c/4))` breaks a claim stated above the proof: `DUPLEXGENATK:26 "attack breaks a security claim made by the"` `DUPLEXGENATK:27 "designers of the NIST lightweight competition candidateXoodyak. This"`, which the designers accept: `KECCAKCRYPT:603 "This forced us to correct our security claim on"` Xoodyak. That attack is generic. It would work with an ideal permutation.

  **2. THE BRIDGE FROM IDEAL TO REAL, AS THE DESIGNERS STATE IT.**

  **The mechanism is a claim.** The Xoodoo designers put it most plainly: a primitive carries its objective as a security claim, and `XOODOODESIGN:128 "In the security proof of the mode, the statements in the security claim are assumed to be"` `XOODOODESIGN:129 "true, and so the security of the scheme is conditional on the validity of these statements."` For the sponge, the claim is the flat sponge claim, Keccak's Claim 1: `KECCAKREF:256 "Claim 1. The expected success probability of any aĴack againstKђѐѐюј[r, c] with a workload equiv-"` alent to `N` calls shall be at most a random oracle's plus `1 − exp(−N(N+1)2^−(c+1))`, and `KECCAKREF:264 "We exclude hereweaknesses due to the mere fact thatKђѐѐюј- f [r + c] can be described com-"` pactly.

  **The hermetic sponge strategy, in its strict form.** `KECCAKREF:2401 "The design philosophy underlyingKђѐѐюј is thehermetic sponge strategy. This consists"` of the sponge for generic security, `KECCAKREF:2403 "calling a permutation (or transformation) that should not have structural properties with the"` exception of a compact description. The logic runs one way. `SPONGEFUNCS:249 "these results show that any aĴack against a sponge function implies that the permutation it"` uses is distinguishable, whence `SPONGEFUNCS:252 "sponge construction and building an underlying permutationf that should not have any"` structural distinguishers. The converse fails, and the designers say so: `SPONGEFUNCS:2980 "for f . However, a distinguisher forf does not necessarily imply an exploitable weakness in"` the sponge.

  **The designers' own departure from it.** Keccak-f[1600] has full-round zero-sum partitions, and `KECCAKREF:2331 "Not increasing the number of rounds, strictly speaking, contradicts the hermetic sponge"` strategy. Xoodyak's designers adopt a weaker form by name. Their strategy chooses `XOODYAKSPEC:821 "ber of rounds in Xoodoo such that the best attacks on Xoodyak are (claimed to be)"` the generic ones, and the strict form `XOODYAKSPEC:828 "in [5] targets the absence of distinguishers on the permutation in an absolute sense, whereas"` `XOODYAKSPEC:829 "we only consider the security of the resulting function Xoodyak. Hence we do not claim"` `XOODYAKSPEC:830 "that Xoodoo[12] is free of distinguishers, only that it is strong enough when plugged in"` Cyclist. Ascon's designers take the same position: its permutations are `ASCONV12:1046 "ered to be ideal 320-bit permutations. However, when used in the recommended"` modes, Ascon keeps a margin.

  **How a bare distinguisher is argued not to reach the mode: two arguments.**
  - **Advantage.** A distinguisher whose advantage is zero below `N` queries, `SPONGEFUNCS:3311 "distinguishing advantage that is zero up to some numberN of queries tof . IfN > 2b/2, such"` a distinguisher cannot touch a sponge at any capacity, since `c ≤ b − 1` and inner collisions end security at `2^(b/2)` anyway. For Keccak-f[1600] the zero-sums `KECCAKREF:2343 "rounds of Kђѐѐюј- f [1600] have zero advantage below something like21575 queries. Only"` `KECCAKREF:2344 "structural distinguishers onf that have non-zero advantage below2800 queries can possibly"` qualify as a threat.
  - **Applicability.** `SPONGEFUNCS:3302 "imposes values to bits in the inner part of the input tof are hard to exploit, as an adversary"` cannot set them directly, and `SPONGEFUNCS:3303 "Applicability must be studied on a case-by-case basis for"` each distinguisher. For zero-sums the adversary must `KECCAKREF:2347 "to the sponge function such that the input tof has the values of her choice, for many diﬀerent"` inputs, which the sponge prevents.

  **The advantage argument does not reach the small widths.** This is this row's arithmetic, and no source makes it. The Keccak team's threshold is `2^(b/2)`. At `b = 320` that is 2^160, and Ascon-p falls to a zero-sum at 2^55 (`HUPEYRIN`, FD-60). At `b = 384` it is 2^192, and Xoodoo falls at 2^33 (`NISTIR8454:1766 "et al. [128] showed a zero-sum distinguisher on the full 12-round Xoodoo with 2 33"`). Ascon's older table lists the full-round zero-sum at 2^130, `ASCONV12:1062 "Distinguisher Permutation 12 / 12 2130 Zero-sum [DEMS15]"`, also below 2^160. By the Keccak team's own sort, every one of these is a distinguisher that "can possibly qualify as a threat". The Ascon and Xoodyak designers answer it with applicability and the absence of a known attack. They make no advantage argument. **So at the widths the family's small `budget` reaches, what separates the mode from the bare permutation is the applicability argument, made case by case.**

  **The dissent, and who has not argued with the designers.** No third party pinned here disputes that a zero-sum distinguisher on Keccak-f, Ascon-p or Xoodoo leaves the modes standing. Hu et al. concede it for Ascon in their own paper. The Gimli attackers dispute the frame instead. `GIMLIATK:387 "This notion of distinguisher breaks down when we look at cryptographic"` permutations, since a keyless permutation is one instance, and `GIMLIATK:395 "mutations from random than it is to distinguish the identity from random. And"` `GIMLIATK:396 "yet, instantiating a sponge with each of these permutations yields hash functions"` with vastly different security levels. They also report the consequence in practice. Their results `GIMLIATK:1762 "Though our results do not pose a direct threat to theGimli NIST candidate,"` and yet low-complexity full-round distinguishers `GIMLIATK:1765 "have been considered in some cases as an issue worth countering by"` tweaking the design. Gimli's designers `GIMLIATK:1771 "but dismissed the distinguishers of Section 3, and did not introduce any change"`, and NIST left Gimli out of the finalists. The pins do not say why.

  **Why keyed modes run fewer rounds, and what that assumes of the attacker.**

  | design | rounds | the reason the source gives |
  |---|---|---|
  | Farfalle, Kravatte at 6, Xoofff at 6 | 6 per permutation, 18 input to output | access. `FARFALLE:112 "than in sponge-based modes, thanks to the fact that in Farfalle an adversary never has"` `FARFALLE:113 "access to both the input and the output of a permutation call."` A keyed sponge exposes partial inputs and outputs, where Farfalle `FARFALLE:881 "never leads to the input and output of a single call to pc, pd or pe being available to"` `FARFALLE:882 "the adversary. This implies that for equal safety margins in Farfalle one can afford to"` take fewer rounds. ### FD-63 every surveyed source counts a halting bounds check as enforcing memory safety and none asks for a static proof first: Schneider's theory makes the terminating monitor its defining enforcement mechanism with memory protection by bounds registers as a worked example, WebAssembly proves memory safety by a soundness theorem whose permitted outcomes include the trap, and Rust, Java and Ada define the out-of-range index as checked at run time; the sources separate the static proof by what it adds, that the check never fires, and SPARK and Schneider together place that addition under availability, which Schneider proves no halting monitor can enforce

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question, dispatched for `records/author-calls.md:96` after the author ruled on 2026-10-01 that an out-of-range request at `nb-bslice` traps (`:97`): **does the published theory of enforcement, and do memory-safe language definitions, count a run-time check that halts execution on an out-of-bounds access as ENFORCING memory safety; and do they distinguish that run-time guarantee from a static proof that the access is in bounds, and if so, how?** Posed so it could come back `no`, where the `no` is "only a proof before execution counts as enforcement, and a halting check is mitigation". **The first half comes back yes from every source that speaks to it.** Schneider's characterization defines its enforcement class by termination and names memory protection through base and bounds registers as an instance. WebAssembly's specification derives memory safety from a soundness theorem that lists the trap among a valid program's outcomes. Rust, Java and Ada define an out-of-range index as checked at run time, and Rust's guide to unsafe code lists aborting the program among the behaviours it calls safe. The formal characterization of memory safety by Azevedo de Amorim, Hrițcu and Pierce is mechanised over a language whose out-of-bounds load is an `Error` outcome. **The second half also comes back yes, and the sources agree on the line.** The static proof enforces the same property and adds one thing: the check provably never fires. Schneider says a proof removes the need for the run-time mechanism, Ada files the two as distinct error categories, and SPARK credits enabled run-time checks with stopping buffer overflow attacks and credits the proof with keeping that guarantee when the checks are compiled out and with keeping the service from crashing. Schneider proves that availability lies outside what any halting monitor can enforce. **No surveyed source withholds the word safe or enforced from a run-time-checked access until a proof exists.**

The theorem carries one precondition: `ENFSECPOLS:305 "enforcement mechanism has sufficient control over the target system to stop"` further steps, and the monitor must see every step the policy names.

  **2. THE STATIC ARM: THE SAME POLICY WITH THE MECHANISM REMOVED, AND ONE PROPERTY NO MONITOR REACHES.** Schneider sets the static route outside his class by the information it uses. `ENFSECPOLS:38 "Excluded from EM are mechanisms that use more information than is"` available from monitoring, so compilers and `ENFSECPOLS:40 "and theorem-provers, which analyze a static representation of the"` target are excluded, and how far that extra information reaches is, in 2000, `ENFSECPOLS:44 "much power is an open question."` Where he returns to it he states the gain as the monitor's absence: `ENFSECPOLS:395 "Finally, there is no need for any run-time enforcement mechanism if"` `ENFSECPOLS:396 "the target system can be analyzed and proved not to violate the security"` policy, which is the proof-carrying code case. **What a halting monitor cannot give is that the program keeps running.** `ENFSECPOLS:140 "Availability defines sets that are properties but not safety properties."` and so `ENFSECPOLS:144 "Thus, there are no enforcement mechanisms in EM for availability-at"` least as he defines it. A time-bounded variant that is a safety property still fails, `ENFSECPOLS:322 "that Real-Time Availability cannot be enforced using any mechanism in EM."` because a monitor cannot stop the clock.

  **3. THE EDIT, FOR THE RECORD OF THE CLAMP HALF.** Schneider files software fault isolation outside his class and says why. `ENFSECPOLS:377 "SFI implements memory protection, as"` his one-state automaton does, but `ENFSECPOLS:381 "The edits insert instructions to check and/or"` `ENFSECPOLS:382 "modify the values of operands, so that illegal memory references are never"` attempted, and `ENFSECPOLS:384 "SFI is not in class EM because SFI involves modifying the target sys-"` tem. A modifying mechanism needs a notion the paper leaves open, `ENFSECPOLS:45 "that modify a target system before executing it. Presumably the modified"` system is equivalent to the original, and the paper says a definition of equivalent is needed to analyse it. A clamp modifies an operand. Under this theory it belongs to a different mechanism class from the trap, and its correctness is a claim about equivalence that a halt never makes. Ligatti, Bauer and Walker's edit automata develop exactly this class and were unreachable (section 8). The author ruled the clamp out on 2026-10-01, so this section closes nothing open.

  **4. LANGUAGE DEFINITIONS: THE OUT-OF-RANGE INDEX IS CHECKED AT RUN TIME, AND THE CHECK SITS INSIDE THE SAFETY CLAIM.**

  **Rust** puts both routes in one sentence: `RUSTREFINDEX:108 "Array access is a [constant expression], so bounds can be checked at compile-time with a constant index value. Otherwise a check will be performed at run-time that will put the thread in a [_panicked state_][panic] if it fails."` The compile-time half is a lint, `RUSTREFINDEX:111 "// lint is deny by default."`, and the variable case is the run-time half, `RUSTREFINDEX:122 "])[n];  // panics"`. The panic is a language mechanism, `RUSTREFPANIC:8 "Some language constructs, such as out-of-bounds [array indexing], panic automatically."` Rust's guide to unsafe code lists what the language prevents after `NOMICONUNSAFE:17 "language cares about is preventing the following things:"` and lists separately what it calls safe, `NOMICONUNSAFE:71 "Rust is otherwise quite permissive with respect to other dubious operations."`, with `NOMICONUNSAFE:78 "* Abort the program"` on that list. Unchecked access is confined to the unsafe dialect, `NOMICONUNSAFE:3 "The only things that are different in Unsafe Rust are that you can:"` with `NOMICONUNSAFE:5 "* Dereference raw pointers"` first.

  **WebAssembly** is the plainest published case of a memory-safety claim resting on a trap. A trap ends the computation, `WASMOVERVIEW:53 "which immediately aborts execution."` and `WASMOVERVIEW:54 "Traps cannot be handled by WebAssembly code,"`, and for memory `WASMOVERVIEW:83 "A trap occurs if an access is not within the bounds of the current memory size."` The formal rule is `WASMEXECSPEC:434 "rule Step_read/load-num-oob:"` under the premise `WASMEXECSPEC:437 "  -- if $(i + ao.OFFSET + $size(nt)/8 > |$mem(z, x).BYTES|)"`, reducing to `TRAP`, and for writes `WASMEXECSPEC:512 "rule Step/store-num-oob:"` with `WASMEXECSPEC:513 "  z; (CONST at i) (CONST nt c) (STORE nt x ao)  ~>  z; TRAP"`. The appendix then states WASMSOUND:7 "The :ref:`type system <type-system>` of WebAssembly is *sound*, implying both *type safety* and *memory safety* with respect to the WebAssembly semantics. For example:" with `WASMSOUND:12 "* No memory location will be read or written except those explicitly defined by the program"` as a listed consequence, and the theorem's conclusion is that `WASMSOUND:1411 "every thread in a valid configuration either runs forever, traps, throws an exception, or terminates with a result that has the expected type."` Validation never looks at an index, WASMSOUND:19 "The typing rules defining WebAssembly :ref:`validation <valid>` only cover the *static* components of a WebAssembly program." **So WebAssembly's memory safety has a static half that proves every access goes through a checking instruction and proves nothing about any index, and a dynamic half that is the trap.**

  **Java** checks every access, `JLS10:195 "All array accesses are checked at run time; an attempt to use an index that is less than zero or greater than or equal to the length of the array causes an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException to be thrown (§15.10.4)."`, and the read rule is `JLS15:1346 "If the value of the index expression is less than zero, or greater than or equal to the array's length, then an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown."` The write rule says that no assignment occurs and the exception is thrown, in one sentence repeated word for word at `JLS15` lines 4361 and 4581 for simple and compound assignment, so it is cited by line and carries no quotation.

  **Ada** classifies the two routes as separate categories of error. `AARM11:1515 "<li>Errors that are required to be detected prior to run time by every Ada implementation;<br /></li>"` are the legality rules, and `AARM11:1530 "<li>Errors that are required to be detected at run time by the execution of an Ada program;<br /></li>"` are the checks, where `AARM11:1532 "Every Ada compiler is required to generate code that raises the corresponding exception if such an error situation arises during program execution."` The same paragraph lets the run-time error move forward when it is certain, `AARM11:1532 "[If such an error situation is certain to arise in every execution of a construct, then an implementation is allowed (although not required) to report this fact at compilation time.]"`, which is Rust's constant-index lint stated as a permission. The index check is one of these, `AARM115:134 "when accessing a component of an array object, check for each dimension that the given index value belongs to the range defined by the bounds of the array object."` Removing it is defined: `AARM115:26 "<b>Term entry: </b><b>suppress a check</b> &mdash; assert that the check cannot fail, and request that the compiler optimize by disabling the check"`, and `AARM115:302 "<p>If a given check has been suppressed, and the corresponding error situation occurs, the execution of the program is erroneous."` Erroneous execution is the category where `AARM11:1542 "Unlike bounded errors, there is no language-specified bound on the possible effect of erroneous execution; the effect is in general not predictable."` **Ada therefore has three tiers for one out-of-range index: refused before run time, detected at run time, and erroneous. `bget` sits in the third today (`docs/definitions/bug-classes.md:46`), the ruled trap moves `str-sub` and `bslice` to the second, and cell J is the first.**

  **5. THE STATIC AND DYNAMIC GUARANTEES STATED SIDE BY SIDE: SPARK.** SPARK's adoption levels put the proof at SPARKUSAGE:97 "#. `Silver level` - absence of run-time errors (AoRTE)". The user's guide states the division this row asks about in one paragraph: `SPARKUSAGE:344 "When run-time checks are enabled during execution, Ada programs are not"` `SPARKUSAGE:345 "vulnerable to the kind of attacks like buffer overflows that plague programs in"` C and C++, and in the `SPARKUSAGE:347 "case where run-time checks are disabled (in general for efficiency, but it"` `SPARKUSAGE:348 "could be for other reasons), proving their absence with |GNATprove| also"` prevents such attacks. **SPARK credits the run-time check with the memory-safety outcome and credits the proof with keeping it after the check is gone.** What the proof adds is named: `SPARKUSAGE:339 "AoRTE is important for ensuring safety in all possible operational conditions"` and `SPARKUSAGE:341 "conditions) or for ensuring availability of a service (absence of DOS attack"` `SPARKUSAGE:342 "that can crash the software)."` The Silver page agrees, `SPARKSILVER:1 "The goal of this level is to ensure that the program does not raise an"` unexpected exception, so that the control `SPARKSILVER:4 "flow of the program cannot be circumvented by exploiting a buffer overflow,"` and `SPARKSILVER:6 "the program cannot crash or behave erratically when compiled without"` run-time checking, and `SPARKSILVER:49 "The proof of AoRTE can be used to compile the final executable without"` run-time exceptions. Removing a check without the proof is the named hazard, after which the `SPARKUSAGE:673 "program is not protected anymore against programming mistakes (for safety) or"` attackers, and with the proof the checks may go SPARKUSAGE:682 "of code using pragma ``Suppress``, knowing that they will never fail at run" time. The price is stated too: `SPARKUSAGE:355 "Typically, 95% to 98% of run-time"` checks prove automatically and the rest need manual provers or a justification, and mixing proof with test has a limit, `SPARKUSAGE:389 "Certainly, formal verification cannot guarantee the same properties"` `SPARKUSAGE:390 "when part of a program is only tested, as when all of a program is proved."` FD-40 section 4 pinned the matching category name in `SPARKPROVE` and found the dynamic semantics unchanged by the proof; this section is the user's guide's account of what the proof is for.

  **6. THE FORMAL DEFINITION OF MEMORY SAFETY ADMITS THE ERROR OUTCOME.** Azevedo de Amorim, Hrițcu and Pierce define memory safety by a reasoning principle. The abstract, as copied in `MEMSAFEABS`, opens `MEMSAFEABS:3 "abstract: 'We give a rigorous characterization of what it means for a programming language to be memory safe, capturing the intuition that memory safety"` and states the principle as `MEMSAFEABS:5 "property: a program can neither affect nor be affected by unreachable parts of the state."` Its application is that `MEMSAFEABS:8 "we evaluate the security of"` `MEMSAFEABS:9 "a previously proposed dynamic monitor for memory safety of heap-allocated data."` **The paper judges a dynamic monitor by its characterization and treats it as a candidate enforcement.** The paper text was unreachable. The Coq development at `arthuraa/memory-safe-language` says in its README that one file builds on the `MEMSAFEREADME:33 "free name restriction construction. It also prove the main results of"` `MEMSAFEREADME:34 "the paper for that semantics."` The README names no title, so tying it to the POST 2018 paper rests on the first author's handle and the matching abstract; the development shows what the characterization admits. Its result type has three outcomes, `MEMSAFEBASIC:353 "computation successfully terminated, returning [x] as a"` `MEMSAFEBASIC:354 "result. [Error] indicates that an error occurred. [NotYet] indicates"` a step bound was hit. A load succeeds only where the heap holds the cell, `MEMSAFEBASIC:462 "        if s.2 p is Some v then Done (setm s.1 x v, s.2)"`, and is `Error` otherwise, and a store is the same, `MEMSAFEBASIC:468 "        if updm s.2 p (eval_expr cast e' s.1) is Some h' then Done (s.1, h')"`. A block holds exactly its allocated offsets, `MEMSAFEBASIC:282 "      if n < size vs then Some (nth VNil vs n)"`, while pointer arithmetic is unrestricted, `MEMSAFEBASIC:307 "  | Add, VNum n, VPtr p sz => VPtr (p.1, p.2 + n) sz"`. **An out-of-bounds load in the reference memory-safe language is therefore an `Error` outcome, and the frame theorems carry that outcome.** `MEMSAFEPROPS:148 "Theorem frame_error s1 s2 c k :"` takes `MEMSAFEPROPS:151 "  eval_com true c s1 k = Error ->"` to `MEMSAFEPROPS:152 "  eval_com true c (s1 ∪ s2) k = Error."`, and `MEMSAFEPROPS:162 "Corollary noninterference s1 s21 s' s22 c k :"` is built from it with the other two frame theorems. The language is checked only at run time: `MEMSAFEBASIC:497 "    | If e ct ce =>"` falls to `Error` on a non-boolean guard, and `grep -iE 'typing|typed|has_type'` over the five files the development's `_CoqProject` lists returns nothing. The formal definition is a property of the run-time semantics, and an execution that stops with an error satisfies it.
