### FD-67 the published field states design rules for an input language and writes them for protocols and file formats: recognize the whole input before acting on it, keep the input language deterministic context-free or weaker so two parsers can be proved to agree, refuse malformed input instead of tolerating it, and bound depth, size and expansion; the record reached carries those rules to a programming language's source reader only in separate pieces that never meet under the field's name, namely one LangSec survey that files Trojan Source as a differential between a programmer and a compiler, Go and CPython bounding the depth of their own source parsers, Go's after a CVE, CompCert, CakeML and CoStar verifying parsers for C, CakeML and Python source, and the Common Lisp, Clojure and Racket readers naming read-time evaluation as the danger in reading untrusted text, and no source surveyed applies the LangSec rule set as a design discipline to a source reader or to a homoiconic reader

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question, dispatched for the surface-syntax rework as research strand `langsec`: **does the published field state design rules for an input language that make its parser secure (input-handling security, "LangSec"), and do those rules reach a programming language's source reader, or only network protocols and file formats?** The answer: the rules are stated, and every source that states them as rules aims them at data a program receives (messages, files, arguments); their reach into source readers is partial, piecemeal, and made by compiler maintainers, verified-compiler authors and Lisp language specifications who do not use the field's vocabulary, with one exception in a LangSec venue that covers a single attack.
- measured: **1. THE RULES, AS THE REACHABLE RECORD STATES THEM.** The founding papers were unreachable (section 10), so the rules arrive here through the field's own later restatements and its toolkit documentation.

  **Full recognition before processing.** Patterson's primer for the Hammer toolkit asks that the code defining the valid inputs come first, `LSCHAMPRIMER:18 "valid inputs are) comes first, before any actions on the data parsed"`, because acting on data `LSCHAMPRIMER:20 "before the entire message has been fully parsed and recognized as"` `LSCHAMPRIMER:21 "correctly formed is the most common weakness that leads to memory"` corruption. The primer addresses `LSCHAMPRIMER:10 "secure parsers in C, C++, and other languages used in production"` programming, and its lectures work through messages: `LSCHAMPRIMER:67 "## Lecture 2 - JSON/HTTP"`, `LSCHAMPRIMER:79 "## Lecture 4 - Samba Base64 Parsing Crash"`.

  **Shotgun parsing is the named anti-pattern.** The 2016 taxonomy by Momot, Bratus, Hallberg and Patterson is reached only through King's verbatim quotation of it, introduced as `LSCPDV:197 "its authors provide the following definition:"`: `LSCPDV:199 "Shotgun parsing is a programming antipattern whereby parsing and input-validating code is mixed with and spread across processing code"`, and `LSCPDV:203 "Shotgun parsing necessarily deprives the program of the ability to reject invalid input instead of processing it."` because `LSCPDV:203 "Late-discovered errors in an input stream will result in some portion of invalid input having been processed"`.

  **The input language's class.** Ali and Smith restate the founding proposal: Sassaman et al. `LSCALI23:83 "made a proposal for keeping the complexity of"` `LSCALI23:84 "input languages within those bounds where the equivalence is"` `LSCALI23:85 "decidable namely, deterministic context-free languages."`

  **2. PARSER DIFFERENTIALS, AND WHAT IS DECIDABLE ABOUT THEM.**

  **The definition and the decidability line.** `LSCALI23:11 "Parser differentials emerge when two (or more)"` parsers read one input two ways. Testing two parsers for agreement is testing two grammars for equivalence, which `LSCALI23:626 "is undecidable for non-determinstic CFGs and higher, but"` `LSCALI23:628 "decidable for deterministic CFGs and lower."`, and the deterministic case's `LSCALI23:81 "decidability for deterministic context-free grammars (CFGs)"` `LSCALI23:82 "was not established [11] until 1997"`. That is weak equivalence, the same accepted strings. For parse trees the survey reports a stronger result: strong equivalence `LSCALI23:645 "of CFGs is decidable"` even for non-deterministic grammars, because two grammars are strongly equivalent exactly when their `LSCALI23:652 "parenthesized versions are weakly equivalent."`, since the `LSCALI23:653 "parentheses embody the parse tree structure."`, and after Reghizzi et al. `LSCALI23:655 "parenthesized CFGs are deterministic."` The authors leave the application open: `LSCALI23:668 "Using these strong-equivalence results and applying them"` to differentials is future work.

  **The model is wider than one grammar.** The crafted input is often `LSCALI23:648 "outside the language being targeted"`, and parsers built for different languages, `LSCALI23:599 "that, combined with overly liberal acceptance, leads to lots of"` places to put it.

  **The cases the brief names.** Android master key, first form: `LSCALI23:90 "The Android OS has two parsers for APK files."`, and `LSCALI23:103 "the verifier read those bytes as 16-bit signed integers"`. Second form: the ZIP `LSCALI23:431 "format allows defining two files with the same name in a"` archive with no rule for which wins, the `LSCALI23:433 "case of duplicates. In the case of a maliciously crafted APK,"`. X.509: `LSCALI23:250 "if null bytes are included in the domain name, then ambi-"`guity over the terminator splits CA and browser. Psychic Paper in iOS worked `LSCALI23:188 "because the parser was more permissive in accepting an input"` than its specification. Zoom's XML stanza smuggling began in a `LSCALI23:274 "mistake in implementing the Unicode spec."` Duplicate keys recur across formats: `LSCALI23:418 "When faced with input with duplicate entries"` each parser picks one.

  **HTTP.** RFC 9112 defines the attack as a differential: `LSCRFC9112:1794 "Request smuggling ([Linhart]) is a technique that exploits"` `LSCRFC9112:1795 "differences in protocol parsing among various recipients to hide"` requests. A message carrying both framing headers (`LSCRFC9112:930 "3.  If a message is received with both a Transfer-Encoding and a"`) `LSCRFC9112:934 "(Section 11.1) and ought to be handled as an error.  An"`, and the RFC warns of its own leniency: `LSCRFC9112:385 "However, lenient parsing can result in request"` `LSCRFC9112:386 "smuggling security vulnerabilities if there are multiple recipients"`.

  **JSON.** RFC 8259 leaves the differential in the standard: `LSCRFC8259:322 "The names within an object SHOULD be unique."`, and with duplicates behaviour is `LSCRFC8259:333 "unpredictable.  Many implementations report the last name/value pair"`, while `LSCRFC8259:545 "A JSON parser MAY accept non-JSON forms or extensions."` RFC 7493 closes three of the gaps as a profile: `LSCRFC7493:159 "Objects in I-JSON messages MUST NOT have members with duplicate"` names, `LSCRFC7493:125 "I-JSON messages MUST be encoded using UTF-8"`, and strings `LSCRFC7493:128 "MUST NOT include code points that identify Surrogates or"` Noncharacters. Seriot's test suite keeps a class of inputs where `LSCJSONTS:21 "parsers are free to accept or reject content"` and a set of files that `LSCJSONTS:25 "These files contain weird structures and characters that parsers may understand differently"`.

  **3. POSTEL'S LAW AND LENIENT PARSING.** RFC 9413 keeps two of the robustness principle's three aspects and narrows the third: tolerance of the unexpected is an `LSCRFC9413:143 "interpretation that advocates for tolerating unexpected inputs is no"` `LSCRFC9413:144 "longer considered best practice in all scenarios."`, and `LSCRFC9413:197 "However, ignoring faulty or ambiguous input is almost always the"` `LSCRFC9413:198 "incorrect solution to the problem."` The decay mechanism: `LSCRFC9413:320 "An implementation that reacts to variations in the manner recommended"` `LSCRFC9413:321 "in the robustness principle enters a pathological feedback cycle."`, until `LSCRFC9413:333 "A flaw can become entrenched as a de facto standard."` The remedy, virtuous intolerance: `LSCRFC9413:510 "Choosing to generate fatal errors for unspecified conditions instead"` `LSCRFC9413:511 "of attempting error recovery can ensure that faults receive"` attention, and `LSCRFC9413:473 "Early implementations of protocols have a stronger obligation to"` `LSCRFC9413:474 "closely follow specifications, as their behavior will affect all"` later ones. Its security section calls the problem `LSCRFC9413:607 "especially acute for any protocol where security depends on agreement"` `LSCRFC9413:608 "about semantics of protocol elements."` The RFC cites no LangSec paper: a search of the pin for Sassaman, LangSec and language-theoretic returns nothing.

  **4. PARSE, DON'T VALIDATE.** King defines `LSCPDV:177 "a parser is just a function that consumes less-structured input and produces more-structured output"` and places it `LSCPDV:179 "right on the boundary between a program and the outside world, and once those checks have been performed, they never need to be checked again"`. She names shotgun parsing from the LangSec taxonomy as the danger validation invites (section 1), and her cure is the full-recognition rule restated for a type system: `LSCPDV:209 "Parsing avoids this problem by stratifying the program into two phases"`, `LSCPDV:209 "where failure due to invalid input can only happen in the first phase"`. Two differences from the LangSec rule are explicit. She says nothing about the input language's class, and she allows more than LangSec's class rule does: `LSCPDV:249 "Avoiding shotgun parsing just means you shouldn"`'t act on input before it is fully parsed, and `LSCPDV:249 "Plenty of useful parsers are context-sensitive."`

  **5. RESOURCE BOUNDS: WHAT A RECOGNIZER MUST BOUND.**

  **The standards permit bounds and require none.** RFC 8259: `LSCRFC8259:547 "An implementation may set limits on the size of texts that it"` `LSCRFC8259:548 "accepts.  An implementation may set limits on the maximum depth of"` nesting, with the same lower-case "may" for number range and string length.

  **Measured consequence for depth.** The suite's results of `LSCJSONRES:14 "<PRE>2019-11-16 19:58:31</PRE>"` list 67 parser columns, the first `LSCJSONRES:128 "<TH class=\"vertical\"><DIV>.NET System.Text.Json 4.6.0</DIV></TH>"` and the last at line 194. This run counted the row `LSCJSONRES:199 "n_structure_100000_opening_arrays.json</TD>        <TD class=\"EXPECTED_RESULT\">"` and found 11 of 67 cells marked CRASH, and the row `LSCJSONRES:198 "n_structure_open_array_object.json</TD>        <TD class=\"EXPECTED_RESULT\">"` with 13 of 67, where the suite's crash code means `LSCJSONTS:12 "the process did crash"`.

  **Expansion needs a ratio bound, and depth does not bound it.** CPython's XML security notes describe the billion laughs attack as one that `LSCPYXML:103 "uses multiple levels of nested entities. Each entity refers to another entity"` and whose `LSCPYXML:105 "The exponential expansion results in several gigabytes of text and"` memory; the quadratic variant is less `LSCPYXML:112 "efficient as the exponential case but it avoids triggering parser countermeasures"` `LSCPYXML:113 "that forbid deeply nested entities."` Expat bounds output against input: it `LSCEXPAT:3267 "Sets the maximum tolerated amplification factor for protection against <a href="` billion laughs, `LSCEXPAT:3269 "attacks</a> (default: <code>100.0</code>) of parser <code>p</code> to"` a chosen factor, computed as `LSCEXPAT:3280 "<pre>amplification := (direct + indirect) / direct</pre>"`, and warns that `LSCEXPAT:3311 "<strong>Note:</strong> Peak amplifications of factor 15,000 for the entire"` `LSCEXPAT:3312 "payload and of factor 30,000 in the middle of parsing have been observed with"` small benign files.

  **Two production source readers carry the same bounds, one after a CVE.** CPython documents its own source parser as crashable: `LSCPYAST:2283 "It is possible to crash the Python interpreter with a"` `LSCPYAST:2284 "sufficiently large/complex string due to stack depth limitations"`. Its literal reader `LSCPYAST:2328 "This function had been documented as \"safe\" in the past without defining"` what that meant, and `LSCPYAST:2332 "attack: A relatively small input can lead to memory exhaustion or to C stack"` `LSCPYAST:2333 "exhaustion, crashing the process. There is also the possibility for"` excessive CPU use, so calling it on `LSCPYAST:2335 "untrusted data is thus not recommended."` The tokenizer bounds nesting, `LSCPYSTATE:9 "#define MAXLEVEL 200        /* Max parentheses level */"` and `LSCPYSTATE:8 "#define MAXINDENT 100       /* Max indentation level */"`, and refuses with `LSCPYLEXER:435 "too many nested parentheses"`; the generated parser bounds recursion at `LSCPYPEGGEN:40 "#  define MAXSTACK 6000"` and refuses with `LSCPYPEGERR:399 "Parser stack overflowed - Python source too complex to parse"`. Go's source parser carried a CVE: `LSCGOVULN:22 "summary: Stack exhaustion due to deeply nested types in go/parser"`, `LSCGOVULN:24 "Calling any of the Parse functions on Go source code which contains deeply"` `LSCGOVULN:25 "nested types or declarations can cause a panic due to stack exhaustion."`, filed as `LSCGOVULN:35 "id: CVE-2022-1962"` under `LSCGOVULN:36 "cwe: 'CWE-674: Uncontrolled Recursion'"` and `LSCGOVULN:5 "- fixed: 1.17.12"`. The fix is a depth bound, `LSCGOPARSER:123 "// maxNestLev is the deepest we're willing to recurse during parsing"`, `LSCGOPARSER:124 "const maxNestLev int = 1e5"`, refused as `LSCGOPARSER:129 "exceeded max nesting depth"`.

  **6. CONSTRUCTION METHODS THE FIELD RECOMMENDS.**

  **Combinators over a chosen backend.** Hammer `LSCHAMMER:1 "it provides a parser combinator interface for writing grammars as inline domain-specific languages"` and runs them on `LSCHAMMER:14 "Packrat parsing"`, `LSCHAMMER:15 "LL(k)"`, `LSCHAMMER:16 "GLR"` or `LSCHAMMER:17 "LALR"` backends, `LSCHAMMER:1 "making it ideal for parsing binary data such as images, network packets, audio, and executables"`.

  **Verified generation, with a definition of a secure parser.** EverParse's output `LSCEVERPARSE:17 "descriptions. The resulting code is verified to be safe (no"` `LSCEVERPARSE:18 "overflow, no use after free), correct (parsing is the inverse of"` `LSCEVERPARSE:19 "serialization) and non-malleable (each message has a unique"` binary representation. A parser `LSCEVERPARSE:158 "is non-malleable (or injective) when it accepts at most one"` representation of each message, and `LSCEVERPARSE:166 "We say that p is a secure parser for V if p is non-malleable"` `LSCEVERPARSE:167 "and complete. If p is secure, then it is also correct and exact"`. Its scope is binary formats, `LSCEVERPARSE:15 "and serializers from tag-length-value binary message format"` descriptions; going `LSCEVERPARSE:1055 "with arbitrary data dependence and lookahead, beyond the"` `LSCEVERPARSE:1056 "class of context-free languages—however, coming up with"` `LSCEVERPARSE:1057 "efficient verified implementations of parsers for such language"` `LSCEVERPARSE:1058 "classes is an open question."` Attempts to `LSCEVERPARSE:984 "create context-free or even regular specifications for X.509."` founder because `LSCEVERPARSE:985 "However, due to the context-sensitive nature of ASN.1, these"` efforts must simplify the format.

  **A verified lexer.** Verbatim `LSCVERBATIM:18 "is implemented and verified with the Coq Proof Assistant."`, and its output `LSCVERBATIM:41 "the string. The resulting list of tokens satisfies a common"` `LSCVERBATIM:42 "specification known as the “maximal munch” principle: each"` `LSCVERBATIM:43 "token is the longest prefix of the remaining input string that"` matches a rule. Its worked instance is JSON: `LSCVERBATIM:360 "Verbatim source code to OCaml, instantiated a JSON lexer,"`.

  **The field's own account of where verification has gone.** The Bohemia paper at the same workshop says verification efforts have `LSCBOHEMIA:30 "focused on specific parsing algorithms or specific kinds of"` `LSCBOHEMIA:31 "grammars (e.g., network formats)."`

  **7. DOES ANY OF IT REACH A SOURCE READER?**

  **In a LangSec venue, once.** Ali and Smith's survey includes `LSCALI23:576 "Example 16: Unicode Trojan Source"`: bidirectional controls can `LSCALI23:580 "be utilized to create source code which looks innocuous to a"` `LSCALI23:581 "programmer reading the displayed text but is actually code"` `LSCALI23:582 "instructing the compiler to do something different."` Line 582 is the pin's only occurrence of the word compiler. The survey classes it as a differential between a human parser and a machine parser, and applies none of the other rules (class, full recognition, bounds) to the compiler.

  **The workshop record reached.** This run converted all 38 papers of the 2021, 2022 and 2023 IEEE LangSec workshops held in `gangtan/LangSec-papers-and-slides` and searched them. Their input subjects are PDF, binary and IoT packet formats, BLE, URLs, x86 instruction decoders, ICC colour profiles and file dialects; the rest are grammar inference, parser-generator testing, program analyses and type systems. None takes a compiler's or interpreter's source reader as its subject. Compilers appear as context or as tools the authors built for their own format languages, as in Bohemia's `LSCBOHEMIA:34 "Parsing is ubiquitous in a variety of tools: compilers,"`; Lisp appears only as an implementation language (Clojure, ACL2) or as a metalanguage notation. In none of the 38 is Lisp source the input analysed.

  **Production compilers, without the vocabulary.** Section 5: CPython and Go bound their source readers by depth and refuse with a message, and Go's case is a CVE against the source parser. Neither source uses LangSec terms.

  **Verified parsers for source languages, framed as correctness.** CompCert's changelog for `LSCCOMPCERT:1181 "# Release 2.3, 2014-05-05"` reads `LSCCOMPCERT:1187 "The parser is now formally verified against the ISO C99 grammar plus"` `LSCCOMPCERT:1188 "CompCert's extensions.  The verification proves that the parser"` `LSCCOMPCERT:1189 "recognizes exactly the language specified by the grammar, and that"` `LSCCOMPCERT:1190 "the grammar has no ambiguities.  For more details, see the paper"` `LSCCOMPCERT:1191 "Validating LR(1) parsers"`. CakeML's parser carries completeness, `LSCCAKEML:5 "a parse tree in the grammar, then the function should return that parse tree"`, soundness, `LSCCAKEML:7 "correct according to the grammar (*soundness*)."`, totality, `LSCCAKEML:13 "well-formed, which means that execution will always terminate (*totality*). As"`, and determinism, `LSCCAKEML:15 "that execution is *deterministic*."` CoStar is `LSCCOSTAR:2 "A parser based on the ALL(*) algorithm, implemented and verified with Coq."` and is benchmarked on Python source, `LSCCOSTAR:103 ": files from the Python 3.6.12 standard library"`. Gross and Chlipala summarize that `LSCPARSES:1004 "Several projects have used proof assistants to apply verified parsers within larger programming-language tools."`, and that Jitawa and CakeML `LSCPARSES:1004 "language implementations include verified parsers, handling Lisp and ML languages, respectively."` None of these sources states its result as input-handling security.

  **8. THE HOMOICONIC READER.**

  **Read-time evaluation is the named danger, and it is on by default.** Common Lisp's `#.` is read as the value of evaluating the next datum; `LSCCLHSDOT:22 "The evaluation is done during the"` read, when the `LSCCLHSDOT:22 "notation is encountered. The <TT>#.</TT> syntax therefore performs a read-time evaluation of"` the datum, and only when `*read-eval*` is false does the reader refuse, `LSCCLHSDOT:23 "In that situation, an error of"` type reader-error. Clojure: `LSCCLJCORE:3803 "Note that read can execute code (controlled by *read-eval*),"`, the flag `LSCCLJCORE:6750 "Defaults to true (or value specified by system property, see below)"`, `LSCCLJCORE:6752 "including syntax that can cause code to execute. It should never be"` `LSCCLJCORE:6753 "used with untrusted sources. See also: clojure.edn/read.***"`, and the disabled form turns off `LSCCLJCORE:6756 "the eval reader (#=) and record/type literal syntax are disabled in read/load."` The language points data elsewhere: `LSCCLJCORE:3806 "For data structure interop use clojure.edn/read\""`. Racket's reader can select another parser in the input itself (`LSCRKTREAD:313 "or @litchar{#!} are allowed for selecting a parser. See"`), and its default parameterization `LSCRKTREAD:337 "provides safety when reading from untrusted sources, since the default"` `LSCRKTREAD:338 "values disable evaluation of arbitrary code via @hash-lang[] or"` `#reader`.

  **A verified Lisp reader proves the round trip.** Jitawa's HOL4 development defines a printer and then `LSCJITAWA:12 "2. we define a function which parses printed s-expressions."`, and its exported theorem is `LSCJITAWA:1331 "!exp. string2sexp (sexp2string exp) = exp"`. In EverParse's terms (section 6) that is correctness, parsing inverts printing. This run found no theorem of the exactness or non-malleability form in the file: its four `Theorem` blocks are at lines 30, 284, 1323 and 1330, and the stream theorem `LSCJITAWA:1388 "val sexp_parse_stream_thm = store_thm("` sits inside a comment opened at line 1380.

  **What none of the Lisp sources does.** None uses the LangSec vocabulary, none discusses the reader's grammar class, none treats two readers of one source as a differential, and none applies full recognition before macro expansion. The danger they name is evaluation during reading, and the remedy they give is a flag or a separate data reader.

  **9. WHAT THIS GIVES A SURFACE-SYNTAX REWORK.** Readings of the pins for a reader designed fresh; this section rules nothing.

  - **Read the whole file to a datum tree before any expansion or evaluation.** The reader is the recognizer and expansion is processing (`LSCHAMPRIMER:18`, `LSCPDV:209`). A refusal anywhere in the file stops everything after it.
  - **Keep the datum grammar deterministic context-free and fully parenthesized.** That class is where agreement between two readers is decidable (`LSCALI23:628`), and a parenthesized grammar carries its parse tree in the string (`LSCALI23:653`, `LSCALI23:655`). A formatter, an editor mode and the compiler can then be checked against one grammar. Each special-case token beyond parentheses and atoms is a place two readers can part.
  - **No read-time evaluation and no reader selection from inside the source.** Common Lisp, Clojure and Racket each name these as the hazard (`LSCCLHSDOT:22`, `LSCCLJCORE:6752`, `LSCRKTREAD:338`); a fresh reader can omit them instead of guarding them with a flag.
  - **Refuse; never repair.** RFC 9413's virtuous intolerance (`LSCRFC9413:510`) and its warning that early implementations set the standard (`LSCRFC9413:473`) apply with most force to a language's first reader. Duplicate keys, two spellings of one datum, and accepted extensions are the JSON precedents of a differential (`LSCRFC8259:333`, `LSCRFC8259:545`); EverParse's non-malleability (`LSCEVERPARSE:158`) is the formal target, one accepted spelling per datum wherever whitespace and comments allow.
  - **Bound depth, token length, file size and any expansion, and refuse at the bound with a message.** CPython bounds parenthesis depth at 200, indentation at 100 and parser recursion at 6000 (`LSCPYSTATE:9`, `LSCPYSTATE:8`, `LSCPYPEGGEN:40`); Go bounds nesting at 1e5 after CVE-2022-1962 (`LSCGOPARSER:124`, `LSCGOVULN:35`). If the reader ever expands anything, bound the ratio of output to input as Expat does (`LSCEXPAT:3280`), since a depth bound alone misses quadratic growth (`LSCPYXML:113`).
  - **Restrict the character repertoire at the reader.** The one LangSec treatment of source code is a Unicode differential between a reader of the screen and the compiler (`LSCALI23:580`), and I-JSON's exclusion of surrogates and noncharacters (`LSCRFC7493:128`) is the nearest standards precedent for refusing code points in a text format.
  - **Specify the reader as a grammar and prove or validate it.** CompCert's validated LR(1) parser proves the parser recognizes exactly the grammar's language and the grammar is unambiguous (`LSCCOMPCERT:1189`, `LSCCOMPCERT:1190`); CakeML's PEG carries soundness, completeness, totality and determinism (`LSCCAKEML:7`, `LSCCAKEML:13`, `LSCCAKEML:15`); Verbatim proves a maximal-munch lexer (`LSCVERBATIM:42`). A print-then-read theorem alone, Jitawa's form (`LSCJITAWA:1331`), proves correctness on the printer's image; exactness (`LSCEVERPARSE:167`) is a separate statement a secure reader owes.
  - **Hand the compiler a type that cannot hold an unread form.** King's stratification (`LSCPDV:209`) puts every reader failure in the first phase, so later passes have no reader errors to report.

  **10. WHAT THE SOURCES DO NOT SETTLE, AND WHAT CAME BACK EMPTY.**

  - **No source applies the LangSec rule set to a programming language's source reader as a design discipline**, and none to a homoiconic reader. The nearest is one example in one survey (section 7), which applies the differential idea and none of the other rules.
  - **No source states which bounds a reader must carry.** RFC 8259 says "may"; the production values (200, 100, 6000, 1e5, a ratio of 100) are each project's choice, and no source derives them.
  - **No source says whether the parenthesized-grammar equivalence result has been applied to a real pair of parsers.** The survey calls it future work (`LSCALI23:668`).
  - **No source measures how often source readers differ.** JSONTestSuite measures JSON parsers; nothing comparable was found for the readers of one programming language.
  - **Primaries reached only through restatement.** The decidability results (Sénizergues on deterministic equivalence, Paull and Unger on structural equivalence), Kaminsky, Patterson and Sassaman's PKI Layer Cake, Freeman's Android master-key analysis and the Seven Turrets taxonomy are quoted here as Ali and Smith or King report them.
  - **Unreachable from this sandbox**, refused by the egress proxy to both `curl` and WebFetch: `langsec.org` (Sassaman et al., "The Halting Problems of Network Stack Insecurity", `;login:` 2011; "Security Applications of Formal Language Theory", TR2011-709; "A Patch for Postel's Robustness Principle"; the Seven Turrets paper; "Curing the Vulnerable Parser", `;login:` 2017; the workshop pages and calls for papers), and `usenix.org`, `cs.dartmouth.edu`, `digitalcommons.dartmouth.edu`, `esat.kuleuven.be`, `ws.engr.illinois.edu`, `repository.ubn.ru.nl` (Poll's LangSec chapter), `seriot.ch` (the "Parsing JSON is a Minefield" article), `lexi-lambda.github.io` (the served post; its repository source was reached), `rfc-editor.org`, `datatracker.ietf.org`, `arxiv.org`, `dl.acm.org`, `semanticscholar.org`, `researchgate.net` and `wikipedia.org`. GitHub code search found no copy of the 2011 papers, and the workshop record before 2021 is absent from the GitHub repositories searched.
  - **Consulted and not pinned.** Narcissus's tutorial (`mit-plv/fiat`, `src/Narcissus/Examples/README.v`) targets a sensor's packet format, the same scope as EverParse. Jourdan and Pottier's C11 parser README (`jhjourdan/C11parser`) was read and adds nothing the CompCert pin lacks. Go's JSON scanner bounds depth at 10000 and repeats the go/parser point.
  - **Four pins are PDF transcriptions.** `LSCALI23`, `LSCBOHEMIA` and `LSCVERBATIM` are two-column workshop papers and `LSCEVERPARSE` the USENIX Security 2019 paper, converted with `pdftotext -layout` 24.02.0. Columns interleave on one line, and every span quoted sits inside one column. Hyphenation at line ends is kept as printed (`ambi-`, `for-`).

- element:  `none`. This row answers a question about the outside world and mints nothing. It is input to the surface-syntax rework, and section 9 bears on the reader rows `records/lenses/problems.md:1434` (PRB-102, bidirectional controls and confusables accepted in source) and `records/lenses/problems.md:1462` (PRB-104, refusals that name nothing), both left unedited.

### FD-68 the published field specifies Unicode in program source as a menu of requirements a language declares against, complete and implementable for identifiers, whitespace, syntax characters and normalization (UAX #31) and for identifier spoofing checks (UTS #39), with bidirectional display handed to editors through UAX #9 HL4 and UTS #55, and silent on what a reader does with an invisible or default-ignorable character inside a string literal; no surveyed production compiler implements the whole menu: Elixir comes nearest by refusing restricted and mixed-script identifiers, rustc denies nine of the twelve bidi controls in comments and literals and only warns on confusables, GCC warns on unpaired bidi controls and non-NFC identifiers with no confusable check, clang keeps both checks in clang-tidy, Python folds identifiers under NFKC with no UTS #39 check, Go, Java and ECMAScript compare identifiers as unnormalized code points, Swift's reference grammar lists the override characters as identifier characters, and Zig keeps identifiers ASCII

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question, dispatched for the reader rework the author asked for (a secure reimplementation of Unicode handling, with `records/lenses/problems.md:1434` PRB-102 recording that the reader today accepts bidi controls, zero-width characters and confusables): **does the published field specify a complete, implementable policy for Unicode in program source (which characters a lexer accepts in identifiers, in comments, in string literals and in whitespace; normalization; confusable and mixed-script checks; bidirectional display), and do production compilers implement that policy in full or in part?** Posed so it could come back `no` on both halves. **The first half comes back partly.** Unicode publishes the policy as numbered requirements a language selects and declares, with data files that make each one mechanical: UAX #31 for identifiers, whitespace, syntax characters and normalization, UTS #39 for restricted characters, confusable skeletons, mixed-script detection and restriction levels, UAX #9 HL4 for display. Both standards place the spoofing defence for programming languages in diagnostics and display and leave the contents of comments and string literals open: UAX #31 asks that comments and strings freely contain the format controls it allows between tokens, and no pinned source states what a reader does with a zero-width or other default-ignorable code point inside a literal. UTS #55, the document the others cite for source code, was unreachable, so its section on that point stands unread. **The second half comes back in part, everywhere.** Each surveyed compiler implements a different subset. Three languages state in writing which UAX #31 requirements they meet: Rust (RFC 2457) claims R3, and C++ and Elixir decline it. Python's reference states that it does not necessarily conform. Trojan Source (CVE-2021-42574, CVE-2021-42694) moved rustc, GCC, the clang-tidy checks, three code hosts and two editors, and Java declared it an editor problem.
- measured: **1. UAX #31 REVISION 43 (UNICODE 17.0): A MENU A LANGUAGE DECLARES AGAINST.**

  Conformance is a declaration. An implementation `UCSUAX31:491 "claiming conformance to this specification shall identify the"` version, and shall describe `UCSUAX31:502 "the following requirements it observes"`: R1 default identifiers, R1b stable identifiers, R2 immutable identifiers, R3a and R3b whitespace and syntax characters, R3c operators, R4 to R7 normalization and case, R8 hashtags. The default identifier is the D1 syntax with Start and Continue set to XID_Start and XID_Continue, `UCSUAX31:663 "Continue to the properties XID_Start and XID_Continue, respectively, and leaving Medial empty."`, and any change is a declared profile. Profiles are expected; `UCSUAX31:562 "example, Java and C++ identifiers include ‘$’, which is a"` Pattern_Syntax character. Stability across Unicode versions is a separate requirement, R1b, that an implementation must `UCSUAX31:815 "guarantee that identifiers are stable across versions of the Unicode"` Standard. The alternative R2 defines an identifier as any string free of `UCSUAX31:2048 "Pattern_White_Space=True"`, Pattern_Syntax, `UCSUAX31:2050 "General_Category=Private_Use, Surrogate, or Control"` and noncharacters, and such identifiers `UCSUAX31:2092 "cannot be compared for NFC, NFKC, or case-insensitive equality"`. The annex anticipates languages leaving R2, since `UCSUAX31:2064 "the inapplicability of measures guarding against spoofing attacks may warrant such a change in definition."`

  **The annex states that conformance leaves the spoofing problem open.** Default identifiers `UCSUAX31:794 "they are still subject to spoofing issues arising from invisible characters,"` visually identical characters and bidi reordering. Default-ignorable code points are problematic `UCSUAX31:924 "because the effects they represent are stylistic or otherwise out of"` scope and are often invisible, and `UCSUAX31:940 "Because variation selectors and joining controls request a difference in display but do not guarantee it, they do not work well in general-purpose identifiers."` `UCSUAX31:941 "A profile should be used to remove them from general-purpose identifiers"`, and section 7.3 defines that profile, `UCSUAX31:3076 "The default-ignorable exclusion profile for default identifiers consists of the exclusion of the code points with property Default_Ignorable_Code_Point from the sets"` Start and Continue. Its own note bounds it: `UCSUAX31:3079 "excluding default-ignorable code points does not prevent spoofing issues."` The placement of the defence is explicit: `UCSUAX31:943 "For programming language identifiers, spoofing issues are more comprehensively addressed by higher-level diagnostics rather than at the syntactic level."`

  **Whitespace (R3a) is fixed to eleven code points with three roles.** `UCSUAX31:2189 "A sequence of one or more of any of the following characters shall be interpreted as a sequence of one or more end of line:"` LF, VT, FF, CR, NEL, `UCSUAX31:2196 "U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR"` and PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR. `UCSUAX31:2200 "The Pattern_White_Space characters with the property Default_Ignorable_Code_Point shall be treated as ignorable format controls"`, which `UCSUAX31:2213 "are U+200E LEFT-TO-RIGHT MARK and U+200F RIGHT-TO-LEFT MARK. The characters to be treated as horizontal space under item 3 of"` R3a-1 are SPACE and TAB. `UCSUAX31:2201 "All other characters in Pattern_White_Space shall be interpreted as horizontal space."` A partial set of line terminators is itself a hazard: failing to treat all seven `UCSUAX31:2219 "as line terminators would lead to spoofing issues; see Unicode Technical Standard #55"`. The two marks exist to repair display order, because without higher-level protocols `UCSUAX31:2232 "tokens may be visually"` `UCSUAX31:2233 "reordered by the Unicode Bidi Algorithm in bidirectional source text,"` `UCSUAX31:2234 "producing a visual result that conveys a different logical intent."` They do not close the hole, `UCSUAX31:2170 "Allowing for the insertion of ignorable format controls does not prevent spoofing based on bidirectional reordering."`, and a mark may stand alone as a separator only at a cost, so a syntax that needs a space should require that at `UCSUAX31:2316 "least one of those be neither LEFT-TO-RIGHT MARK nor RIGHT-TO-LEFT MARK."`, since else⟨LRM⟩if reads as one word and parses as two. Literals and comments are carved out: `UCSUAX31:2174 "An exception must be made for comments and strings, which should be able to freely contain these characters."`, and `UCSUAX31:2331 "Implementations should permit these characters in string literals, but in such a literal, their insertion has an effect on the meaning of the program"`.

  **Syntax characters (R3b, R3c).** Pattern_Syntax is the set of characters with syntactic use, `UCSUAX31:2375 "with syntactic use. The following sets shall be disjoint:"` identifier characters, whitespace, syntax characters. Any other character `UCSUAX31:2403 "can still be allowed in a program, for instance, as part of string literals or comments."` Both property sets are `UCSUAX31:2142 "invariant, not changing with successive versions of Unicode."` For user-defined operators, `UCSUAX31:2409 "In order to avoid ambiguities in lexical analysis, operators should not be allowed to contain characters that may be found at the beginning of an identifier or literal"`.

  **Normalization and case (R4 to R7).** `UCSUAX31:2507 "Normalization Form C is appropriate; whereas, if the programming"` `UCSUAX31:2508 "language has case-insensitive identifiers, then Normalization Form KC"` is more appropriate. Implementations `UCSUAX31:2511 "have two choices: to treat variants as equivalent, or to disallow"` them: R4 says identifiers with the `UCSUAX31:2524 "same Normalization Form shall be treated as equivalent by the"` implementation, R6 says `UCSUAX31:2546 "containing excluded characters, allowed identifiers must be in the"` specified form. NFKC costs mathematical languages their letter styles, which they must filter out with `UCSUAX31:2601 "Decomposition_Type=Font."` The XID properties make identifiers `UCSUAX31:2653 "closed under all four Normalization Forms."` toNFKC_Casefold `UCSUAX31:2580 "case folds and normalizes a string, and also removes default-ignorable code points."`, and wherever display and comparison forms differ, `UCSUAX31:944 "Default_Ignorable_Code_Points should be ignored for comparison."` Section 1.3 allows a display form `UCSUAX31:454 "that differs from the internal form used to"` compare. The mathematical profile (7.1) is admitted with a caution: such characters `UCSUAX31:3005 "are discouraged in general use, as they are confusing to most readers."`

  **2. UTS #39 REVISION 32: THE SECURITY LAYER, WITH DATA THAT MAKES IT MECHANICAL.** The premise: `UCSUTS39:305 "Deliberately restricting the characters that can be used in identifiers"` is an important security technique. The General Security Profile `UCSUTS39:383 "permit any characters in \p{Identifier_Status=Restricted}, unless it documents the"` additions. Restricted types include `UCSUTS39:424 "Unassigned characters, private use characters,"` surrogates and controls, default-ignorables, non-NFKC characters, excluded and limited-use scripts, obsolete, technical and uncommon characters. `UCSUTS39:490 "In Unicode 15.0, the Joiner_Control characters (ZWJ/ZWNJ) have been removed from"` the Inclusion type, and `UCSUTS39:495 "Their inclusion in programming language identifier profiles has usability and security implications."` The 17.0.0 data lists the allowed set explicitly, `UCSIDSTATUS:30 "# @missing: 0000..10FFFF; Restricted"`, with `UCSIDSTATUS:1685 "# Total code points: 33791"` allowed.

  Confusable detection maps each string to a skeleton: NFD, then `UCSUTS39:1157 "Remove any characters in X that have the property Default_Ignorable_Code_Point."`, then `UCSUTS39:1158 "Concatenate the prototypes for each character in X according to the specified data, producing a string of exemplar characters."`, then NFD again. The data holds rows such as `UCSCONFUS:1748 "CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER A → LATIN SMALL LETTER A"` and `UCSCONFUS:2378 "CYRILLIC CAPITAL LETTER EN → LATIN CAPITAL LETTER H"`, the second being the substitution in the Trojan Source homoglyph demonstration, which marks `UCSTSPAPER:1194 "Cyrillic Н in red. This program outputs the text Goodbye,"` World!. The bidi variant first must `UCSUTS39:1163 "Reorder the code points in X for display by applying the rules of the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm"`, and the standard names programming languages as its case, using it when strings cannot be forced to one script `UCSUTS39:1198 "or at least single-directionality; this is the case in programming language identifiers."`, with a pointer to UTS #55 section 5.1, `UCSUTS39:1199 "Confusability Mitigation Diagnostics"`. Skeletons move with the data: `UCSUTS39:1218 "they can only be interchanged between systems that use the same version of Unicode to compute"` them. The mechanism is deliberately coarse, `UCSUTS39:1169 "However, that is computationally much more expensive, and requires more sophisticated data, so at this point in time the simpler mechanism has been chosen."` A string is mixed-script `UCSUTS39:1394 "if its resolved script set is empty and defined to be"` single-script otherwise. Restriction levels run from ASCII-Only, `UCSUTS39:1516 "All characters in the string are in the ASCII range."`, through Single Script and Highly Restrictive to Moderately Restrictive, covered `UCSUTS39:1542 "by Latin and any one other Recommended script, except Cyrillic, Greek"`, then Minimally Restrictive and Unrestricted. For email local parts the same standard requires that a quoted string `UCSUTS39:1102 "It must not contain any stateful bidirectional format characters."`, the nearest UTS #39 comes to a rule for quoted text.

  **3. UTR #36 AND UTS #55: ONE STABILIZED, ONE UNREACHED.** UTR #36 `UCSUTR36:63 "has been stabilized: There are no"` plans to update it, `UCSUTR36:67 "This Technical Report has not been maintained since 2014."`, some of its material is superseded by UTS #39, UTS #55 and UAX #31, and the recommendations `UCSUTR36:70 "made in UTR #36 may conflict with the ones given in these more up-to-date standards or"` mislead. Both CVE records still send readers to it (section 5). **UTS #55 itself is known here only by what the pinned standards cite of it:** section 3.3, language evolution (`UCSUAX31:2064`), section 4.1, bidirectional ordering of program text (`UCSUAX9:2803`), section 5.1, confusability mitigation diagnostics (`UCSUTS39:1199`), and section 5.2, conversion to plain text, which `UCSUAX31:2304 "specifies an algorithm for the automatic insertion of LRM characters."`

  **4. UAX #9 REVISION 51: DISPLAY OF SOURCE IS A HIGHER-LEVEL PROTOCOL.** Higher-level protocols are recommended wherever the semantics of segment order are more `UCSUAX9:2523 "significant than those of displayed order, as is the case for source text."` HL4 applies the algorithm to segments of structured text. For x + תו == 1, where the Hebrew identifier drags == 1 to its left in plain display, `UCSUAX9:2722 "It would be better to apply protocol HL4 when displaying these expressions, treating each identifier as a separate"` segment. Copying out of such a display needs repair: `UCSUAX9:3298 "program text must be converted to plain text in a semantics-preserving way,"` `UCSUAX9:3299 "by inserting characters that are ignored by the compiler."`, and `UCSUAX9:3301 "It is recommended that computer languages allow for the insertion of some"` formatting characters without changing a program's meaning. The bidi controls themselves are twelve code points in the 17.0.0 data: `UCSPROPLIST:28 "; Bidi_Control # Cf       ARABIC LETTER MARK"`, `UCSPROPLIST:29 "; Bidi_Control # Cf   [2] LEFT-TO-RIGHT MARK..RIGHT-TO-LEFT MARK"`, `UCSPROPLIST:30 "; Bidi_Control # Cf   [5] LEFT-TO-RIGHT EMBEDDING..RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE"`, `UCSPROPLIST:31 "; Bidi_Control # Cf   [4] LEFT-TO-RIGHT ISOLATE..POP DIRECTIONAL ISOLATE"`.

  **5. TROJAN SOURCE: THE ATTACK, THE CVES, THE DISCLOSURE AND WHO MOVED.** The bidi record reads `UCSCVE42574:23 "An issue was discovered in the Bidirectional Algorithm in the Unicode Specification through 14.0."` and carries Unicode's counter-statement, which points to UTR #36, UTS #39 and UAX #31 and adds that `UCSCVE42574:23 "the BIDI specification allows applications to tailor the implementation in ways that can mitigate misleading visual reordering in program text; see HL4 in Unicode Standard Annex #9"`. The homoglyph record reads `UCSCVE42694:23 "An issue was discovered in the character definitions of the Unicode Specification through 14.0."`, and in Unicode's wording `UCSCVE42694:23 "an adversary could produce source code identifiers using homoglyph characters that render visually identical to but are distinct from a target identifier."` CISA's enrichment scores it `UCSCVE42694:138 "\"baseScore\": 8.3"`. Boucher and Anderson report both CVEs issued `UCSTSPAPER:1374 "two CVEs [36]: CVE-2021-42574 for tracking the Bidi attack, and CVE-2021-42694 for tracking the homoglyph attack."` and `UCSTSPAPER:1375 "These CVEs were issued by MITRE against the Unicode specification."` The repository lists the attack in twelve languages and says `UCSTSREADME:38 "We note that this list of affected languages is non-exhaustive"`.

  The paper's defences, in order: `UCSTSPAPER:1239 "The simplest defense is to ban the use of text directionality control characters both in language specifications and in"` compilers, with escapes for legitimate output; a better one might `UCSTSPAPER:1250 "be to ban the use of unterminated Bidi control characters"` `UCSTSPAPER:1251 "within string literals and comments. By ensuring that each"` control is terminated; and defences `UCSTSPAPER:1256 "Trojan Source defenses must be enabled by default on all"` `UCSTSPAPER:1257 "compilers that support Unicode input, and turning off the defenses should only be permitted when a dedicated suppression"` flag is passed. On responsibility the authors hold that the attacks are `UCSTSPAPER:1299 "While Trojan Source attacks are strictly speaking a matter"` `UCSTSPAPER:1300 "for the language rather than the compiler, we are of the view"` that compiler protection serves the ecosystem.

  The disclosure: `UCSTSPAPER:1392 "We contacted nineteen independent companies and organizations in a coordinated disclosure effort"`, `UCSTSPAPER:1406 "all confirmed receipt of our disclosure, and ultimately nine of"` `UCSTSPAPER:1407 "them committed to releasing a patch."` The outcome: `UCSTSPAPER:1469 "GitHub now shows a warning banner and code"` point visualization, Bitbucket and GitLab visualize the controls, `UCSTSPAPER:1473 "Studio Code now visualizes both Bidi control characters and"` `UCSTSPAPER:1474 "potential homoglyphs by default [59]. Emacs now uses a"` heuristic. `UCSTSPAPER:1478 "Rust released a new set of lints in the rustc compiler that will throw errors upon detection of non-escaped"` Bidi characters. `UCSTSPAPER:1479 "GCC released a new warning detecting"` `UCSTSPAPER:1480 "Bidi misuse, -Wbidi-chars, which is enabled by default [62]."` `UCSTSPAPER:1481 "LLVM added a set of checks to the official clang-tidy linter,"` `UCSTSPAPER:1482 "but did not add compiler warnings for performance considerations [63]. The Java team, on the other hand, declared the"` `UCSTSPAPER:1483 "Trojan source attack to be an issue for code editors rather than"` for the language. The paper reports that `UCSTSPAPER:1485 "a new working group was proposed within Unicode"`, and UAX #31 credits a Source Code Working Group with its later revisions, `UCSUAX31:3091 "The attendees of the Source Code Working Group meetings assisted with the substantial changes made in Versions 15.0 and 15.1:"`.

  The paper also measured the neighbouring attacks. Invisible characters in function names mostly failed: every compiler `UCSTSPAPER:1172 "emitted compilation errors when this technique was employed,"` `UCSTSPAPER:1173 "with the exception of Apple clang v12.0.5 (which emitted a"` `UCSTSPAPER:1174 "warning instead of an error), SQL, and shell scripts on zsh."` Homoglyph function names worked in C, C++, C#, JavaScript, `UCSTSPAPER:1230 "Java, Rust, Go, Python, SQL, and Bash all appear to be vulnerable."` The paper names three exceptions, `UCSTSPAPER:1203 "concept. There were only three exceptions. GNU’s gcc"` `UCSTSPAPER:1204 "and its C++ counterpart, g++, both emitted stray token errors. Of particular note is the Rust compiler, which threw"` `UCSTSPAPER:1205 "a ‘mixed_script_confusables’ warning while producing the"` binary. A later variant uses an invisible character inside a comment terminator, where `UCSTSPAPER:1182 "tack, an adversary uses an invisible character to divide multiline comment terminating sequences."`

  **The empirical evidence is two scans.** GitHub ran the authors' regex for unterminated controls in comments and strings over public commits from January to mid-October 2021: `UCSTSPAPER:1315 "This yielded 7,444 commits of the"` `UCSTSPAPER:1316 "over over 1 billion commits scanned, which resolved to 2,096"` files, and `UCSTSPAPER:1319 "98.8% of the results were false positives."` The Rust project scanned every crate version on crates.io, `UCSRUSTCVE:56 "published on crates.io (as of 2021-10-17), and only 5 crates have the affected"` codepoints, none malicious.

  **6. PRODUCTION COMPILERS: WHAT EACH IMPLEMENTS.**

  **rustc implements R1, R3 and R4 and the UTS #39 checks as lints.** The reference: `UCSRUSTIDENT:24 "Identifiers follow the specification in [Unicode Standard Annex #31][UAX31] for Unicode version 17.0"`, Start is XID_Start `UCSRUSTIDENT:35 "plus the underscore character (U+005F)"`, `UCSRUSTIDENT:46 "Zero width non-joiner (ZWNJ U+200C) and zero width joiner (ZWJ U+200D) characters are not allowed in identifiers."`, and `UCSRUSTIDENT:60 "Two identifiers are equal if their NFC forms are equal."` Whitespace is R3a: `UCSRUSTWS:29 "Whitespace is any non-empty string containing only characters that have the"` Pattern_White_Space property, the left-to-right and right-to-left marks included. RFC 2457 declares the conformance, `UCSRFC2457:173 "* UAX31-C1: The Rust language conforms to the Unicode® Standard Annex #31 for Unicode Version 10.0.0."`, with R3 stated as `UCSRFC2457:180 "Rust only uses characters from these categories for whitespace and syntax."` Outside literals and comments the lexer refuses a character that starts no token, and flags it as invisible when it is one of `UCSRUSTLEXER:39 "'\u{200b}', '\u{200c}', '\u{2060}', '\u{2061}', '\u{2062}', '\u{00ad}', '\u{034f}', '\u{061c}',"` reported with `UCSRUSTLEXER:500 "invisible: INVISIBLE_CHARACTERS.contains(&c),"`. For bidi, `text_direction_codepoint_in_comment` is deny by default, `UCSRUSTLINTS:3904 "To avoid potential problems or confusion, such as in CVE-2021-42574, by default we deny"`, and `text_direction_codepoint_in_literal` covers nine characters that `UCSRUSTLINTS:3920 "make the flow of text on screen change"` direction; the advisory lists them as `UCSRUSTCVE:73 "U+202A, U+202B, U+202C, U+202D, U+202E, U+2066, U+2067, U+2068, U+2069."` and shipped them in `UCSRUSTCVE:50 "Rust 1.56.1 introduces two new lints to detect and reject code containing the"` affected codepoints, recommending that legitimate uses `UCSRUSTCVE:66 "If your code has legitimate uses for the codepoints we recommend replacing them"` with escapes. The three marks LRM, RLM and ALM fall outside those nine. The identifier checks are lints: `UCSRUSTNONASC:37 "pub NON_ASCII_IDENTS,"` at Allow, `UCSRUSTNONASC:71 "pub UNCOMMON_CODEPOINTS,"` at Warn, which fires on any code point outside the UTS #39 allowed set, `UCSRUSTNONASC:61 "This lint is triggered by identifiers that contain a codepoint that is"` not Allowed, `UCSRUSTNONASC:110 "pub CONFUSABLE_IDENTS,"` at Warn, reporting distinct identifiers X `UCSRUSTNONASC:101 "and Y in the same crate where"` the two skeletons are equal, and `UCSRUSTNONASC:146 "pub MIXED_SCRIPT_CONFUSABLES,"` at Warn. RFC 2457 explains the level: `UCSRFC2457:106 "Note: The confusable detection is set to"` warn for forward compatibility, since `UCSRFC2457:106 "The list of confusable characters will be extended in the future and programs that were once valid would fail to compile."` Its mixed-script lint exempts Latin, which `UCSRFC2457:157 "is made because the standard library is Latin-script."` The advisory adds that homoglyph mitigation predates the disclosure, `UCSRUSTCVE:99 "identifiers. Rust already includes mitigations for that attack since Rust"` 1.53.0.

  **The C++ standard implements R1 and R4 and declines R3.** Identifier characters are `UCSCPPLEX:912 "with the Unicode property XID_Start or the Unicode property ID_Compat_Math_Start"`, and a program is ill-formed if an identifier does not conform to `UCSCPPLEX:954 "Normalization Form C as specified in the Unicode Standard."`, so the draft filters as R6 does while claiming R4. The informative annex: `UCSCPPUAX31:12 "this document conforms by meeting the requirements"` R1 and R4 of UAX #31, and states R4 as `UCSCPPUAX31:96 "This document requires that identifiers be in Normalization Form C and"` therefore NFC-equal identifiers are equivalent; `UCSCPPUAX31:36 "For \Cpp{} we apply the Mathematical Compatibility Notation profile,"`, R1b is out, `UCSCPPUAX31:61 "\Cpp{} does not make this guarantee,"`, case is significant and the standard `UCSCPPUAX31:104 "does not do any case folding."`, and for whitespace and syntax `UCSCPPUAX31:87 "This document does not claim conformance with this requirement from"` UAX #31.

  **GCC adds bidi and normalization warnings and no confusable check.** `GCCWARN:9446 "Warn about possibly misleading UTF-8 bidirectional control characters in"` `GCCWARN:9447 "comments, string literals, character constants, and identifiers.  Such"` characters; the default is `GCCWARN:9454 "@option{-Wbidi-chars=unpaired}, which warns about improperly terminated"` bidi contexts, `any` warns on every use, and `GCCWARN:9459 "By default, this warning does not warn about UCNs."` The lexer recognizes `UCSGCCLEX:1226 "NONE, LRE, RLE, LRO, RLO, LRI, RLI, FSI, PDF, PDI, LTR, RTL"`, eleven of the twelve Bidi_Control code points, with ARABIC LETTER MARK absent. For identifiers, `GCCWARN:11075 "In ISO C and ISO C++, two identifiers are different if they are"` different sequences, and the default is `GCCWARN:11085 "@option{-Wnormalized=nfc}, which warns about any identifier that is"` outside NFC; turning it off invites bugs `GCCWARN:11102 "literally impossible to see."` A search of the pinned option manual for homoglyph and confusable returns nothing.

  **clang warns on lookalike symbols and invisible identifier characters, and leaves bidi and confusables to clang-tidy.** Lexer diagnostics: Unicode whitespace is `UCSCLANGDIAG:152 "\"treating character %0 as whitespace\">,"` and an error by default (`UCSCLANGDIAG:153`), a symbol lookalike is `UCSCLANGDIAG:155 "treating character %0 as an identifier character rather than"` a symbol, and `UCSCLANGDIAG:158 "identifier contains character %0 that is invisible in"` some environments. clang-tidy carries the rest: `UCSTIDYBIDI:6 "Warns about unterminated bidirectional unicode sequence, detecting potential attack"`, `UCSTIDYCONF:6 "Warn about confusable identifiers, i.e. identifiers that are visually close to"` each other, and `UCSTIDYMISID:6 "Finds identifiers that contain Unicode characters with right-to-left direction,"`. The confusable check's page attributes its attack to `UCSTIDYCONF:8 "attack described in [CVE-2021-42574](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2021-42574)."`, the bidi record; the homoglyph record is CVE-2021-42694.

  **Python normalizes under NFKC, names no UTS #39 check, and departs from R3.** PEP 3131: `UCSPEP3131:94 "All identifiers are converted into the normal form NFKC while parsing;"` `UCSPEP3131:95 "comparison of identifiers is based on NFKC."` UTS #39 was raised and left open, `UCSPEP3131:144 "It's not clear how that can precisely apply to this PEP; possible"` consequences listed include `UCSPEP3131:149 "* somehow perform Confusable Detection"`, and the PEP's open questions include `UCSPEP3131:248 "1. What to do about bidi format control characters?"`, `UCSPEP3131:254 "F.  Which normalization form should be used, NFC or NFKC?"` and `UCSPEP3131:256 "G.  Should source code be required to be in normalized form?"`. The reference keeps NFKC, `UCSPYLEX:539 "NFKC while parsing."`, says `UCSPYLEX:566 "Note that Python does not necessarily conform to"` UAX #31, defines `UCSPYLEX:353 "whitespace:  ' ' | tab | formfeed"` and `UCSPYLEX:138 "newline: <ASCII LF> | <ASCII CR> <ASCII LF> | <ASCII CR>"`, so NEL, LS and PS are outside R3a's line terminators. PEP 672 catalogues the hazards and `UCSPEP672:15 "This document does not give any recommendations and solutions."`; the issues `UCSPEP672:34 "They should be solved in code editors and review tools"`; Python allows bidi controls only in strings and comments, which limits them, and `UCSPEP672:250 "These characters essentially allow arbitrary reordering of the text that"` follows. Its planned `UCSPEP672:366 "* Recommendations for Text Editors and Code Tools"` remain an open issue.

  **Go, Java and ECMAScript compare code points with no normalization and specify no bidi or confusable rule.** Go: source text is not `GOSPEC:84 "canonicalized, so a single accented code point is distinct from the"` same character built from a combining accent, `GOSPEC:91 "Each code point is distinct; for instance, uppercase and lowercase letters"` differ, a letter is any code point in a Letter category (`GOSPEC:113`), and export depends on the first character being a `GOSPEC:2312 "letter (Unicode character category Lu); and</li>"`. Java: a Java letter `UCSJLS3:255 "is a character for which the method Character.isJavaIdentifierStart(int) returns true."`, `UCSJLS3:265 "Two identifiers are the same only if, after ignoring characters that are ignorable, the identifiers have the same Unicode character for each letter or digit."` and `UCSJLS3:265 "Identifiers that have the same external appearance may yet be different."` `UCSJLS3:269 "Unicode composite characters are different from their canonical equivalent decomposed characters."` Unicode escapes are translated before lexing, `UCSJLS3:68 "A compiler for the Java programming language (\"Java compiler\") first recognizes Unicode escapes in its raw input"`. ECMAScript: identifiers follow UAX #31 `ECMA262:17200 "are tokens that are interpreted according to the Default Identifier Syntax given in Unicode Standard Annex #31, Identifier and Pattern Syntax, with some small modifications."` with ID_Start and ID_Continue, `ECMA262:16661 "Conforming ECMAScript implementations are not required to perform any normalization of source text, or behave as though they were performing normalization of source text."`, `ECMA262:16945 "All format control characters may be used within comments, and within string literals, template literals, and regular expression literals."`, and white space includes `ECMA262:17014 "any code point in general category “Space_Separator”"`, so `ECMA262:17025 "U+0020 (SPACE) and U+00A0 (NO-BREAK SPACE) code points are part of &lt;USP>."`

  **Swift's reference grammar admits the controls Trojan Source uses.** Among identifier-head characters it lists `UCSSWIFTLEX:240 "> *identifier-head* → U+200B–U+200D, U+202A–U+202E, U+203F–U+2040, U+2054, or U+2060–U+206F"`, a range set that holds zero-width space, ZWNJ, ZWJ, the five embeddings and overrides, and the four isolates. Whitespace is space, LF, CR, tab, VT, FF `UCSSWIFTLEX:30 "and null (U+0000)."`, outside R3a. In raw identifiers `UCSSWIFTLEX:188 "a left-to-right mark (U+200E) or right-to-left mark (U+200F)"` `UCSSWIFTLEX:189 "is allowed and considered whitespace."` Whether the shipping compiler matches the book was outside the pinned sources.

  **Elixir implements the most.** It conforms to UAX #31 R1, R1b and R4 (`UCSELIXIR:51 "Elixir conforms to the standards outlined in the"` annex, version 17.0), excludes ZWJ and ZWNJ, and `UCSELIXIR:75 "Bidirectional control characters are also not supported."` It normalizes to NFC, `UCSELIXIR:107 "Elixir normalizes all atoms and variables to NFC form. Quoted-atoms and strings can, however, be in any form and are not verified by the parser."` From UTS #39 it implements C1, `UCSELIXIR:119 "Elixir will not allow tokenization of identifiers with codepoints in"` Identifier_Status=Restricted, C2 as a warning, `UCSELIXIR:43 "Finally, Elixir will also warn of confusable identifiers in the same file."`, with ASCII-only identifiers exempt (`UCSELIXIR:133`), and C3 as a refusal, `UCSELIXIR:137 "Elixir will not allow tokenization of mixed-script identifiers unless it is via chunks separated by an underscore"`. It declines R3, accepting four whitespace characters, `UCSELIXIR:101 "and therefore does not follow requirement R3."`, and C4.

  **Zig refuses what the others negotiate.** `ZIGLANGREF:14722 "Zig source code is encoded in UTF-8. An invalid UTF-8 byte sequence results in a compile error."` `ZIGLANGREF:14723 "Throughout all zig source code (including in comments), some code points are never allowed:"` legacy controls and `ZIGLANGREF:14726 "<li>Non-Ascii Unicode line endings: U+0085 (NEL), U+2028 (LS), U+2029 (PS).</li>"` Identifiers are ASCII, `ZIGLANGREF:15809 "&lt;- !keyword [A-Za-z_] [A-Za-z0-9_]* skip"`, with an escape for foreign names, `ZIGLANGREF:1909 "If a name that does not fit these requirements is needed, such as for linking with external libraries"`. The pinned reference gives no reason for the ASCII rule.

  **Editors.** VS Code highlights `UCSVSCODE:4322 "* Controls whether characters that just reserve space or have no width at all are highlighted."` and `UCSVSCODE:4327 "* Controls whether characters are highlighted that can be confused with basic ASCII characters"`, both on by default (`UCSVSCODE:4374 "invisibleCharacters: true,"`, `UCSVSCODE:4375 "ambiguousCharacters: true,"`), inside strings too (`UCSVSCODE:4377 "includeStrings: true,"`).

  **7. NORMALIZATION: WHAT EACH CHOICE LOSES, AND WHO REFUSES NON-ASCII.** NFC keeps compatibility variants distinct and makes canonically equivalent spellings one identifier (rustc, Elixir, C++ as a filter, GCC as a warning). NFKC folds them: Python treats a ligature-and-superscript spelling as finalization, `UCSPYLEX:542 "so Python treats them as the same name::"`, and `UCSPEP672:285 "(There are several normal forms; Python uses"` NFKC. RFC 2457 chose NFC for three reasons, `UCSRFC2457:199 "NFC normalization was chosen over NFKC normalization for the following reasons:"` mathematicians use symbols `UCSRFC2457:201 "like π and ϖ in the same context."`, NFKC mangles some words `UCSRFC2457:202 "in surprising ways."`, and `UCSRFC2457:203 "Naive (search) tools can"` miss NFKC variants. No normalization (Go, Java, ECMAScript) leaves Á and A followed by a combining acute as two identifiers (`UCSJLS3:269`). Case folding appears only as UAX31-R5 and R7; C++ declines it (`UCSCPPUAX31:104`) and no surveyed compiler folds. **Refusal of non-ASCII identifiers outright** appears in Zig's grammar (`ZIGLANGREF:15809`), in Rust at specific sites, `UCSRUSTIDENT:49 "Identifiers are restricted to the ASCII subset of"` XID for extern crates, filesystem modules, no_mangle and foreign items, in Elixir aliases, `UCSELIXIR:97 "Aliases in Elixir only allow ASCII characters"`, and as an opt-in Rust lint at forbid. The stated reasons are in the drawbacks of RFC 2457, `UCSRFC2457:188 "As source code should be written in English and in English only (source: various people)"` and `UCSRFC2457:192 "Homoglyph attacks are possible. Without confusable detection identifiers can be distinct for the compiler but visually the same."`, and in the PEP 3131 debate, `UCSPEP3131:190 "2. Python will become vulnerable to a new class of security exploits;"` and `UCSPEP3131:201 "6. The Unicode bidi algorithm yields an extremely confusing display"` order.

  **8. WHAT A POLICY THE FIELD SUPPORTS CONTAINS, AND WHAT NO PINNED SOURCE SPECIFIES.** This section is this row's reading of the pins. A supported policy declares its UAX #31 version and requirements; takes R1 with a declared profile that removes default-ignorables (7.3) and the joiners (as Rust does), and R1b; takes R3a whitespace whole, or refuses NEL, LS and PS anywhere as Zig does, since a partial terminator set is the spoofing case UAX #31 names; keeps identifier, whitespace and syntax sets disjoint (R3b) with a declared profile for any operator characters; takes R4 or R6 under NFC for a case-sensitive language; applies the General Security Profile, mixed-script refusal and bidiSkeleton confusable detection; refuses explicit bidi controls outside literals and comments, and either refuses them unpaired inside or refuses them always with an escape suggestion; and treats display through HL4 and visible rendering of invisible characters in tools. **Left unspecified by every pinned source:** what a reader does with a default-ignorable code point other than a bidi control inside a string literal or comment (U+200B, U+2060, variation selectors, TAG characters). UAX #31's only text on literals is that the two marks be permitted there (`UCSUAX31:2331`), and its advice to escape default-ignorables is recommended practice for pattern languages, `UCSUAX31:2474 "practice to quote or escape all literal whitespace and default-ignorable code points as well."` rustc and GCC check only bidi controls in literals, ECMAScript admits every format control there, and RFC 9839's subsets exclude only surrogates, noncharacters and legacy controls, `UCSRFC9839:177 "\"Surrogate\" or \"Noncharacter\" and to \"legacy controls\" as defined in"`, calling its own bar low, `UCSRFC9839:163 "This is a low bar; the PRECIS"`. For problematic input it names `UCSRFC9839:278 "Two reasonable options for dealing with problematic input are either"` `UCSRFC9839:279 "rejecting text containing problematic code points or replacing the"` them, and warns that `UCSRFC9839:282 "Silently deleting an ill-formed part of a string is a known security"` risk. Also unsettled: unpaired versus any bidi control as the default (GCC unpaired, rustc any of nine, the paper both); the scope of confusable comparison (rustc a crate, Elixir a file, UTS #39 silent); warn versus deny, given that skeletons change with each Unicode version; and how a diagnostic reports a column in text with bidi controls or combining marks. UTS #55 may settle some of these and was unreachable.
