### FD-69 controlled evidence on surface syntax exists and is small, novice-heavy and centred on Java and C: randomized trials found Perl and Java no more usable to first-time programmers than a placebo language with random keywords, identifier-style and indentation-depth results split between studies, omitted braces and implicit operator precedence measurably raise misreading, and no surveyed trial, review or mapping study measures parenthesized prefix syntax against any alternative, so every Lisp-family move off s-expressions (M-expressions, Dylan, SRFI 105, 110 and 119, Pyret, Rhombus) and Go's choices of braces and one machine format rest on adoption judgment, designer experiment, case studies and stated engineering experience

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question, dispatched as the readability strand of a surface-syntax rework: **does controlled empirical evidence exist on which surface-syntax features help or hurt program reading and writing, for novices and for experts; does any of it measure s-expression (parenthesized prefix) syntax against alternatives; and what have the Lisp family's own attempts at a more readable surface found?** Posed so it could come back `no` on each part: the field could have had no controlled syntax studies, and it could have had a trial of Lisp notation. **The first part comes back yes, with heavy qualifications; the second comes back no.** Controlled studies exist for whole-language syntax with novices (Stefik and Siebert), for identifier style, indentation depth, block delimiters, small confusing patterns and control constructs, and two reviews map them. They are small, mostly students, mostly Java, C and Pascal, and two of the best-known effects failed to replicate or reversed between studies. The authors of the whole-language trials list prefix notation among the features still to be tested, the formatting review holds no Lisp study, and the 95-experiment mapping study lists 21 snippet languages with no Lisp-family language among them. The Lisp family's attempts report rationale, anecdote, two-program experience reports and two case studies; none reports a user study. Canonical formatting and the rejection of significant indentation are argued from engineering experience in Go's own texts, and no source measures what either does to comprehension.
- measured: **1. THE WHOLE-LANGUAGE TRIALS: STEFIK AND SIEBERT, AND WHAT THEY LEAVE UNTESTED.**

  The 2013 article reports two surveys and two randomized accuracy studies. `RDXSTEFIK:21 "Randomo was designed by randomly choosing some"` `RDXSTEFIK:22 "keywords from the ASCII table (a metaphorical placebo)."`, and the headline is that `RDXSTEFIK:23 "more traditional C-style syntax (both Perl and Java) did not afford accuracy rates significantly higher than"` `RDXSTEFIK:24 "a language with randomly generated keywords, but that languages which deviate (Quorum, Python, and"` Ruby did. Study 3 ran on `RDXSTEFIK:1938 "Of the remaining 18 participants"`, and in it `RDXSTEFIK:2163 "Perl users were not able to"` `RDXSTEFIK:2164 "program significantly more accurately than Randomo users, p = .458."` Study 4 recruited `RDXSTEFIK:1943 "September 2011 and June 2012, again from non-computer programming classes at"` a university, `RDXSTEFIK:1947 "12 participants, which adds to 72."`, and confirmed that `RDXSTEFIK:2193 "initial accuracy rates of novices"` `RDXSTEFIK:2194 "did, in fact, vary by programming language, F(5, 66) = 4.889, p = .001, ηp2 = .270."` Post-hoc tests put `RDXSTEFIK:2209 "(Quorum (p = .033), Python (p = .011), and Ruby (p = .003)), and (2) for others, there"` was too little evidence that novices did `RDXSTEFIK:2243 "more accurately than placebo (Java (p = .922), Perl (p = .573))."`; the one pairwise difference among real languages was Ruby over `RDXSTEFIK:2246 "Java (p = .044)."`

  At the token level, the authors conclude `RDXSTEFIK:2328 "the single equals sign is a superior"` choice for novices: double equals was used correctly by one participant `RDXSTEFIK:2335 "of 48 students in the other four languages."`, and `RDXSTEFIK:2459 "Ironically, the double"` `RDXSTEFIK:2460 "equals did so poorly that our randomly chosen operator, bang (!) did just as well (if"` not better. In the surveys the usual loop keywords for, while and foreach `RDXSTEFIK:868 "science, for, while, and foreach, were rated as the three most unintuitive choices by"` non-programmers. The take-home list reads `RDXSTEFIK:2545 "(a) Looping constructs that use intuitive word choices afford higher accuracy (e.g.,"` repeat 10 times), `RDXSTEFIK:2547 "(b) If statements that remove parentheses, braces, and use a single equal sign"` afford higher accuracy, and `RDXSTEFIK:2549 "(c) Type annotations and semicolons appear to cause minor deficits in novice"` accuracy; on semicolons the authors agree with prior work that `RDXSTEFIK:2438 "shows, semicolons are a relatively trivial issue for novices anyway [Denny et al. 2012],"`.

  **Experts enter only as raters.** Self-reported C++ experience moved intuitiveness ratings: `RDXSTEFIK:2523 "individuals rated C++ constructs an average of about half a point higher per"` year, so designers are advised `RDXSTEFIK:2526 "to check their assumptions before claiming a design is intuitive."` The tasks are small and not `RDXSTEFIK:2469 "representative of what professionals do in the field"`; the authors note an `RDXSTEFIK:2476 "number of archival quality randomized controlled trials on language design in the aca-"` demic literature that is astonishingly small, and they name as future work `RDXSTEFIK:2479 "testing new features (e.g., closures, prefix"` `RDXSTEFIK:2480 "notation, enum syntax, other loop constructs, switch statements) in a controlled and"` systematic way. **Prefix notation is on the authors' own list of untested features.**

  **The evidence-based design line.** Stefik's public reply to criticism of the 2011 pilot states the programme: the community `RDXSTEFIKRESP:86 "really needs to do is to move away from a largely pseudo-scientific"` `RDXSTEFIKRESP:87 "view of programming language design toward one based on"` evidence, and languages should be tested with `RDXSTEFIKRESP:27 "novices, professionals, and everyone in between."` The PLIERS process paper places that line among others, `RDXPLIERS:84 "Some authors, such as Stefik and Hanenberg, have focused on using quantitative approaches [88,"` 89], and separates audiences: `RDXPLIERS:435 "Designing languages for novices is substantially different from"` designing for experienced programmers. From its own studies it reports that borrowed syntax misleads when the `RDXPLIERS:1900 "mantics do not match precisely, confusion can result; this can be addressed by choosing distinct"` syntax. Its evidence for the process is that `RDXPLIERS:21 "showed that the PLIERS process resulted in languages that could be used effectively by many programmers"`. Stefik and Hanenberg's own evidence-standards papers (Onward! 2014, and the 2017 methodology critique) were unreachable; only their citation in PLIERS is pinned.

  **2. SYNTAX DETAILS: IDENTIFIERS, INDENTATION, DELIMITERS, PRECEDENCE, CONSTRUCTS.**

  **Identifier style split between two studies.** Binkley and colleagues ran `RDXBINKLEY:15 "An empirical study of 135 programmers and non-programmers was conducted"`; `RDXBINKLEY:15 "Results indicate that camel casing leads to higher accuracy among all subjects regardless of training"`, and `RDXBINKLEY:15 "those trained in camel casing are able to recognize identifiers in the camel case style faster than identifiers in the underscore style."` The task was recognizing a phrase among moving clouds, which the authors concede `RDXBINKLEY:57 "Although this task is very different from a standard programming task"`. Sharif and Maletic replicated it with an eye tracker: `RDXSHARIF:1816 "One main difference is that subjects were trained mainly in the underscore style and were all programmers."` `RDXSHARIF:1816 "While results indicate no difference in accuracy between the two styles, subjects recognize identifiers in the underscore style more quickly."` Training, the variable the first study controlled for, is the one that changed.

  **Indentation depth failed to replicate.** Miara and colleagues (1983), as summarized by the formatting review, tested `RDXFMTSLR:1122 "students and 32 experienced students to evaluate the inﬂuence of indenta-"` tion, found `RDXFMTSLR:1135 "showed that there are signiﬁcant diﬀerences between novices and experts"` and between depths, `RDXFMTSLR:1137 "where two characters produced the best results."` Bauer and colleagues repeated it with eye tracking: `RDXINDENT19:9 "we asked 22~participants to calculate the output of Java code snippets with different levels of indentation"`, and `RDXINDENT19:10 "We could not find any indication that the indentation levels affect program comprehension or visual effort, so we could not replicate the findings of Miara and others."`; the review records no significant difference `RDXFMTSLR:1203 "between indentation levels, unlike in the previous study."` Hanenberg's group has since compared indented with unindented code, titling one trial `RDXHANENBERG:31 "Intendation in Source Code: A Randomized Control Trial on the Readability of Control Flows in Java Code with Large Effects"` and another `RDXHANENBERG:27 "Indentation and reading time: a randomized control trial on the differences between generated indented and non-indented if-statements"`. Only the titles and designs are pinned; the result sections sit on Springer and SciTePress, which were unreachable.

  **Block delimiters and small confusing patterns.** The Atoms of Confusion experiment tested minimal C snippets: `RDXAOC:14 "code. We show empirically in an experiment with 73 participants"` `RDXAOC:15 "that these code patterns can lead to a significantly increased rate of"` misunderstanding. Of the candidates, `RDXAOC:667 "in Table 2, of the 19 atom candidates we proposed, we accepted 15"`, all of them `RDXAOC:670 "from a medium to a very large effect size."` Two results bear on surface syntax directly. `RDXAOC:1291 "our subjects made 22% more errors"` `RDXAOC:1292 "when braces were omitted."`, against the Linux and NASA style guides; and for assignment inside a condition, `RDXAOC:1279 "Our data shows a 38% increase in the number of correctly evaluated assignments when"` the assignment moved out. The subjects were mostly students, so `RDXAOC:1462 "the effect sizes reported may be overstated for some"` populations. For labelled closers, the review reports Sykes and colleagues (1983, 36 students): `RDXFMTSLR:1327 "the subjects performed better using the ENDIF delimiters than using the"` `RDXFMTSLR:1328 "REQ-BE (p = 0.074) and BE (p = 0.073) delimiters."`, significant only at the α = 0.1 the study chose. It is the nearest measured analogue to the uniform `)` closer of an s-expression, and it is weak.

  **Operator precedence.** SRFI 105 reports Derek Jones's ACCU 2006 survey of experienced developers (secondary; the primary was unreachable): `RDXSRFI105:892 "In this experiment only 66.7% of the answers were correct (standard"` deviation 8.8), `RDXSRFI105:894 "this was not much better than random chance (50%)."`, `RDXSRFI105:902 "and the more-experienced developers did not do better (!)."`, and in large C code bases `RDXSRFI105:884 "(102,822/154,575) of the operator pairs were explicitly parenthesized"` where precedence could have applied. SRFI 105 draws `RDXSRFI105:905 "Nevertheless, these results clearly suggest that precedence rules may harm,"`.

  **Control constructs, with professionals.** Ajami, Woodbridge and Feitelson measured `RDXAJAMI:64 "220 professional programmers"` reading equivalent snippets: `RDXAJAMI:68 "for loops are significantly harder than ifs, that some but not all"` negations harm, `RDXAJAMI:73 "and that syntactic structures are not necessarily the most important"` factor, and time and `RDXAJAMI:75 "errors made are not necessarily equivalent."` (abstract as reproduced by the review site; the paper text was out of reach).

  **3. THE REVIEWS: SMALL STUDIES, LOW POWER, AND NO LISP.**

  Oliveira and colleagues' review of formatting and legibility found `RDXFMTSLR:93 "12 papers that compare alternative formatting elements."` Some formatting `RDXFMTSLR:97 "matting elements were found to be statistically better than other equivalent"` ones while others showed no difference, with `RDXFMTSLR:100 "e.g., one study found a signiﬁcant diﬀerence in favor of 2-space indentation,"` and two others finding none. Comparisons that `RDXFMTSLR:1570 "hibit statistically signiﬁcant results (e.g., Pretty-printed layout vs. Disrupted"` layout) failed to reach significance. On power: `RDXFMTSLR:1699 "These low sample sizes imply that these studies"` `RDXFMTSLR:1700 "are only able to detect large eﬀect sizes."`, and of the fMRI layout study, `RDXFMTSLR:1703 "Since this study involved only 11 participants, its"` power is very low. The review's text names no Lisp-family or parenthesized-prefix study: a search of the pin for Lisp, Racket, Clojure, s-expression, parenthes and prefix returns nothing, and its few uses of scheme name Pascal layout schemes.

  Wyrich, Bogner and Wagner `RDXMAP40:54 "We therefore conducted a systematic mapping study of 95 source code comprehension experiments published"` between 1979 and 2019. The snippets used a total `RDXMAP40:957 "of 21 unique languages (plus pseudocode)."`; Java is `RDXMAP40:961 "the most used language in our sample. It is followed by C (14 studies), C++ (10), and Pascal (10)."` The figure lists the 21 as `RDXMAP40:980 "# of studiesJavaCC++Pascaln/aC#PythonFortranCobol"` `RDXMAP40:980 "JavaScriptAlgolBasicDartDelphiJ#Modula-2Objective CPL/IProcessingpseudocodeRubyScalaVisual Basic"`, which contains no Lisp-family language. `RDXMAP40:917 "About half of the 95 papers (53.7%) reported a sample that consisted entirely of students."`, and for only `RDXMAP40:918 "9 papers (9.5%), only professionals were included in the sample."`

  **4. THE LISP FAMILY'S OWN ATTEMPTS, AND WHAT EACH OFFERS AS EVIDENCE.**

  **M-expressions.** McCarthy's account reaches this row through SRFI 110's quotation (the Stanford pages were unreachable and no GitHub copy holds the text): `RDXSRFI110:4968 "M-expressions (or meta-expressions) are a notation"` intended as the primary notation, and the project `RDXSRFI110:4976 "explicitly abandoned. It just receded into the indefinite future, and a"` new generation of programmers preferred internal notation `RDXSRFI110:4978 "to any FORTRAN-like or ALGOL-like notation that could be devised."` A machine form would have needed redefinition `RDXSRFI110:5025 "because the pencil-and-paper M-notation used characters"` missing from the IBM 026 key punch. SRFI 110's diagnosis is `RDXSRFI110:5017 "The fundamental problem with M-expressions was that they were not general."` Rhombus cites the same history: `RDXRHOMBUS:438 "M-expression notation for Lisp famously never materialized (McCarthy 1978)"`. Steele and Gabriel's prediction reaches this row through Wheeler's quotation (the HOPL II paper was unreachable): `RDXWHEELER:219 "Therefore we expect future generations of Lisp programmers to continue"` `RDXWHEELER:220 "to reinvent Algol-style for Lisp, over and over and over again, and we"` `RDXWHEELER:221 "are equally confident that they will continue, after an initial period"` `RDXWHEELER:222 "of infatuation, to reject it."`

  **SRFI 105, curly infix.** The rationale is testimony: `RDXSRFI105:121 "notation. Even some Lisp advocates, like Paul Graham, admit that"` prefix math feels unnatural, and `RDXSRFI105:129 "Infix is not going away; standard mathematical notation uses infix,"`. Beside the authors' own trials, as in `RDXSRFI105:1807 "Experimentation found that separating parameters solely by whitespace"` worked well, its one appeal to measurement is the precedence data, `RDXSRFI105:856 "In addition, there is some experimental evidence that developers"` rarely use precedence and often misapply it, which with the reader-composition problem decides `RDXSRFI105:842 "In short, building precedence into a"` Lisp reader creates many complexities, so curly infix has none.

  **SRFI 110, sweet-expressions.** The rationale opens `RDXSRFI110:256 "Many software developers find Lisp s-expression notation inconvenient and"` unpleasant to read, then sets the bar that most past notations missed: being `RDXSRFI110:323 "general (i.e., the notation is independent of an underlying semantic) or"` `RDXSRFI110:324 "homoiconic (i.e., the underlying data structure is clear from the syntax)."` Extra bracket pairs failed in practice: `RDXSRFI110:2501 "relatively few people use these alternatives in practice, and no one"` claims parity with Python, R7RS voted `RDXSRFI110:2505 "(out of 15 voters, 11 voted against supporting [...])."`, and `RDXSRFI110:2510 "Part of the problem may be that (), [], and {}"` look too alike. The case for indentation is that `RDXSRFI110:2544 "Making indentation syntactically meaningful eliminates many"` parentheses and that indentation and grouping `RDXSRFI110:2556 "they are automatically kept in sync."` The evidence offered for the notation is use: `RDXSRFI110:6839 "At least two programs have been written using sweet-expressions:"`, which the authors read as showing `RDXSRFI110:6857 "shows that sweet-expressions are mature enough to be standardized."`

  **SRFI 119, wisp.** It aims at `RDXSRFI119:50 "This SRFI describes a simple syntax which allows making scheme easier to read for newcomers"`, asserting that `RDXSRFI119:94 "the parentheses at the beginning of lines hurt readability and scare away newcomers."` and that indentation-defined structure `RDXSRFI119:94 "using it directly to define the structure avoids errors due to mismatches between indentation and actual meaning."` It disputes SRFI 110 on the same ground: `RDXSRFI119:117 "These additional syntax-elements however hurt readability for newcomers (obviously the authors of"` SRFI 110 disagree). It names its own error mode, the leading period that `RDXSRFI119:171 "can lead to errors when trying to return a variable from a procedure and forgetting the period."`, and its experience is that `RDXSRFI119:161 "the biggest program in wisp is still its implementations"`. Neither SRFI 110 nor SRFI 119 cites a user study, and each claims newcomer readability against the other.

  **Dylan.** `RDXDYLANHIST:57 "Harlequin's Dylan was originally implemented using the prefix syntax"` `RDXDYLANHIST:58 "and later converted to the current infix syntax."` The reason given in the project's own history pages is adoption: the Apple Cambridge team `RDXDYLANEULOGY:39 "understood that C programmers would be generally unwilling to convert to"` `RDXDYLANEULOGY:40 "a parenthesized, prefix syntax: for this reason, Dylan was given a"` Pascal-like syntax, `RDXDYLANEULOGY:45 "but in fact many barriers to language adoption are"` cultural and practical. Wheeler records the same switch: `RDXWHEELER:242 "Dylan actually <i>switched</i> from S-expressions to a more"` `RDXWHEELER:243 "traditional syntax, when they wanted &#8220;normal&#8221; people to use it."`

  **Pyret.** Brown's teaching language left Racket partly for syntax: `RDXPYRET:41 "We wanted to experiment with syntax. Much as many of us love"` `RDXPYRET:42 "parentheses, we fear that Racket will always bump into an acceptance"` `RDXPYRET:43 "threshold due to its syntax."` It also refuses implicit precedence outright: `RDXPYRETPREC:9 "Pyret has only one rule for using multiple operators in a single expression:"` `RDXPYRETPREC:10 "different operators must be explicitly grouped by parentheses, and evaluation"` proceeds left to right, because `RDXPYRETPREC:55 "Implicit operator precedence is a common source of errors among even"` experienced developers.

  **Rhombus and shrubbery notation.** The paper's motive is that the message of macros `RDXRHOMBUS:74 "of macros has been diﬃcult to detangle from Lisp’s minimalistic, parenthesis-oriented notation."`; `RDXRHOMBUS:81 "Rhombus is a programmable programming language with conventional notation, designed from"` the start around macros. S-expressions give conceptual simplicity `RDXRHOMBUS:437 "at the price of lots of parentheses."`; `RDXRHOMBUS:439 "Some characterize programming with S-expressions as"` writing in ASTs, the `RDXRHOMBUS:441 "sense that programmers must write out a kind of parse tree with all grouping made explicit."` Shrubbery's bounded nesting limits the `RDXRHOMBUS:92 "transformations that macros can perform, so programmers do not need to know every macro"` `RDXRHOMBUS:93 "before making some sense of unfamiliar code."` The authors hold that the details of the indentation `RDXRHOMBUS:490 "rules, as well as the choice of indentation-sensitive parsing, are less important than (1) the approxi-"` mate size and shape of the grammar. **The evaluation is two case studies:** `RDXRHOMBUS:1196 "two larger eﬀorts: a video game framework (section 7.1) and a language for teaching (section 7.2)."` The first is by `RDXRHOMBUS:1199 "One of the authors, while still a relative newcomer to the language, used Rhombus to implement"` a game framework and reports that shrubbery's rules `RDXRHOMBUS:1206 "to consider lower-level parsing concerns, but its rules for grouping and indentation closely match"` developer intuitions; the second ports a teaching language, `RDXRHOMBUS:1234 "Shplait is a successor to Plait,13 which has the same constructs and type system but resembles"` Racket, and measures the port by implementation size, `RDXRHOMBUS:1289 "parable part of Shplait is split across more than 40 modules that total only 3k lines of code, primarily"`, with no report of student outcomes. The conclusion offers, `RDXRHOMBUS:1520 "evidence that this combination is practical and eﬀective, we oﬀer the Rhombus implementation,"`. The project's 2021 status note records how the surface was chosen: `RDXRHSTATE:122 "Matthew tried several experiments and found Python-style notation"` `RDXRHSTATE:123 "most straightforward to work with, and he’s been the primary"` implementor, and `RDXRHSTATE:126 "Making the “correct” decision about surface syntax isn’t our goal at"` this stage; `RDXRHSTATE:131 "next. We don’t believe that shrubbery notation is perfect."`

  **The one mitigation a parenthesized language ships for paren errors.** DrRacket's teaching languages require an identifier at the head of every call, which `RDXDRRLANG:221 "confusing misuses of parentheses, such as @racket[(1)] or"` `RDXDRRLANG:222 "@racket[((+ 3 4))], which is a common mistake among beginners"` `RDXDRRLANG:223 "who are used to the optional parentheses of algebra.}"` The documentation states the error class from teaching experience and cites no count.

  **5. SIGNIFICANT INDENTATION: CLAIMED BENEFITS, SHIPPED REFUSALS, AND NO ERROR-RATE MEASUREMENT.**

  Python's design FAQ gives the benefit as an identity of readings: `RDXPYFAQ:17 "Since there are no begin/end brackets there cannot be a disagreement between"` `RDXPYFAQ:18 "grouping perceived by the parser and the human reader."`, opening with `RDXPYFAQ:13 "Guido van Rossum believes that using indentation for grouping is extremely"` elegant. The cost every indentation-sensitive surface surveyed pays is a column rule, and each ships a refusal for it. Python: `RDXPYLEX:280 "Indentation is rejected as inconsistent if a source file mixes tabs and spaces"` `RDXPYLEX:281 "in a way that makes the meaning dependent on the worth of a tab in spaces; a"` TabError is raised, while a form feed elsewhere `RDXPYLEX:291 "in the leading whitespace have an undefined effect (for instance, they may reset"` the count. Haskell 2010 fixes `RDXHSLAYOUT:183 "Tab stops are 8 characters apart."`, treats every Unicode character as one column, `RDXHSLAYOUT:188 "are considered to be of the same, fixed, width as an ASCII character."`, and advises `RDXHSLAYOUT:189 "However, to avoid visual confusion, programmers should avoid writing programs in which "` `RDXHSLAYOUT:190 "the meaning of implicit layout depends on the width of non-space characters."`; its layout algorithm is coupled to the parser, since `RDXHSLAYOUT:295 "Note 1 implements the feature that layout processing can be stopped"` `RDXHSLAYOUT:296 "prematurely by a parse error."` Shrubbery counts a column that `RDXSHRUBTOK:90 "increments once per Unicode @defterm{grapheme cluster}, except that tabs"` are special, a column is `RDXSHRUBTOK:96 "indented than another only if it extends the other column's sequence."`, and when two columns `RDXSHRUBTOK:98 "are incomparable; if parsing depends on an order between incomparable"` columns, the parse fails with a mix-tabs error. Its block colon `RDXSHRUBRAT:35 "is mostly a kind of consistency check to"` `RDXSHRUBRAT:36 "enable better and earlier errors when indentation goes wrong."`; `RDXSHRUBRAT:13 "Parentheses in shrubbery notation do not disable indentation, unlike"` some notations; and the designers accept a residual risk that an operator line will `RDXSHRUBRAT:39 "be treated as continuing a group, but hopefully that will be rare."` SRFI 110 requires that `RDXSRFI110:3210 "users must be consistent; if a line is indented with"` `RDXSRFI110:3211 "eight spaces, the next line cannot be indented with a tab."`, a rule it says `RDXSRFI110:3220 "This simple rule completely eliminates the problems caused by variances"` in tab display, and it concedes `RDXSRFI110:3225 "is that horizontal whitespace can get lost in many transports"`; wisp adds a leading underscore for that case, `RDXSRFI119:290 "<p><i>requirement: share code in environments which do not preserve whitespace.</i></p>"`

  **Go rejects significant indentation from experience.** `RDXGOSPLASH:109 "Some observers objected to Go's C-like block structure with braces, preferring the use of spaces for indentation, in the style of Python or Haskell."` Google had tracked failures in cross-language builds where an embedded Python snippet `RDXGOSPLASH:112 "is subtly and _invisibly_ broken by a change in the indentation of the surrounding code."`, so `RDXGOSPLASH:115 "It is better to forgo convenience for safety and dependability, so Go has brace-bounded blocks."` This is a field report with no counts. **No pinned source measures how many errors significant indentation causes or prevents.** The formatting review's indentation studies vary depth or presence inside brace languages, and the Python, Haskell, SRFI and shrubbery texts give design reasons.

  **6. CANONICAL FORMATTING: THE GO TEAM'S REASONS, AND NO COMPREHENSION MEASUREMENT.**

  Go ties syntax to readers and tools together: `RDXGOSPLASH:447 "Syntax is the user interface of a programming language. Although it has"` limited semantic effect, it determines readability, and `RDXGOSPLASH:462 "Unlike C and Java and especially C++, Go can be parsed without"` `RDXGOSPLASH:463 "type information or a symbol table;"`. `RDXGOSPLASH:479 "Declarations introduced by keyword are easier to parse both for people and"` computers. On formatting, `RDXGOSPLASH:1023 "From the beginning of the project, we  intended Go programs"` `RDXGOSPLASH:1024 "to be formatted by machine, eliminating an entire class of argument"`, and uniform presentation `RDXGOSPLASH:1037 "makes code easier to read and therefore faster to work on."` Because the formatter prints from the parse tree, `RDXGOSPLASH:1045 "This makes it possible to _edit_ the parse tree before formatting it,"` which is how the rewrite tools arose. The blog states the reader benefit as `RDXGOFMT:21 "easier to **read**: when all code looks the same you need not mentally convert"`, measured adoption at `RDXGOFMT:33 "about 70% of them are formatted according to gofmt's rules."`, and names the review benefit: `RDXGOFMT:69 "One of the greatest virtues of machine-formatted code is that it can be"` `RDXGOFMT:70 "transformed mechanically without generating unrelated formatting noise in the diffs."`

  The nearest measurement concerns review load. Allamanis, Barr, Bird and Sutton define `RDXALLAMANIS:17 "A coding convention is a syntactic restriction not imposed by a programming language’s grammar."` and found developers enforce conventions `RDXALLAMANIS:17 "with roughly one third of code reviews containing feedback about following them (Section 4.1)."` **No pinned source measures whether an enforced canonical format changes comprehension or review outcomes**; the one layout comparison in the review (pretty-printed against disrupted, 11 participants) found no significant difference at very low power.

  **7. WHAT THIS GIVES A SURFACE-SYNTAX REWORK.** This section reads the pins against the rework's stated aims and rules nothing.

  - **The choice of s-expressions against an alternative is unmeasured either way.** The only sources that state an effect for prefix or parenthesized notation are testimony (SRFI 105, 110, 119), adoption judgments (Dylan, Pyret) and designer experiment (Rhombus). A rework that keeps or drops s-expressions has no trial to cite; the PLIERS process and Stefik's placebo design are the published ways to obtain one.
  - **Measured hazards that a parenthesized surface already avoids:** implicit operator precedence (Jones via SRFI 105, Pyret's refusal) and optional block delimiters (Atoms of Confusion, 22% more errors). Every s-expression form delimits its extent and carries no precedence, and both properties should survive any rework, including an infix layer, as SRFI 105 and Pyret keep them.
  - **The hazard every surveyed Lisp reformer names is indentation that disagrees with grouping** (SRFI 110, wisp, Python FAQ, shrubbery's consistency check). A reader that keeps parentheses can refuse that disagreement instead of adopting significant indentation; shrubbery's colon check is the nearest shipped precedent, and no source measures the refusal.
  - **Any rule that reads columns needs a defined column.** Python refuses tab-dependent meaning, shrubbery counts grapheme clusters and refuses incomparable tab and space prefixes, and Haskell counts every Unicode character as one column and warns against width-dependent layout. Any column rule in this tree meets the Unicode handling that `records/lenses/problems.md:1434` (PRB-102) records as open, and the position reporting of `records/lenses/problems.md:1448` (PRB-103).
  - **A canonical printer from the parse tree is a design decision with stated engineering reasons** (Go) and a measured review-load target (one third of reviews), with no measured comprehension effect.
  - **Refusals that name the misuse have a precedent in a parenthesized teaching language:** DrRacket refuses a non-identifier call head to catch `(1)` and `((+ 3 4))`, which bears on `records/lenses/problems.md:1462` (PRB-104).

  **8. WHAT THE SOURCES DO NOT SETTLE, AND WHAT CAME BACK EMPTY.**

  - **No controlled study compares s-expressions with infix, M-expression-style or indentation syntax for comprehension or writing.** Searched: the Stefik and Siebert article (prefix notation listed as untested), the formatting review (no Lisp study in the text), the 95-experiment mapping study (no Lisp-family snippet language), the Rhombus paper and repository (two case studies, a design-process document with no survey), SRFI 105, 110 and 119 (rationale and two-program experience), the Open Dylan history pages, the Pyret rationale, Wheeler's survey of readable-Lisp attempts, GitHub code search for parenthesized-prefix experiments, and web search for prefix-against-infix comprehension trials. Ebrahimi (IJHCS 1994) compared novice errors across Pascal, C, FORTRAN and LISP courses; its text was unreachable, so this row makes no claim about it.
  - **No study measures error rates caused or prevented by significant indentation**, and none measures braces against indentation directly.
  - **No study measures the comprehension or review effect of an enforced canonical format.**
  - **Expert evidence is thin.** Stefik's experts appear only as survey raters; the Atoms of Confusion and identifier studies drew mostly on students; Ajami and colleagues (220 professionals) is the one professional sample here, and its full text was out of reach.
  - **Two headline syntax effects did not hold across studies** (identifier style, indentation depth), and the formatting review attributes the instability partly to low power.
  - **Unreachable from this sandbox**, refused by the egress proxy or absent from GitHub: McCarthy's History of Lisp (`www-formal.stanford.edu`, `jmc.stanford.edu`); Steele and Gabriel, The Evolution of Lisp (`dreamsongs.com`); Miara and colleagues 1983 (`cs.umd.edu`); Binkley and colleagues, EMSE 2013, Ajami, Woodbridge and Feitelson, EMSE 2019, and Hanenberg, Morzeck and Gruhn, EMSE 2024 (`link.springer.com`); Morzeck and colleagues, ICSOFT 2023; Stefik and Hanenberg, Onward! 2014 and the 2017 methodology paper, and Stefik and colleagues, PLATEAU 2011 (`dl.acm.org`, `ecs.victoria.ac.nz`); Stefik's site and `quorumlanguage.com`; Oliveira and colleagues' ICSME readability review and Feitelson's pitfalls paper (`arxiv.org`, with no GitHub text copy found); Ebrahimi 1994 (`sciencedirect.com`); Bachrach and Playford, D-Expressions (`csail.mit.edu`); Marceau, Fisler and Krishnamurthi's DrRacket error-message study (the readscheme mirror path returned 404); Jones's ACCU 2006 paper (`knosof.co.uk`); the Racket survey and Discourse threads on Rhombus (`racket-lang.org`, `racket.discourse.group`); `rhombus-lang.org`. ### FD-70 the field gives the method in two published halves and both ship: write the grammar in a deterministic class, LL(1) or conflict-free LR(1), which is unambiguous by construction and is checked by a generator's conflict report because ambiguity in general is undecidable, then verify the parser against that grammar, which Menhir's Rocq back end does for CompCert C with a generated unambiguity theorem and CakeML does for its PEG parser with soundness, completeness, totality and a proved-unambiguous grammar; no source measures how small a usable grammar can be, the published counts for whole languages run from 25 to 166 productions and every small one moves its lexis, its precedence or a residual ambiguity into prose, and the canonical s-expression form is published as RFC 9804 (June 2025), two ABNF rules over length-prefixed strings, unique per expression, motivated by digital signatures

- state:    OPEN
- claim:    The question, dispatched for the surface-syntax rework strand: **does the published field give a method to specify a programming language's concrete syntax so that the grammar is provably unambiguous, small, and parsed by a parser that can itself be verified; is there published evidence on how small such a grammar can be for a usable language; and is there a published canonical form for s-expressions?** Answer: yes to the method and yes to the canonical form, and the size question has counts without a measurement. The method is a deterministic grammar class checked mechanically plus a parser proved or validated against the grammar, and two languages publish both halves for their source: CompCert C and CakeML. Each verified front end starts from tokens and leaves named parts outside the proof (in CompCert, termination, positions, error messages and the lexer feedback loop), and every surveyed small grammar resolves something in prose.
- measured: **1. AMBIGUITY IS UNDECIDABLE IN GENERAL, AND THE DETERMINISTIC CLASSES ARE UNAMBIGUOUS BY CONSTRUCTION.**

  The encyclopedia statement is `GMNPMAMBIG:70 "Deciding whether a context-free grammar is ambiguous is undecidable unless it has only one terminal symbol."` The same entry gives the class result at the level of languages, that every regular language is unambiguous `GMNPMAMBIG:86 "and so is any deterministic context-free language"`, and shows unambiguity belongs to the grammar as written, since `GMNPMAMBIG:80 "every context-free language can be generated by an ambiguous grammar"`. The entry cites Ginsburg (1966) and Kozen (1997).

  Bison's manual states the construction direction: `GMNBISON:9680 "Ambiguous grammars, since they have strings with more than one possible"` `GMNBISON:9681 "sequence of reductions cannot have deterministic parsers in this sense."` The converse fails, `GMNBISON:724 "apply the grammar rules to get the same inputs.  Even unambiguous"` `GMNBISON:725 "grammars can be @dfn{nondeterministic}, meaning that no fixed"` lookahead suffices. So a clean conflict report proves unambiguity and a conflict proves nothing by itself: `GMNBISON:10187 "One difficulty is that conflicts occur in the @emph{automaton}, and it can"` `GMNBISON:10188 "be tricky to relate them to issues in the @emph{grammar} itself."` Bison's counterexample generator, `GMNBISON:10194 "initially developed by Chinawat Isradisaikul and Andrew Myers"`, prints two derivations of one string when it finds a unifying example, `GMNBISON:10218 "This shows two different derivations for one single expression, which proves"` ambiguity.

  Wirth states the LL(1) conditions as checks a program can run. For alternatives, `GMNWIRTHCC:600 "The terms must not have any common start symbols."`, and for options and repetitions `GMNWIRTHCC:603 "[exp] or {exp}       The sets of start symbols of exp and of symbols"` that may follow must be disjoint. His exercise asks for a program that decides whether a syntax `GMNWIRTHCC:1255 "can be parsed top-down with a lookahead of a single symbol. If this is not so, the program displays the"` `GMNWIRTHCC:1256 "conflicting productions in a suitable way."` His stance is `GMNWIRTHCC:472 "languages; ambiguous programming languages, however, are simply useless."`, and the book will `GMNWIRTHCC:787 "restrict our attention to languages which can be parsed with a lookahead of a single symbol."`

  The generalized camp moves the question to parse time. A Bison GLR parser that meets two parses with no declared preference resolves nothing: `GMNBISON:9728 "the result.  Otherwise, it reports an ambiguity."` CoStar (section 3) proves the same per-input report.

  **2. PEGS REMOVE AMBIGUITY BY DEFINITION, AND THE LARGEST PEG USER DOCUMENTS WHAT ORDERED CHOICE HIDES.**

  Ford's abstract claims PEG `GMNPEGABS:332 "solves the ambiguity problem by not introducing ambiguity in the first place"`: `GMNPEGABS:332 "Where CFGs express nondeterministic choice between alternatives, PEGs instead use prioritized choice."` CPython adopted the claim when it replaced its LL(1) parser, `GMNPEP617:122 "Unlike LL(1) parsers, PEG-based parsers cannot be ambiguous: if a string parses,"` and `GMNPEP617:120 "order in which they are written. This makes the choice operator not commutative."` The PEP's reason for leaving LL(1) is readability: an LL(1) conflict `GMNPEP617:90 "The rule may be transformed to equivalent LL(1) rules, but then it may"` be harder for a human to read.

  CPython's own parser guide documents the cost. Ordered choice `GMNCPYPARSER:101 "how PEG parsers work) has deep consequences, other than removing ambiguity."` Two rules that denote one language in EBNF denote two in PEG, `GMNCPYPARSER:113 "In a regular EBNF grammar, both rules specify the language"` {aa, aaa}, and the guide warns `GMNCPYPARSER:126 "> The effects of ordered choice, such as the ones illustrated above, may be"` `GMNCPYPARSER:127 "> hidden by many levels of rules."` Its worked case is the dangling `else`: with the short alternative first, `GMNCPYPARSER:138 "In this example, the second alternative will never be tried because the first one will"` succeed. **This is the criticism the strand names, stated by the production user**: the PEG has one parse per string, and the grammar's choice of which parse is fixed by alternative order, invisible from the rule that is wrong. Tratt's essays, the usual citation for it, were unreachable.

  **3. VERIFIED AND VALIDATED PARSERS: WHAT EACH PROVES.**

  **Menhir's Rocq back end (Jourdan, Pottier and Leroy, ESOP 2012).** Each generated parser carries `GMNMENHIRMAIN:29 "(** Correction theorem. **)"`, `GMNMENHIRMAIN:42 "Theorem parse_complete"` and `GMNMENHIRMAIN:57 "(** Unambiguity theorem. **)"`, whose conclusion is `GMNMENHIRMAIN:62 "pt_sem tree1 = pt_sem tree2."`: two parse trees of one word yield one semantic value. The manual reads it as `GMNMENHIR:4268 "These results imply that the grammar is unambiguous: for every input, there is"` `GMNMENHIR:4269 "at most one valid interpretation."` The price is stated beside it. Completeness needs a conflict-free grammar, `GMNMENHIR:4175 "That is, the grammar must be LR(1). Conflict resolution via"` priority declarations is refused because `GMNMENHIR:4178 "The reason is that there is no simple formal specification"` `GMNMENHIR:4179 "of how conflict resolution should work."` `GMNMENHIR:4162 "Location information is not propagated."` Termination is outside the proof, `GMNMENHIR:4213 "crucial. For this reason, we did not formally establish the termination of the"` parser, which runs on fuel. The failure result's state and token are `GMNMENHIR:4242 "the validity of these two pieces of information is not certified by either the correctness"` or the completeness theorem.

  **CompCert C.** Release 2.3 (`GMNCCLOG:1181 "# Release 2.3, 2014-05-05"`): `GMNCCLOG:1187 "The parser is now formally verified against the ISO C99 grammar plus"` CompCert's extensions, and the proof shows it `GMNCCLOG:1189 "recognizes exactly the language specified by the grammar, and that"` `GMNCCLOG:1190 "the grammar has no ambiguities.  For more details, see the paper"`. The verified grammar receives identifiers already classified, `GMNCCPARSER:25 "%token<Cabs.string * Cabs.loc> VAR_NAME TYPEDEF_NAME OTHER_NAME"`. The classification is made by a pre-parser that records declarations as it goes, `GMNCCPRE:35 "let declare_typename (i,_,_) ="`, and the Menhir manual describes CompCert's pattern as `GMNMENHIR:4318 "a \textit{non-verified} separate parser"`, one that may also aid `GMNMENHIR:4319 "languages (such as C) that need a lexical feedback loop for correct parsing."` That pre-parser resolves conflicts by precedence and says so, `GMNCCPRE:19 "WARNING: The precedence declarations tend to silently solve"` conflicts, expecting `GMNCCPRE:23 "2 shift/reduce conflicts were silently solved."`, one of them `GMNCCPRE:79 "(* These precedence declarations solve the dangling else conflict. *)"`. The verified grammar, barred from precedence declarations, splits statements instead into `GMNCCPARSER:879 "selection_statement_dangerous:"` and `GMNCCPARSER:888 "selection_statement_safe:"`. It defines 92 nonterminals after `GMNCCPARSER:118`, a count this row made.

  **CakeML.** The parser is a PEG proved against a context-free grammar over tokens, `GMNCAKEREADME:4 "Here conforming means that if a sequence of tokens has"` a parse tree in the grammar, the function returns it `GMNCAKEREADME:6 "(*completeness*). Dually, if the function returns a parse tree, it should be"` correct (soundness), and the PEG is proved `GMNCAKEREADME:13 "well-formed, which means that execution will always terminate (*totality*). As"` a function it is `GMNCAKEREADME:15 "that execution is *deterministic*. (The necessary background theory of PEGs"`. The grammar itself is proved unambiguous: `GMNCAKECOMP:3601 "Theorem cmlG_unambiguous:"` concludes, for two valid trees with `GMNCAKECOMP:3605 "real_fringe pt2 = real_fringe pt1 ∧"`, that `GMNCAKECOMP:3607 "     pt1 = pt2"`. This is tree equality, stronger than Menhir's equality of semantic values. The grammar (`GMNCAKEGRAM:2 "Definition of CakeML's Context-Free Grammar."`) defines 75 nonterminals in `GMNCAKEGRAM:130 "val cmlG_def = mk_grammar_def ginfo"`, two more being commented out, a count this row made.

  **Vermillion (verified LL(1) generator, Lasser et al., ITP 2019).** The generator is proved sound and complete, `GMNVERM:44 "Theorem parseTableOf_complete :"` stating that it returns a table whenever a correct LL(1) table exists for the grammar. The parser has `GMNVERM:72 "Theorem parse_sound :"`, `GMNVERM:91 "Theorem parse_terminates_without_error :"` and `GMNVERM:111 "Theorem parse_complete :"`, whose conclusion `GMNVERM:119 "-> parse tbl s (w ++ r) = inr (v, r)."` fixes one semantic value per derivable prefix. Termination comes from well-founded recursion, `GMNVERM:67 "match parseSymbol tbl s ts NtSet.empty (triple_lt_wf _) with"`, so no fuel is needed.

  **CoStar (verified ALL(*), Lasser et al., PLDI 2021).** It parses any non-left-recursive grammar and reports ambiguity per input: `GMNCOSTAR:47 "Theorem parse_sound__ambiguous_derivation :"` states that a result `GMNCOSTAR:53 "-> parse g x ts = Ambig t"` comes with a second, distinct derivation; `GMNCOSTAR:99 "Theorem parse_complete__unique_derivation :"` returns `Accept` on a uniquely derivable input; `GMNCOSTAR:79 "Theorem parse_terminates_without_error :"` holds under the non-left-recursion hypothesis. It proves nothing about the grammar's ambiguity in advance.

  **4. HOW SMALL: THE PUBLISHED COUNTS, AND WHERE EACH SMALL GRAMMAR PUTS THE REST.** Every count is this row's, made on the pinned text.

  | grammar | productions | what lives outside the productions |
  |---|---|---|
  | Wirth's EBNF, CACM 1977 | 6 (`GMNWIRTH77` lines 40 to 48) | identifier and character, left undefined |
  | HOL4's verified s-expression PEG | 11 nonterminals (`GMNHOLSEXPPEG` lines 76 to 148) | nothing; it reads characters |
  | Lua 5.4 | 25 (`GMNLUA54` lines 9343 to 9448) | lexis and the precedence table; one ambiguity |
  | Oberon-0 (Wirth's book) | 27 (`GMNWIRTHCC` lines 1311 to 1348) | letter and digit |
  | Oberon-07 report | 61 (`GMNOBERON07` lines 758 to 835) | type-guard and call share one notation |
  | CakeML | 75 nonterminals (`GMNCAKEGRAM` lines 130 to 248) | lexis, which the grammar takes as tokens |
  | CompCert C, verified | 92 nonterminals (`GMNCCPARSER` after line 118) | typedef classification, by an unverified pre-parser |
  | R7RS Scheme | 137 (`GMNR7RSSYN` lines 27 to 477), of which 57 lexical and 9 for `datum` | three prose rules and a TeX note |
  | Go 1.28 | 166 (`GMNGOSPEC` ebnf blocks), of which 123 syntactic and 43 lexical | semicolon insertion and three prose rules |

  Wirth's notation is defined in itself, and its operators are `GMNWIRTH77:50 "Repetition is denoted by curly brackets, i.e. {a} stands for e | a"` repetitions, brackets for options and parentheses for grouping. The copy is a third party's transcription in a code comment.

  Lua's appendix says `GMNLUA54:9331 "Here is the complete syntax of Lua in extended BNF."`, then sends the reader elsewhere for `GMNLUA54:9335 "(For operator precedences, see @See{prec};"` and the terminals. The manual states `GMNLUA54:1254 "This possibility leads to an ambiguity in Lua's grammar."`, about a statement beginning with a parenthesis, and resolves it by the implementation, `GMNLUA54:1266 "The current parser always sees such constructions"` as a call.

  Wirth's check shows that Oberon-0 `GMNWIRTHCC:1510 "handled by the method of recursive descent using a lookahead of one symbol."` The Oberon-07 report is `GMNOBERON07:25 "This report is not intended as a programmer's tutorial. It is intentionally kept concise."` Its appendix lets a `factor` be a designator followed by optional actual parameters (line 790) and lets a selector be a parenthesised qualified identifier (line 792), the type guard `GMNOBERON07:277 "The typeguard v(T0) asserts that v is of type T0"`. Under those two productions `p(x)` has two derivations, a call and a guard, and a compiler tells them apart by looking `x` up. That reading is this row's; the report names no ambiguity.

  R7RS gives `GMNR7RSSYN:12 "This section provides a formal syntax for Scheme written in an extended"` BNF. `datum` is what `read` `GMNR7RSSYN:222 "successfully parses.  Note that any string that parses as an"` expression also parses as a datum. The lexical grammar overlaps itself: `+i`, `-i` and the infinities `GMNR7RSSYN:102 "below are exceptions to the"` peculiar-identifier rule and read as numbers. Quasiquote templates can be read two ways and the unquotation reading `GMNR7RSSYN:375 "un\-quo\-ta\-tion $D$} takes precedence."` The TeX source keeps an open note at the character syntax, `GMNR7RSSYN:142 "\todo{Explain what happens in the ambiguous case.}"`. The expression grammar holds only while keywords are bound as the report binds them, `GMNR7RSSYN:243 "the syntax keywords defined in this report have been properly imported"` `GMNR7RSSYN:244 "from their libraries, and that none of them have been redefined or shadowed."` So the s-expression layer is context-free and small, and the form layer above it depends on bindings.

  Go's notation separates the lexical layer by case, `GMNGOSPEC:57 "Lowercase production names are used to identify lexical (terminal) tokens."`, and adds a rule outside the grammar, `GMNGOSPEC:189 "When the input is broken into tokens, a semicolon is automatically inserted"`. Three ambiguities are resolved in prose: `GMNGOSPEC:2673 "A parsing ambiguity arises when the type parameter list for a generic type"`, `GMNGOSPEC:3218 "A parsing ambiguity arises when a composite literal using the"`, where `GMNGOSPEC:3223 "In this rare case, the opening brace of the literal is erroneously parsed"`, and conversions whose type must be parenthesised when `GMNGOSPEC:5417 "necessary to avoid ambiguity:"`. The FAQ claims the language `GMNGOFAQ:2104 "has been designed to be easy to analyze"` `GMNGOFAQ:2105 "and can be parsed without a symbol table.  This makes it much easier"` for tools.

  **No surveyed source measures the smallest grammar a usable language needs, or ties grammar size to defects.** The counts above are the evidence there is.

  **5. CANONICAL S-EXPRESSIONS: PUBLISHED, SMALL, AND MOTIVATED BY SIGNATURES.**

  Rivest's draft dates from `GMNSEXP97:7 "draft-rivest-sexp-00.txt"`, May 1997, with the goal `GMNSEXP97:80 "canonicalization: it should be easy to produce a unique"` form for digital signatures. Its BNF `GMNSEXP97:511 "For canonical and basic transport:"` defines `<sexpr>` (line 513) while its list rule repeats `GMNSEXP97:521 "<sexp>*"`, a symbol it never defines, and it carries the no-leading-zeros rule for lengths as a comment (lines 519, 533). That reading is this row's.

  The revival was published as `GMNRFC9804:6 "Request for Comments: 9804"`, `GMNRFC9804:12 "Simple Public Key Infrastructure (SPKI) S-Expressions"`, Informational, June 2025, Rivest and Eastlake. The canonical form: `GMNRFC9804:648 "It is uniquely defined for each S-expression.  It is not particularly"` readable and is meant to be easy `GMNRFC9804:650 "to parse, reasonably economical, and unique for any S-expression."`, writing every string `GMNRFC9804:654 "in verbatim mode, and represents each list with no blanks separating"` elements. The ABNF for it is two rules, `c-sexp` (`GMNRFC9804:777 "*c-sexp"`) and `c-string` (line 779), over `verbatim` and a `decimal` that now refuses leading zeros in the grammar itself, `GMNRFC9804:738 "decimal        =  %x30 / (%x31-39 *DIGIT)"`. The advanced transport form takes 23 rules (lines 714 to 773, this row's count). Outside verbatim strings the character set is limited to the `GMNRFC9804:264 "following characters in ASCII"` letters, digits, six whitespace characters, eight pseudo-alphabetic marks and eleven reserved punctuation marks (lines 266 to 302); the rest of printable ASCII is unavailable outside verbatim and quoted strings. The security rationale is the canonical form itself: `GMNRFC9804:915 "considerations to S-expressions.  A canonical form is required for"` `GMNRFC9804:916 "the consistent creation and verification of digital signatures.  This"`. A companion draft `GMNRFC9804:186 "S-expressions and formally demonstrates that the examples and ABNF in"` the RFC are correct; section 10 lists it among the unpinned. The format is `GMNRFC9804:167 "The S-expressions specified herein are in active use today between"` GnuPG and RNP.

  **Two other s-expression formats.** R7RS `datum` is 9 productions (section 4). edn says `GMNEDN:40 "Currently this specification is casual, as we gather feedback from implementors. A more rigorous"` `GMNEDN:41 "e.g. BNF will follow."`

  **A verified s-expression reader.** HOL4 ships one, used by CakeML for `GMNCAKEREADME:28 "Definitions of functions for conversion between an S-expression encoding of"` its abstract syntax. The grammar is a PEG over characters, `GMNHOLSEXPPEG:77 "sexpPEG : (char, sexpNT, sexp, string) peg ="`, proved well-formed, `GMNHOLSEXPPEG:316 "Theorem wfG_sexpPEG:"`, which in the PEG theory is the termination condition CakeML's README names totality. Its printer and reader are tied by `GMNHOLSEXPPARSE:1182 "Theorem parse_print:"`, `GMNHOLSEXPPARSE:1183 "valid_sexp s ⇒ print_sexp s = MAP FST sl ⇒ parse_sexp sl = SOME s"`: what the printer writes, the reader reads back to the same value. String contents are restricted to printable characters other than quote and backslash, `GMNHOLSEXPPEG:144 "tok (λc. isPrint c ∧ c ≠"`. It states no unambiguity theorem against a context-free grammar, and none is needed for the round trip.

  **A reader that executes code.** Clojure's `read` carries the warning `GMNCLJCORE:3803 "Note that read can execute code (controlled by *read-eval*),"`, and the flag's documentation says the full reader is `GMNCLJCORE:6752 "including syntax that can cause code to execute. It should never be"` `GMNCLJCORE:6753 "used with untrusted sources. See also: clojure.edn/read.***"`. The language ships a second reader, edn's, for data.

  **6. LOSSLESS TREES AND ROUND-TRIPPING, AND THE STATED REASON.**

  Roslyn: `GMNROSLYN:97 "syntax trees hold all the source information in full fidelity"`, and `GMNROSLYN:99 "A syntax tree obtained from the parser is completely round-trippable back to the text it was parsed from."`, so that `GMNROSLYN:99 "syntax trees can be used as a way to construct and edit source text"`. Malformed input keeps the property: `GMNROSLYN:171 "Even when the source text contains syntax errors, a full syntax tree that is round-trippable to the source is exposed."` The parser `GMNROSLYN:173 "it may insert a missing token into the syntax tree in the location that the token was expected"` and attaches what it skips as trivia, `GMNROSLYN:175 "the skipped tokens that were skipped are attached as a trivia node with the kind SkippedTokens"`. `GMNROSLYN:141 "Each node, token, or trivia knows its position within the source text"`.

  rust-analyzer (rowan) takes its terms from Roslyn, `GMNRASYNTAX:38 "Red-green terminology comes from Roslyn"`. Its goals: `GMNRASYNTAX:18 "Syntax trees are lossless, or full fidelity. All comments and whitespace get preserved."` and `GMNRASYNTAX:22 "Parsing is lossless (even if the input is invalid, the tree produced by the parser represents it exactly)."` `GMNRASYNTAX:73 "The original text can be recovered by concatenating the texts of all tokens in order."` `GMNRASYNTAX:78 "If an extra erroneous input is present, it is wrapped into a node with"` an error kind. `GMNRASYNTAX:261 "SyntaxNode knows its *absolute* text offset in the whole file"`. The parser is permissive by design and a later pass refuses: `GMNRASYNTAX:492 "For example, parser accepts visibility modifiers on trait methods"`, then flags them. `GMNRASYNTAX:528 "We use a boring hand-crafted recursive descent + pratt combination"`.

  swift-syntax: `GMNSWIFTPARSER:49 "so that a syntax tree can be rendered back into text that is byte-for-byte identical to the original source"`, and the parser `GMNSWIFTPARSER:42 "It has no side effects, and in particular produces no errors regardless of how ill-formed the input source text is."` Errors are missing and unexpected nodes in the tree, diagnosed by a separate pass.

  **Canonical formatting.** Go's `gofmt` `GMNGOFAQ:1019 "whose purpose is to enforce layout rules; it replaces the usual"` style guide. The stated reason across all four is tools: Roslyn's construction and editing of source, rust-analyzer's IDE (`GMNRASYNTAX:524 "In practice, incremental reparsing doesn't actually matter much for IDE use-cases"`), Swift's fixes, since missing tokens `GMNSWIFTPARSER:45 "can also be used by tools to provide fixes for the source code"`, and Go's `GMNGOFAQ:2106 "to build tools such as debuggers, dependency analyzers, automated"` documentation extractors.

  **7. ERROR POSITION AND MESSAGES AS A GRAMMAR PROPERTY.**

  grmtools states the LR guarantee: `GMNGRMERR:13 "parsing guarantees to report syntax errors at the first point that an error can"` `GMNGRMERR:14 "be definitively proven to have occurred (though note that this might not be the"` point the user meant. Bison qualifies it by table construction: canonical LR without default reductions is `GMNBISON:9412 "guaranteed to detect a syntax error as soon as possible without performing"` extra reductions, and with default reductions `GMNBISON:9475 "Thus, the parser sometimes fails to detect the syntax error until it reaches"` a later state. Menhir builds merged states with default reductions, and `GMNMENHIR:3551 "reductions}. These techniques \emph{defer} error detection by allowing"` extra reductions.

  Menhir's message approach is `GMNMENHIR:3522 "An apparently simple-minded approach to error reporting,"` proposed by Jeffery and further explored by `GMNMENHIR:3524 "Pottier~\cite{pottier-reachability-cc-2016}, consists in selecting a diagnostic"`, which picks a `GMNMENHIR:3525 "message (or a template for a diagnostic message) based purely on the current"` automaton state; the tool enumerates the error states and checks that a messages file is irredundant and complete (lines 3713 to 3736). CompCert ships one: `GMNCCMSG:18 "# This file contains a complete list of sentences that cause the pre_parser to"` detect an error, 243 entries by this row's count, each to `GMNCCMSG:69 "# Show a list of the permitted continuations: \"at this point, one of the"` following is expected. It has shipped such explanations since 2.6, `GMNCCLOG:972 "- Production of detailed explanations for syntax errors during parsing."`

  A PEG has no such position. CPython: the `GMNCPYPARSER:82 "PEG parser doesn't have a concept of"` where the error is, so pegen reports `GMNCPYPARSER:694 "the location of *generic* syntax errors is reported to be the furthest token that"` was tried, and the heuristic works because `GMNCPYPARSER:699 "As the Python grammar was primordially written as an"` LL(1) grammar.

  Wirth ties error handling to language design: `GMNWIRTHCC:1565 "problem has so far eluded formal treatment."`, and `GMNWIRTHCC:1579 "much as the technique of error treatment. Without doubt, a simple language structure significantly"` simplifies diagnostics, while `GMNWIRTHCC:1580 "a complicated syntax complicates error handling"`. Constructs that begin with reserved symbols `GMNWIRTHCC:1595 "are therefore never skipped. They serve as synchronization points in the text, where parsing can be"` resumed.

  **8. LANGUAGES THAT PUBLISH BOTH A MACHINE-CHECKED UNAMBIGUOUS GRAMMAR AND A VERIFIED PARSER.** Two were found. **CompCert C** (section 3), whose generated `Parser.unambiguous` theorem covers the grammar the verified parser reads, after an unverified pre-parser; the Rocq model takes the lexer as given, `GMNMENHIR:4199 "We model the lexer as an object of type"` a token stream. **CakeML** (section 3), whose `cmlG_unambiguous` covers its token-level grammar and whose PEG parser is proved sound, complete and total against it. Vermillion and CoStar are verified tools for any grammar of their class, and their published uses are benchmarks. Among s-expression formats, HOL4's reader (section 5) is verified for totality and print-then-read identity, and RFC 9804's correctness argument is a formal model of its ABNF and examples.

  **9. WHAT THIS GIVES A SURFACE-SYNTAX REWORK.** This section reads the pins against the question and rules nothing.

  - **Pick a deterministic class and let a tool check it.** Unambiguity is undecidable for an arbitrary grammar (`GMNPMAMBIG:70`) and follows from a clean LL(1) or LR(1) check (`GMNBISON:9680`, `GMNWIRTHCC:600`). An s-expression reader is the case Wirth's book targets, one symbol of lookahead (`GMNWIRTHCC:787`).
  - **Encode every disambiguation in the productions.** The verified tools refuse precedence declarations (`GMNMENHIR:4178`), CompCert's unverified half warns that they hide conflicts (`GMNCCPRE:19`), and CPython warns that ordered choice hides them (`GMNCPYPARSER:126`). CompCert's safe and dangerous statements show the grammar-only form (`GMNCCPARSER:879`).
  - **Resolve nothing in prose.** Go, Lua, R7RS and Oberon-07 each carry a rule outside the grammar (section 4), and each is a place where two readers may disagree.
  - **Keep the reader free of binding-dependent parsing.** CompCert's unverified part is the lexical feedback loop (`GMNMENHIR:4319`), Go claims parsing without a symbol table (`GMNGOFAQ:2105`), and R7RS's form grammar assumes unshadowed keywords (`GMNR7RSSYN:244`). A datum grammar of R7RS's size (9 productions) is context-free, and form recognition can sit over data with its own named refusals.
  - **Publish one canonical printed form and a formatter that produces it.** RFC 9804's form is unique per expression (`GMNRFC9804:648`) and puts the leading-zero rule into the grammar (`GMNRFC9804:738`). Go's formatter replaces the style guide (`GMNGOFAQ:1019`). RFC 9804 limits non-verbatim text to ASCII (`GMNRFC9804:264`); R7RS admits U+200C and U+200D in identifiers (`GMNR7RSSYN:51 "or Co, or is U+200C or U+200D (the zero-width non-joiner and joiner,"`), the class PRB-102 records.
  - **Prove the printer and reader inverse.** HOL4's `parse_print` (`GMNHOLSEXPPARSE:1182`) is the published theorem shape for an s-expression reader, and its PEG's well-formedness (`GMNHOLSEXPPEG:316`) gives termination.
  - **Keep the tree lossless with exact source positions.** Roslyn, rust-analyzer and swift-syntax keep every byte and an offset per node (`GMNROSLYN:141`, `GMNRASYNTAX:261`, `GMNSWIFTPARSER:49`), which bears on PRB-103's blob coordinates.
  - **Attach a message to each error state and enumerate them.** Menhir's per-state messages with a completeness check (`GMNMENHIR:3525`) and CompCert's list of expected continuations (`GMNCCMSG:69`) are the published form of a refusal that names what was expected, the gap PRB-104 records.
  - **Make the reader execute nothing.** Clojure's warning (`GMNCLJCORE:6752`) is the hazard, and its separate data reader is the remedy it ships.
  - **Expect a verified reader to leave termination, positions and messages outside the proof** unless they are built in, as Menhir's manual lists (`GMNMENHIR:4162`, `GMNMENHIR:4213`, `GMNMENHIR:4242`). CakeML proves totality (`GMNCAKEREADME:13`) and Vermillion proves error-free termination (`GMNVERM:91`).

  **10. WHAT THE SOURCES DO NOT SETTLE, AND WHAT CAME BACK EMPTY.**

  - **No source measures grammar size against usability or defects.** Section 4 is counts.
  - **No source ties a syntax-caused vulnerability class to grammar ambiguity by measurement.** Clojure's reader warning and RFC 9804's signature rationale are the two security statements found.
  - **Menhir's unambiguity is equality of semantic values** (`GMNMENHIRMAIN:62`), which equals tree uniqueness only when the actions build the tree. CakeML's is tree equality.
  - **Unreachable from this sandbox**, refused by the egress proxy for `curl` and WebFetch alike: Wirth, Good Ideas, Through the Looking Glass (`inf.ethz.ch`, `pascal.hansotten.com`, `norayr.am`, and a `gist.github.com` extract that WebFetch summarized as Pascal-compiler history, read as a pointer only); the full CACM 1977 text of Wirth's EBNF note; Ford's POPL 2004 paper (`bford.info`), present here only as its abstract; Jourdan, Pottier and Leroy, ESOP 2012, and Pottier, CC 2016 (`gallium.inria.fr`, `link.springer.com`); Lasser et al., ITP 2019 and PLDI 2021 (`tupl.cs.tufts.edu`, `arxiv.org`); Tratt's two parsing essays (`tratt.net`); Lippert's red-green post; the IETF datatracker and `rfc-editor.org`, whose RFC 9804 came instead from a GitHub mirror; Petit-Huguenin's formal-model draft, known only by its metadata; Knuth 1965, Redziejowski on PEG language hiding, Maidl et al. on PEG error reporting, and Blaudeau and Shankar's verified packrat interpreter, none found as text on GitHub. The GitHub API answered 403 for repository listings, so paths were found through code search and probing.
  - **The venues named for Vermillion (ITP 2019) and CoStar (PLDI 2021) come from search results and the paper titles, unpinned.** The pinned READMEs and theorem files name neither venue.
  - **Two pins are transcriptions and six are third-party copies.** `GMNWIRTHCC` is `pdftotext -layout` of the PDF served from `tpn/pdfs` (one production line, `IdentList`, starts with a form feed). `GMNOBERON07` is a text conversion of Wirth's report PDF stored in the `Spirit-of-Oberon/Oberon-Language-revisions` repository by its maintainers; Wirth's own PDF was unreachable. Third-party copies: `GMNWIRTH77` (Wirth's notation inside a C++ comment), `GMNPEGABS` (Ford's abstract inside a JSON listing of POPL 2004), `GMNPMAMBIG` (a PlanetMath entry), `GMNMENHIR` (Menhir 20260209's manual vendored in an opam switch in a third-party repository), `GMNRFC9804` (a mirror, identical across four fetches from two mirrors) and `GMNSEXP97` (a copy in a Lisp library).
